docs.title: django-service-specs
docs.text:
A service contract for Django. An operation is declared once - what it takes, who may run it, how its arguments are validated, what it returns - and any transport dispatches it: an HTTP view, an MCP tool, an agent tool, a management command, a background task.

Each transport would otherwise restate the operation in its own terms: a serializer for the view, a JSON Schema for the tool, argparse options for the command, and a permission check in whichever of them remembered one. Declared once, the operation carries all of that itself, and a transport reads the declaration rather than repeating it.

docs.title: Two positions, three layers
docs.text:
Everything else follows from two decisions, and both read as limitations.

Django is the base, and the only one. There is no pure-Python protocol layer beneath the kernel and no Django-free subpackage inside it. A principal is a Django user, a target is a model row, a transaction is Django's. Django is the only framework the package depends on, and typing_extensions its only other dependency.

DRF is an adapter, never a dependency. The package exists so a Django project with business logic and no API framework can hand its operations to an agent, a command or a queue. Nothing in django_service_specs imports rest_framework, and the test suite runs without it installed.

On that base the package is in three layers. Every subpackage is classified into one, and a test fails if core imports anything classified outside it:

  • Core is what every transport needs to run a spec: the declaration, the registry and dispatch, with authorization always on, because dispatch always authorizes. It is what dispatch and the registry import, and nothing more.
  • Opt-in modules are subpackages core never imports: model writes, relation writes and the schema projection. Opt-in is a classification, not a switch. No setting turns a module on or off; a spec that uses none of them dispatches without them. The validator adapters for dataclasses, forms and pydantic sit outside core the same way, as libraries a project writes against.
  • A transport only wires a protocol onto specs and dispatch, and belongs in a distribution of its own. The HTTP views are django-spec-html and the management command is django-spec-cli.

Where the transports stand. djangorestframework-services depends on this package, never the reverse: its ServiceSpec is the DRF adapter over this kernel. The family's MCP server and Pydantic AI toolset reach specs through it today, so both still require DRF. What they read off a spec besides dispatch is here - see affordances and paging and projection - and transport distributions that read kernel specs with no DRF at all are planned. Until then a project without DRF dispatches its specs from its own views, commands, tasks and agent tools.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install django-service-specs

The package has no models and needs no entry in INSTALLED_APPS. A principal is a user of django.contrib.auth, and a generic-relation write needs django.contrib.contenttypes. Listing "django_service_specs" there is optional and adds nothing: the system check reporting every spec a management command serves that authorizes nothing is django-spec-cli's.

Minimum Python 3.10 Django 4.2

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
A write that renames a note. Note is a model with a title and an owner who is a user; the examples on these pages import their models from the package's own test suite, which is where they run.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any

from django_service_specs import (
    DataclassPresenter,
    DataclassValidator,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    PermissionCheck,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    ServiceSpec,
    dispatch,
    present,
)
from tests.dispatch_app.models import Note  # a title, and an owner who is a user


@dataclass
class Rename:  # what the operation takes
    title: str


@dataclass
class NoteOut:  # what it returns
    id: int
    title: str


class IsOwner(PermissionCheck):
    message = "Only the note's owner may rename it."

    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any) -> bool:
        return principal.is_authenticated

    def has_object_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any, target: Any) -> bool:
        return target.owner_id == principal.pk


def rename_note(*, instance: Note, title: str) -> Note:
    instance.title = title
    instance.save(update_fields=["title"])
    return instance


rename_note_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=rename_note,
    permissions=[IsOwner()],
    validator=DataclassValidator(Rename),
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=lambda *, pk: Note.objects.filter(pk=pk),  # the row, or none
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)),
    ),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteOut),
)


def rename(user: Any, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> Any:
    result = dispatch(rename_note_spec, principal=user, arguments=arguments)
    if result.kind == "not_found":
        return None  # a transport answers this in its own terms: a 404, an exit code
    return present(rename_note_spec, result)

What each part is:

  • Rename, wrapped in DataclassValidator, declares what the operation takes. A transport reads the declaration as Parameters to describe itself - a JSON Schema, argv options - and dispatch validates the arguments against it.
  • The instance selector finds the row the service acts on, from the pk argument its reads declare. A missing row is reported as not-found and the service never runs.
  • IsOwner is a PermissionCheck: has_permission runs before any row is looked up, has_object_permission on the row once it is.
  • rename_note is the service. It is called with the keywords it declares and nothing else: the resolved row as instance, and each validated value by name.
  • NoteOut, wrapped in DataclassPresenter, declares what comes back and renders it, reading each field off the row by attribute.

rename(owner, {"pk": 1, "title": "Final"}) returns {"id": 1, "title": "Final"}. For another user it raises NotPermitted, and for a note that does not exist it returns None, because dispatch reports a missing row as kind="not_found" rather than raising: an HTTP view answers it with a 404, a command with an exit code, a tool with an error result.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Declaring an operation: the two spec types, Parameters, the Validator contract and its dataclass adapter, Output and the Presenter.
  • Dispatching: the seven steps, results, grants, a target resolved ahead of the call, the async entry point, and pool seeds.
  • Arguments and refusals: the shape check, the error tree, flat transports, and the two error families.
  • Affordances: when an operation is possible right now, the refusal's stable code, offering only what a call could pass, and asking for one more value.
  • Relation writes: writing a row and its related rows in one operation.
  • The registry: one named set of operations for several transports.
  • The forms adapter: a Django form class, ModelForm included, as the Validator.
  • The pydantic adapter: a pydantic model as the Validator and the Presenter, with the pydantic extra.
  • JSON Schema: the input and output schema a transport describes an operation with.
  • Paging and projection: a list served a page at a time, and each row shaped for an agent reading it.
  • API reference: every public name.

docs.title: Affordances
docs.text:
Some operations are impossible right now as a fact about the world rather than about the caller: an archived note cannot be renamed, refunds are closed while the books are. An affordance says so on the operation, once, so every transport reads the same rule. A call is refused with a stable code beside the sentence, and a transport listing operations before anyone calls them can leave out one that no call could pass.

# An ambient fact a condition may read, registered like any other pool seed.
seeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS.extend(
    read_only=lambda: getattr(settings, "NOTES_READ_ONLY", False),
)

rename_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=rename_note,
    permissions=[IsOwner()],
    validator=DataclassValidator(Rename),
    instance_selector_spec=rename_note_spec.instance_selector_spec,
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteOut),
    affordances=[
        Affordance(  # a condition on nothing in particular: a callable over the seeds
            code="notes_read_only",
            reason="Notes are read-only during maintenance.",
            when=lambda *, read_only: not read_only,
        ),
        Affordance(  # a condition on the row: an ORM expression, answered in SQL
            code="note_archived",
            reason="An archived note cannot be renamed. Restore it first.",
            when=Q(archived=False),
        ),
    ],
    idempotent=True,  # renaming twice to one title leaves what renaming once did
)

ServiceSpec's affordances takes a sequence of conditions, each an Affordance with three fields:

  • code names the rule, never the state that tripped it, and does not change when the sentence is reworded. It is what a transport or a client branches on.
  • reason is the sentence people and models both read, and the message of the refusal. Say what is not possible and, where it helps, what would make it possible.
  • when is true when the operation is available.

Not a fact about the caller: that is permissions, which is always checked first, so a principal who may not see a row is never told what state it is in.

docs.title: Two kinds of condition
docs.text:
when's type decides which kind it is. It is derived, never declared, so it cannot drift from what it describes:

  • An ORM boolean expression - a Q, an Exists, a lookup - is a condition on the row. It reads exactly as Note.objects.filter(when) does, relations included, and is answered in SQL: every condition on the row in one query, however many are declared. A NULL is not true.
  • A callable is a condition on nothing in particular. It is called with the pool seeds it names - user, progress and any registered pool seed, like read_only above - and never with the call's target, its validated values or a client's argument: the caller does not get to decide whether the operation is available. Its result is read for truth, so a callable that returns nothing means unavailable. It is sync-only and never awaited: an answer still to be awaited is refused with ImproperlyConfigured rather than read as met, since a coroutine is truthy.

A Python callable over the row is refused. A rule that has to run once per row turns every list reporting availability into a query per row, and prefetching does not fix it. A rule the ORM cannot express is not an affordance: it stays in the service, which raises a ServiceConflict and advertises nothing.

docs.title: Refused where it is written
docs.text:
Every mistake below raises ImproperlyConfigured when the spec is built, so it fails at import rather than on the first call through a transport that never asked:

  • a code or reason that is not a non-empty string;
  • an ORM expression that is not boolean, such as F("title");
  • a callable naming data, instance, collection, result or queryset, the names dispatch seeds per call;
  • a when that is neither an expression nor a callable, or is an async callable - an async def, an object whose __call__ is one, or an async generator function;
  • affordances that is not a sequence - a single Affordance, a set whose order would decide which refusal a caller sees, a generator the first call would exhaust;
  • an entry that is not an Affordance, or a code declared twice;
  • a condition on the row on an operation with a collection_selector_spec, which has no single row to answer it against.

docs.title: Offering an operation
docs.text:
A transport that lists operations before anyone calls them - an MCP server building its tool list, an agent assembling its next toolset - asks unmet_operation_affordance for the first callable condition not met now, or None.

OPERATIONS = {"list_notes": list_notes_spec, "rename_note": rename_spec}


def tools_for(user: Any) -> dict[str, str | None]:
    """Each operation a transport could offer, with the code of what withholds it."""
    pool = base_pool(user=user, seeds=seeds)  # the seeds a call would be handed
    tools: dict[str, str | None] = {}
    for name, spec in OPERATIONS.items():
        unmet = unmet_operation_affordance(spec, pool, reserved=seeds.reserved)
        tools[name] = None if unmet is None else unmet.code
    return tools

Conditions on the row are skipped without a query, because at list time there is no row; they go on being answered at the call. A SelectorSpec answers None. operation_affordances returns the conditions that would be asked, so a transport can skip building a pool when there are none.

Build the pool the way the call's would be: base_pool with the same seeds=, and reserved=seeds.reserved beside it, or a condition reading a registered seed is asked without it. A condition that raises propagates: one that cannot be answered is not a no.

The answer is advisory. An operation listed a moment before a condition flips is refused when it is called, with the code this would answer if asked again then. A condition driven by a clock has no event, so nothing announces the moment it flips.

On an event loop, await aunmet_operation_affordance instead. It gives the same answer, with every condition asked in one sync_to_async hop, since a condition may query; a spec with nothing to ask at list time costs no hop at all, and most declare nothing.

docs.title: Enforcing at the call
docs.text:
dispatch and adispatch answer a service spec's affordances themselves, after object-level authorization and the Validator and before the run's transaction opens. The first one not met refuses the call with ActionUnavailable, carrying its reason as the message and its code, and the service never runs. A callable condition sees every registered seed, and whatever a transport seeds per call, such as progress. A selector spec's affordances refuse nothing: they are answers about each row.

def rename(user: Any, pk: int, title: str) -> Note:
    # dispatch answers the affordances itself, after the object-level check and
    # the Validator: an archived note is refused before the service runs.
    result = dispatch(
        rename_spec, principal=user, arguments={"pk": pk, "title": title}, pool_seeds=seeds
    )
    return result.value

enforce_affordances is that step, exported for a transport that runs a service itself. It calls it after authorization and validation and before the service, with the pool seeds' reserved set, or a condition the direct path refuses is skipped on that one, and with the call's call_context=, so a condition naming it is handed the dict the call's other stages share (the parameter, else one the pool carries, else a fresh one; two different dicts are refused):

def rename_step(user: Any, note: Note, title: str) -> Note:
    """One step of a chain that resolved its row itself and runs the service in hand."""
    grant = authorize(rename_spec, user)
    authorize_target(rename_spec, user, note, grant=grant)
    data = bind_arguments(rename_spec, {"pk": note.pk, "title": title}, principal=user, target=note)
    pool = base_pool(user=user, seeds=seeds)
    pool.update({**data, "data": data, "instance": note})  # the pool the service receives
    enforce_affordances(rename_spec, pool, instance=note, reserved=seeds.reserved)
    return rename_spec.service(**resolve_callable_kwargs(rename_spec.service, pool))

A transport running a service from an event loop awaits aenforce_affordances, which refuses and lets through as enforce_affordances does, answering every condition in one sync_to_async hop, and none for a spec declaring none.

Declaration order decides which refusal a caller sees, and nothing after the first unmet condition runs. A condition on the row is read from the table, not from the instance in hand. Two other answers come from the row: one that vanished since it was resolved is ServiceNotFound, and a condition on the row reached with no model instance to answer it for is ImproperlyConfigured.

ActionUnavailable is a ServiceConflict, so a transport that has never heard of it still answers a conflict. One that wants the code matches it before its generic conflict and service-error handlers.

A transport answering over HTTP puts the code beside the detail a client already reads, as django-spec-html's error_response does at 409:

{"detail": "An archived note cannot be renamed. Restore it first.", "code": "note_archived"}

docs.title: Asking for one more value
docs.text:
A service that gets far enough to discover it needs something else - usually because of what it found - raises AdditionalInputRequired with a message and a schema. It is not a validation error, because what was sent is not wrong, and it is a ServiceError, so a transport that has never heard of it still reports why the operation did not complete.

@dataclass
class Purge:
    confirmed: bool = False  # declared, so the second call may send it


def purge_archived(*, user: Any, confirmed: bool) -> int:
    doomed = Note.objects.filter(owner=user, archived=True)
    count = doomed.count()
    if count > 1 and not confirmed:
        raise AdditionalInputRequired(
            f"{count} archived notes will be deleted. Confirm to proceed.",
            schema={"confirmed": {"type": "boolean"}},
        )
    doomed.delete()
    return count


purge_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=purge_archived,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=DataclassValidator(Purge),
)


def purge(user: Any, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> int:
    return dispatch(purge_spec, principal=user, arguments=arguments).value

schema describes what is missing, keyed by the argument the service expects it back under. The answer comes back as an ordinary argument on the next call, so the operation declares it like any other, and there is no session to resume. A transport answering over HTTP puts the schema beside the detail when there is one, as django-spec-html's error_response does at 422:

{"detail": "2 archived notes will be deleted. Confirm to proceed.", "schema": {"confirmed": {"type": "boolean"}}}

A schema one transport cannot render is the raiser's error, not the caller's, so a service asks the same question on every route or on none. check_requested_input is that rule, for a transport to call before it renders the question. It reads the spec's top-level parameters and the schema, runs no query, and raises ImproperlyConfigured naming the key for a key no top-level parameter declares, for a fragment that is not a schema object, for a shape some transport cannot render, and for a type the declared parameter does not take. A declared key the server fills - one a provider is annotated to fill, or a seed the call's pool_seeds registers - is refused too, because dispatch drops the caller's value for it and the answer would never arrive. The narrowest renderer is an MCP elicitation form: a string, number, integer or boolean, or an array whose items list enum values. On a many spec the top level is the list and the spec's reads, so a confirmation asked once for the whole call is a reads parameter.

def check_the_question() -> None:
    # What a transport calls before it renders the question: `confirmed` is a
    # declared boolean, so a form can ask it. A key the spec does not declare
    # would raise ImproperlyConfigured naming it.
    check_requested_input(purge_spec, {"confirmed": {"type": "boolean"}})

docs.title: Declaring idempotency
docs.text: ServiceSpec(idempotent=True) states that repeating the call with the same arguments leaves the state making it once did. Nothing in this package reads it, because idempotency is a property of the service the author writes, not something a dispatcher can arrange; it is stated once so that a retry policy, a queue's redelivery handling and an agent tool annotation all read the same answer. None, the default, means undeclared, so a transport can tell "nothing was said" from a declared False. atomic answers a different question: a single call is all-or-nothing, not that a second one is a no-op.

docs.title: Answers for each row of a list
docs.text:
A SelectorSpec declares which operations' affordances each of its rows is answered for, keyed by a name the caller chooses:

# The list, declaring which operations' answers its rows are asked for.
list_notes_with_answers_spec = replace(list_notes_spec, affordances={"rename": rename_spec})

The values are the ServiceSpecs themselves rather than registry names, so a read takes no registry dependency and the declaration is the one the operation enforces. Each answer is named affordance__<name>__<code> - here affordance__rename__notes_read_only and affordance__rename__note_archived. A name colliding with a key of the selector's annotations, or two entries generating one name, is refused when the spec is built, because a generated answer silently replacing a project's own annotation is the worst way for this to fail.

Dispatch answers them wherever the selector runs: a selector spec's own, or a service spec's output selector. On a queryset, every answer joins the spec's annotations in the one .annotate() call shaping makes, before extend_queryset and before a transport pages the rows, so the list still costs one query and a page's rows carry what the whole list would have. A condition on the row is the same correlated EXISTS the call is refused by, so the list and the call agree about every row; a callable condition is answered once per call, against the seeds alone, as it is at the call. Rows a selector returns directly are answered too: instances by one query per model class, mappings with their callable answers only, because a mapping has no row to find.

present then adds an affordances object to every row it presents, and so does every response the HTTP views serve and every payload present_for_audience hands an agent, reason included:

def list_notes(user: Any) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    # dispatch answers every row's affordances as it runs the selector, in the
    # one query the list costs; present adds them to each row it presents.
    result = dispatch(list_notes_with_answers_spec, principal=user, arguments={}, pool_seeds=seeds)
    return present(list_notes_with_answers_spec, result)

[
  {"id": 1, "title": "Draft", "affordances": {"rename": {"available": true}}},
  {
    "id": 2,
    "title": "Old",
    "affordances": {
      "rename": {
        "available": false,
        "code": "note_archived",
        "reason": "An archived note cannot be renamed. Restore it first."
      }
    }
  }
]

Each name answers with the first condition its row does not meet, in declaration order, as the call would refuse. A row deleted between the selector returning it and its answers being asked is {"available": false} with no code and no reason, because no condition's sentence is true of a row that no longer exists. A selector spec's affordances refuse nothing: the archived note is still listed, and says why it cannot be renamed.

spec_output_schema describes the object on each item, with or without a projection, and with each name's codes enumerated so a client can switch on them:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "rename": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "available": {"type": "boolean"},
        "code": {"type": "string", "enum": ["notes_read_only", "note_archived"]},
        "reason": {"type": "string"}
      },
      "required": ["available"]
    }
  },
  "required": ["rename"]
}

Presenting refuses what would lose or garble the answers: a spec declaring affordances with no presenter, a presented row that is not an object or already has an affordances key, and a row that did not come through the selector declaring them. Dispatch refuses a condition on the row beside mapping rows, and a row that is neither a model instance nor a mapping.

A target lookup - a service spec's instance_selector_spec or collection_selector_spec - that declares affordances has its rows answered too, as djangorestframework-services' dispatch answers them, and nothing presents them: a service spec presents only its output selector's answers. The declaration costs a subquery, or a query of its own when the lookup returns a bare row, and buys nothing. Declare the answers on the read that lists the rows, or on the output selector.

shape_queryset answers none: a transport that shapes a selector's rows itself, rather than through dispatch, hands present rows with no answers on them, and is refused.

docs.title: Arguments and refusals
docs.text: Parameters are declared; arguments are supplied. This page is about the arguments: what is checked before an operation runs, the shape a refusal takes, how a flat transport's strings become typed values, and the two families of error a transport answers.

docs.title: The shape check
docs.text:
check_arguments is step one of every dispatch, and of bind_arguments. It checks what a caller can get wrong that the declaration can see - presence, JSON type, format, choices and nullability - at every level of nesting, with no query. It returns a cleaned copy and never modifies what it was given.

It is no stricter than the libraries behind it. A decimal accepts a JSON number as well as a string, because every decimal validator does, and a check stricter than the worker would refuse calls that would have run. A required parameter with a declared default is not refused when absent, because the Validator will supply the default. A JSON true is neither an integer nor a number, although Python makes bool an int: sent for a count, it is a caller's mistake, not the number one. An integral float is an integer: JSON Schema counts 5.0 as one, so the {"type": "integer"} the kernel advertises admits it, and the check hands the Validator 5 wherever the declaration reaches, so the Validator's own type check and bounds read the int. 5.5 is still refused, and a number keeps its float. DRF's IntegerField, like Django's form field, reads str(value), so given 1e16 it reads "1e+16" and refuses it; the check follows JSON Schema and hands on 10000000000000000.

A string spelling a number is that number where an integer or a number is declared, wherever the declaration reaches, and the number is handed on: "3", "3.0" and " 3 " are 3, and a number's "1e3" is 1000.0. Django's forms and pydantic's lax mode both read these strings so, and the reading is the one coerce_flat makes, which the check shares. Where the two differ it is Django's: an integer's "5." and "5 .0" are 5, which pydantic's int refuses. A string that spells no such number is refused as the type it is not, and true is still neither. The number goes on rather than the string because a Validator stricter than those two, the dataclass adapter's, refuses "3" for an int.

A number's string is read as a JSON decoder reads its literal: digits alone are the exact integer they spell, and a point or an exponent makes a float. So "9007199254740993" goes on as that integer, as the JSON literal does, where a float would round it to its neighbour, and "3" goes on as the 3 a JSON body's 3 is. Digits alone that Python's int refuses, past the 4300 it reads from Python 3.10.7 on, spell no number either, even where zeros in front leave a float able to read them. A fraction finer than a float holds is rounded, as the JSON literal is; a value that must be exact is declared a decimal, and so is each element of an array that must be: items="string" with format="decimal", as a django-filter CSV number filter declares, keeps every digit of each element and still splits ?pks=1,2.

Only an ASCII string spells an integer or a number, and this is one of three places the check is stricter than the libraries behind it, the others being a declared minimum or maximum and the length of a list. Python's int and float, and so Django's number fields, read Arabic-Indic and fullwidth digits and strip any Unicode space; no JSON number is spelled so, and pydantic refuses them. "\u0665", the JSON spelling of an Arabic-Indic five, is refused as the type it is not, by the check and by coerce_flat alike. A decimal string is not read this way, and on purpose: it is checked as Python's Decimal reads it, which takes those digits too, because every decimal field behind the check reads it so - Django's DecimalField, DRF's and pydantic's Decimal each hand the string to Decimal - and the string is handed on unchanged. "\u0665" sent for a decimal is 5 to all of them, as "5" is.

A file is a Django File, an upload included, and nothing else is one: no JSON value can be, so a JSON caller's string for one is refused at its name.

An any declares no type, so every value is one and is handed on exactly as it arrived: a "3" stays the string, never read as the number it spells. null is still refused unless the parameter is nullable, and NaN and the infinities are still no JSON value. Nothing is checked against a type, so a value of no JSON type is handed on too: a Python caller's, or a multipart upload sent under the parameter's name.

NaN and the infinities are refused, and that is a type rule rather than a stricter check: JSON has no spelling for either, so they are outside the number type, and only a decoder reading an overflowing literal such as 1e400, or a Python caller, can produce one. Two validators would take one all the same - pydantic's float and the dataclass adapter's - where Django's number fields refuse both. A number, a decimal or an element of an array with no items is refused with "Enter a number."; any other type refuses one as the wrong type. Like every rule here, it holds wherever the declaration reaches: inside a free-form object, or an object or array element that nothing declares, the contents are the Validator's.

A Parameter's json_schema_extra is never read here. The keywords it carries, such as a pattern, a string's maxLength or uniqueItems, are advertised in the schema and checked by nothing before the Validator, so what one states holds only where the spec's Validator enforces it.

docs.title: How long a list may be
docs.text:
An array's length is read before any of its elements, so a list longer than it takes is refused whole, at its name, and costs no per-element work. A parameter's min_length and max_length bound it inclusively. One that declares no max_length is still bounded, by the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting: 1000 unless the project sets another count, the line Django's DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_NUMBER_FIELDS draws for a form body, or None, which bounds no array. A declared max_length outranks the setting either way, wider or narrower. The setting is read at the call, so override_settings reaches a spec built at import, and so checking an array with no max_length, by the shape check or coerce_flat, needs Django's settings configured.

IDS = Parameters.of(Parameter("ids", "array", items="integer"))  # no max_length declared
PAGE = Parameters.of(Parameter("ids", "array", items="integer", min_length=1, max_length=50))

# check_arguments(IDS, {"ids": list(range(1001))}) refuses, at the list:
TOO_LONG = {"ids": ["Ensure this field has no more than 1000 elements."]}
# check_arguments(PAGE, {"ids": []}) refuses too:
TOO_SHORT = {"ids": ["Ensure this field has at least 1 elements."]}


def unbounded(arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    with override_settings(SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH=None):  # bounds no array
        return check_arguments(IDS, arguments)

Like the ASCII rule and a declared minimum or maximum, this is a place the check can be stricter than the library behind it, on purpose: a list is a cost its caller controls the size of. Each row of a many call is a Validator run inside one transaction, and each value of a django-filter in lookup is one query variable, past whose limit the database refuses the query and the caller gets a 500 rather than a refusal. The default reaches every array the declaration reaches - a row's own array included, a CSV filter's, a many call's list of rows - and a project whose Validator takes longer lists raises the setting or declares the max_length. A min_length past the setting on a parameter with no max_length of its own is a declaration no call could meet, refused as ImproperlyConfigured at the call and when its schema is built, since the setting cannot be read where the parameter is written.

The messages are DRF's, "Ensure this field has no more than {max_length} elements." and "Ensure this field has at least {min_length} elements.": no Django catalog entry counts a list's elements, and DRF's catalog translates these wherever DRF is installed.

Under partial=True no absent parameter is refused, at any depth: a partial update sends only what changes. A value that is present is checked as it would be otherwise, and an unknown key is still refused. Dispatch relaxes a partial write's Validator parameters, and a parameter a provider is annotated to fill, so a transport checking a call as dispatch will calls bind_arguments rather than check_arguments(partial=True).

It runs before the Validator by design, so a Validator is only ever handed well-shaped arguments - and a test of a Validator fed a malformed argument passes without exercising the Validator.

docs.title: The closed argument set
docs.text:
An argument no parameter declares is refused where it appeared, under "Unknown argument.". That holds at every level, inside each row and each nested object as well as at the top: closed only at the top, an unknown key in a row would reach the row's constructor and come back as a TypeError naming no row.

UnknownArguments.REJECT is the default everywhere. An untrusted caller's undeclared key is refused before it costs a query, and a trusted caller's typo - a command's misspelt option, a task enqueued with last month's argument name - fails where the caller can see it instead of being dropped. IGNORE drops undeclared keys instead, at every level:

def lenient(arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return check_arguments(AUTHOR, arguments, unknown_arguments=UnknownArguments.IGNORE)


SENT = {"name": "Ursula", "nickname": "UKL", "books": [{"title": "Lathe", "price": 7, "isbn": 1}]}
KEPT = {"name": "Ursula", "books": [{"title": "Lathe", "price": 7}]}

There is no third policy that passes an undeclared argument through. Reaching a callable is exactly what the closed set prevents: on a read, with no Validator in front of it, it would let a caller supply a keyword the operation's author never offered. The enum does carry a third member, PASSTHROUGH, kept as a name for the transports of the current djangorestframework-services release, which compare a policy against it. It is not a policy: every function that takes one raises ValueError for it rather than running it as IGNORE.

dispatch, adispatch, check_call and bind_arguments each take unknown_arguments=.

A spec's shapes are declared parameters like any other here: an argument sent for one passes the closed set and is shape-checked, choices and lengths included, before anything runs, and an undeclared one beside them is refused as any is. Only what happens after differs: the value goes to the presenter alone, on PresentationContext.shapes, and never to the Validator, a selector or the service (declaring an operation).

docs.title: The refusal tree
docs.text:
Every refusal of arguments is InvalidArguments, whoever made it: the shape check, the closed argument set, coerce_flat, a Validator, or a relation write. It carries every problem found, not the first, as one tree in .detail addressed by path:

from django_service_specs import (
    InvalidArguments,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    UnknownArguments,
    check_arguments,
    coerce_flat,
)

BOOK = Parameters.of(
    Parameter("title", "string", required=True),
    Parameter("price", "string", format="decimal", required=True),
)
AUTHOR = Parameters.of(
    Parameter("name", "string", required=True),
    Parameter("books", "array", items=BOOK),
)


def refusal(arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[Any, Any]:
    try:
        check_arguments(AUTHOR, arguments)
    except InvalidArguments as refused:
        return refused.detail
    return {}


ARGUMENTS = {
    "name": "Ursula",
    "books": [
        {"title": "The Dispossessed", "price": "9.99"},
        {"price": "a lot", "colour": "red"},
        "Always Coming Home",
    ],
}

REFUSED = {
    "books": {
        1: {
            "title": ["This field is required."],
            "price": ["Enter a number."],
            "colour": ["Unknown argument."],
        },
        2: {"non_field_errors": ["Expected an object."]},
    },
}
  • A field's messages are a list under its name: {"title": ["..."]}.
  • A nested object's are a tree under its name: {"author": {"name": ["..."]}}.
  • An array's rows are keyed by their int index, and only the rows that failed appear: the first book above is fine, so there is no key 0.
  • A message about a row itself, rather than one of its fields, sits under non_field_errors inside the row. The third book is not an object at all, so it has no field to hang the message on. non_field_errors is Django's and DRF's spelling of the same idea, so a transport that renders either's errors reads these without a translation table.

A many write's rows are addressed the same way, under its many_argument: {"items": {2: {"title": [...]}}}, a message about a row itself under non_field_errors inside it, and the list's own refusal - absent, null, not a list - as {"items": [...]}. The shape check's refusals of some rows and the Validator's of others come back in the one tree. A Validator that validates the list as one may refuse the list itself after its rows pass on their own - too many rows, two rows that clash - and that message sits under non_field_errors in the list's node, after the rows: {"items": {2: {...}, "non_field_errors": [...]}}.

Every leaf is a list of strings, so the tree is JSON-serializable once the integer keys are written as strings, which is what json.dumps does. The messages are spelled as Django's own form fields spell them wherever one has the message, so Django's catalogue translates them and a project adds nothing. Each also carries a code, which the next section reads.

DataclassValidator answers in the same tree, and so does a relation write that refuses a row, so a transport reads one shape whichever of them refused.

docs.title: The codes a refusal carries
docs.text:
A message is for a person, and is translated. A program reading the tree needs something that is not, so every refusal the kernel and its shipped adapters make is a CodedMessage: a str carrying a code. The code is the one a DRF field gives the same mistake, so an adapter building DRF's ErrorDetail from the tree maps each one across unchanged, and a client of both reads one get_codes().

def codes(detail: Any) -> Any:
    """The tree with each message's code in its place, and ``"invalid"`` where it has none."""
    if isinstance(detail, Mapping):
        return {key: codes(value) for key, value in detail.items()}
    if isinstance(detail, list):
        return [codes(message) for message in detail]
    return getattr(detail, "code", "invalid")


CODES = {
    "books": {
        1: {"title": ["required"], "price": ["invalid"], "colour": ["unknown"]},
        2: {"non_field_errors": ["invalid"]},
    },
}
Refusal Code Raised by A required argument is absent required the shape check A null where none is allowed null the shape check A key nobody declared, under REJECT unknown the shape check A value of the wrong type, a malformed date, date-time or UUID, a decimal or number that is not finite, a row that is not an object invalid the shape check A value that is not an array where one is declared not_a_list the shape check A number past its maximum, or short of its minimum, an array's element at its index max_value, min_value the shape check A value outside its choices invalid_choice the shape check An array longer than it takes, or shorter max_length, min_length the shape check, coerce_flat A flat string that spells no integer, number or boolean, or one sent for a parameter with nested parameters invalid coerce_flat A read a selector, its extend_queryset or a precondition asks for that nothing filled required dispatch, as the shape check would A value a FilterSet refuses its form field's own code, invalid where it has none the FilterSet, through dispatch A number past a signed 64-bit integer sent to a filter on an integer column, a range filter's bound at its own argument and a CSV filter's element at its index max_value, min_value dispatch, applying the FilterSet A model choice filter's key past the range of the column its rows are matched on invalid_choice dispatch, applying the FilterSet A null row in a relation's list null a relation write A row's data Django fails to write the ValidationError's own code, invalid where it has none and for a TypeError or ValueError a relation write

The shipped Validators code theirs the same way:

Validator Its refusals DataclassValidator required, null, unknown, invalid_choice, and invalid for a wrong type, a decimal or date that does not parse, and a ValueError from __post_init__; a Django ValidationError from __post_init__ keeps its own code, invalid where it has none FormValidator Django's own code on each message, the field's and the form's: required, max_length, invalid_choice, unique_together and the rest; invalid for a message raised with none PydanticValidator pydantic's error type mapped to DRF's code: missing is required, a None a type refuses null, a length max_length or min_length, a bound (an exclusive one too) max_value or min_value, a Literal or Enum invalid_choice, a list's type not_a_list, a decimal's digits max_digits, max_decimal_places or max_whole_digits, a forbidden extra key unknown; any other of pydantic's own types, and a ValueError in a validator, invalid; a PydanticCustomError keeps its type as its code

Django's codes are Django's, and not always DRF's: a pair a model holds unique together says unique_together from a form, where DRF's serializer validator says unique. They come through as Django raised them rather than translated to a guess.

One has no DRF field to follow. DRF ignores a key a serializer does not declare, so it has no code for refusing one, and unknown names the policy that refused it. A free-form object is invalid, as a nested serializer's refusal is, where DRF's DictField would say not_a_dict. An empty many list refused by many_min_length=1 is min_length, as its message says, where a ListSerializer with allow_empty=False says empty.

A CodedMessage is its message to everything else. It equals and hashes as its str, and json.dumps writes the plain message, so the codes never reach a body a transport writes and a test comparing a tree with plain strings is unchanged by them. A copy and a pickle keep the code.

A Validator's messages reach the tree as it raised them, on one call and row by row on a many call. Dispatch does not rewrap them: a library's own coded message, DRF's ErrorDetail among them, keeps its code, and a plain str stays one, with no code. So does a project's own Validator raising plain strings, so read a code with getattr(message, "code", ...) and choose the default, as the example's "invalid" is DRF's own for a message raised with none.

One check answers a field. The shape check runs before the Validator, so a call it refuses is never validated, and only its codes come back: a title that is blank and sent beside an unknown key reads unknown alone, not blank too. A many call reads the same way row by row: a row the shape check refuses is never handed to the Validator, while every row it lets through is, so the two checks' refusals of different rows come back in one tree.

docs.title: Flat transports
docs.text:
Argv and a query string carry strings. Validation libraries read strings differently from one another, so turning them into what a JSON caller would have sent is the kernel's job rather than each transport's: coerce_flat, directed by the declaration.

FILTERS = Parameters.of(
    Parameter("limit", "integer"),
    Parameter("published", "boolean"),
    Parameter("ids", "array", items="integer"),
    Parameter("price_below", "string", format="decimal"),
)


def from_argv(raw: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return check_arguments(FILTERS, coerce_flat(FILTERS, raw))


ARGV = {"limit": "10", "published": "true", "ids": "3", "price_below": "9.99"}
TYPED = {"limit": 10, "published": True, "ids": [3], "price_below": "9.99"}
  • An integer or a number is parsed. An integer is read as Django's IntegerField reads one: "5.0" and "5." are 5, and "5.5" is refused with "Enter a whole number.". A number is read as a JSON decoder reads the same literal: "3" is the integer 3, exactly, and "2.5" and "1e3" are floats, so ?pks=9007199254740993 is that key and not its neighbour. Each element of an array, a repeated query-string key's included, is read the same way.
  • A boolean is parsed from exactly four spellings - true, false, 1, 0, in any case - and anything else is refused with "Enter true, false, 1 or 0.". Libraries disagree about every other spelling (a Django BooleanField reads "no" as true), so refusing is the one answer that cannot set a flag the caller meant to clear.
  • A decimal, a date-time, a date and a UUID stay strings, for the Validator to decode, exactly as they would arrive off a JSON wire; the shape check then refuses one that does not parse, ?project=null included, and hands a UUID on in its canonical spelling. So does each element of an array of decimal strings, which the shape check then reads and bounds as a decimal, at its index.
  • An any stays the string it arrived as: it declares no type to read the string as, so ?pk=3 reaches the Validator as "3", not 3.
  • An array's elements are coerced by its items type, and a single value becomes a one-element list, since a flat transport sends a one-element list as a bare value. An array longer than it takes is refused whole, before any element is parsed, by the same length rule as the shape check's. A query string's ?ids=1,2,3 is split into no more than one element past the most the array takes, so a value of a million commas is refused without becoming a million elements first: Django's DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_NUMBER_FIELDS counts keys, and a comma list is one.
  • A parameter with nested Parameters is refused by name - an object, or an array of rows, has no flat spelling - with "This argument has nested parameters, which a flat transport cannot send.", rather than passing the string on to fail as a type error that does not say why.
  • A key the parameters do not declare passes through untouched, so the closed argument set in check_arguments stays the one place that refuses it.

docs.title: Two families of error
docs.text:
Every error a transport answers belongs to one of two families, and the family says who refused.

Family Members Who refused DispatchError InvalidArguments, NotPermitted, PrincipalUnavailable Dispatch, before the operation ran ServiceError ServiceValidationError, ServiceConflict, ServiceNotFound The operation itself

Neither subclasses the other, and none of their members crosses over. That reads like an oversight and is the point:

  • Every consumer reads a service error as a refusal the caller adapts to: an agent turns one into a result the model reads and routes around, and the run goes on. A denial declared that way becomes something the model retries, where a denial should end the attempt.
  • An MCP server tells "invalid arguments" from "a business rule refused well-shaped arguments" by exactly this type difference. So InvalidArguments is not a ServiceValidationError: the first says the input was not well-shaped or did not validate, the second states a business rule about input that did.

A service raises the second family. ServiceValidationError carries a detail (a string, a field-keyed mapping, or a list), ServiceConflict says the request collides with the current state and a caller may re-read and try again, and ServiceNotFound says the thing is absent, or not the caller's to see - the same answer for both, since refusing a row the caller cannot see confirms that it exists.

A transport answers each type in its own terms. One HTTP-shaped ladder:

from typing import Any

from django_service_specs import (
    DispatchError,
    InvalidArguments,
    NotPermitted,
    PrincipalUnavailable,
    ServiceConflict,
    ServiceError,
    ServiceNotFound,
    ServiceSpec,
    ServiceValidationError,
    dispatch,
    present,
)


def answer(spec: ServiceSpec, principal: Any, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[int, Any]:
    """One HTTP-shaped answer per outcome. Another transport maps the same types its own way."""
    try:
        result = dispatch(spec, principal=principal, arguments=arguments)
    # Dispatch refused, before the operation ran.
    except InvalidArguments as refused:
        return 400, refused.detail
    except (NotPermitted, PrincipalUnavailable) as refused:
        return 403, {"detail": refused.message}
    # The base may be raised bare, so it is answered below its subclasses.
    except DispatchError as refused:
        return 400, {"detail": refused.message}
    # The operation refused. The subclasses first: each is also a ServiceError.
    except ServiceValidationError as refused:
        return 400, field_map(refused.detail)
    except ServiceNotFound as refused:
        return 404, {"detail": refused.message}
    except ServiceConflict as refused:
        return 409, {"detail": refused.message}
    except ServiceError as refused:
        return 422, {"detail": refused.message}
    if result.kind == "not_found":
        return 404, {"detail": "Not found."}
    return 200, present(spec, result)


def field_map(detail: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Every 400 body is a field map: a message about the input as a whole has its own key."""
    if isinstance(detail, dict):
        return detail
    return {"non_field_errors": detail if isinstance(detail, list) else [detail]}

The subclasses of ServiceError are matched before ServiceError itself, or the base class swallows them. A transport that has never heard of ServiceConflict still handles it as a ServiceError.

Every 400 is a field map, whichever family refused: a service's string or list detail goes under non_field_errors, where a message about the input as a whole sits in an InvalidArguments tree too. A service's own refusal that names no field (ServiceError itself) is a 422: the request was understood and refused, which is not the same as malformed.

The statuses are djangorestframework-services'. A transport answering over HTTP need not write its own ladder: django-spec-html ships one, and its documentation has the whole of it.

Configuration errors are neither family. A spec with no permission check, a parameter named after a pool seed, shaping declared on a selector that returns no queryset: each raises Django's ImproperlyConfigured, because it is the declaration that is wrong, for every caller.

docs.title: Running operations from the command line
docs.text:
The management command that serves a registry's specs, one subcommand per spec, is django-spec-cli, a distribution of its own:

pip install django-spec-cli

It runs each operation through dispatch as every other transport does, and its documentation covers declaring a command, the user a run is made as, the output formats, the exit codes, and the report of open specs. This package no longer ships a command.

docs.title: Open specs: --explain and the system check
docs.text: Both are django-spec-cli's, in its documentation. The registry fact they report is this package's: open specs, reported.

docs.title: Declaring an operation
docs.text:
An operation is a spec: a frozen dataclass that says what the operation takes, who may run it, what it acts on and what it returns. There are two.

  • SelectorSpec is a read: a list or a retrieve.
  • ServiceSpec is a write: a service, the row or rows it acts on, and what it returns.

Specs are usually built at module level, at import time. Anything that could need the app registry - reading a Validator's declaration, resolving an annotation - happens on first use instead, so building a spec never does. A declaration no reader could act on is refused where it is written, with ImproperlyConfigured naming the field: a Validator class where an instance belongs, both an instance and a collection selector, a presenter declared on a service and on its output selector, a string where select_related wants a sequence.

docs.title: Every callable declares what it receives
docs.text:
The service, the selector, extend_queryset, the providers, the preconditions and a pool seed's resolver are all called the same way: with the keywords their signature declares, picked from a pool dispatch builds for the call, and nothing else. A callable that takes **kwargs receives the whole pool but call_context and shapes, which reach a callable only by their names.

Name Holds In the pool of user The principal Every callable progress The transport's progress reporter, or null_progress Every callable; the caller's reporter only in the run's pool and its spec's callable affordance conditions' each validated value, by name What the Validator returned The service data The Validator's data: the validated values as one mapping, or the instance a DataclassValidator built The service what the Validator binds, by name A value bound for the call, its Validated.pool The service instance The row an instance selector resolved The service, its providers collection The rows a collection selector resolved The service, its providers each of a selector's reads, by name The checked argument That selector, its kwargs provider each of a service spec's reads, by name The checked argument The service, its providers each key a kwargs provider returns The author's value, outranking the caller's The selector or service it is declared on result The service's return The output selector, which is handed it as instance too queryset The shaped queryset so far extend_queryset a registered seed Its resolver's value Every callable call_context The call's context: the transport's dict, or a fresh one Every callable dispatch resolves that names it, never a **kwargs catch-all; not a seed's resolver or a filter_set shapes The call's shapes: what the caller sent for the spec's shapes, read-only, empty on a spec declaring none Every callable dispatch resolves that names it but an affordance condition and a write's target selector, never a **kwargs catch-all; not a seed's resolver, a filter_set or the Validator

The fixed names - user, progress, data, instance, collection, result, queryset, call_context and shapes - are reserved: a parameter declared under one is refused, and so is a validated value returned under one, so an argument can never outrank a value dispatch put in the pool itself. A caller naming an argument user is the case that matters. Pool seeds add names of your own, reserved the same way.

A parameter with no default that the call's pool lacks, where a caller could have filled it, is refused before the callable runs, on dispatch and adispatch alike, as InvalidArguments keyed by the parameter with the shape check's own "This field is required.", rather than reaching the callable as a TypeError. That is a read declared optional that the caller left out, whether the selector, its extend_queryset, the service or a precondition takes it, or a Validator parameter the caller left out, which the service takes - unless the spec is partial, whose calls may leave any of those out.

Any other parameter the pool lacks is the declaration's error, and raises as the callable's own TypeError. The argument set is closed, so a name that is none of the selector's reads - or, for the service, none of its Validator's parameters, which is every name when it has no Validator - can never be sent: REJECT refuses it as unknown and IGNORE drops it. A Validator parameter the caller did send, and the Validator did not hand back under that name - a form that pops it in clean(), a pydantic field returned under its own name rather than its alias - has been sent already. Refusing either as a missing argument would ask for a value the caller cannot send or already did, and a client that reads InvalidArguments as its own mistake would send the call again. It is decided at dispatch rather than when the spec is declared, because a registered seed may fill such a parameter, and the seeds are known only then.

Four kinds of parameter are never missing: one with a default, **kwargs, *args, and a positional-only one, which dispatch never passes by name. Nothing the output selector declares is refused either: its pool carries no argument, and the service has already run. Where an argument may be left out, give the parameter a default.

docs.title: Typing a callable
docs.text:
Nothing above reads an annotation, so a service is typed for its author and the type checker rather than for dispatch. Seven Protocols name the shapes dispatch calls: CreateService takes data, UpdateService takes instance and data, and DeleteService takes instance with data optional; ListSelector and RetrieveSelector type a selector's result, and Selector and AsyncSelector describe any selector at all. Every other key of the pool arrives through **extras. implements states the Protocol on the definition, where a type checker such as ty reports a callable that does not conform, and returns the callable unchanged:

@dataclass
class NoteIn:
    title: str


@implements(CreateService[NoteIn, Note])
def create_note(*, data: NoteIn, **extras: Any) -> Note:
    return Note.objects.create(owner=extras["user"], title=data.title)


@implements(DeleteService[NoInput, Note, None])  # reads no input, so no `data`
def delete_note(*, instance: Note, **extras: Any) -> None:
    instance.delete()


create_note_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=create_note, permissions=[IsSignedIn()], validator=DataclassValidator(NoteIn)
)
delete_note_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=delete_note, permissions=[IsSignedIn()], instance_selector_spec=the_note
)

NoInput fills the input type of a service that reads none. A delete that does take input declares data with a default of its own, since the Protocol's caller may leave it out.

docs.title: A read
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Annotated, Any

from django.db.models import QuerySet

from django_service_specs import (
    UNSET,
    DataclassPresenter,
    DataclassValidator,
    FieldMarking,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    PermissionCheck,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    UnsetType,
)
from tests.adapter_app.models import Status
from tests.dispatch_app.models import Note


class IsSignedIn(PermissionCheck):
    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any) -> bool:
        return principal.is_authenticated


@dataclass
class NoteRow:
    id: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()]
    title: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]


def notes_of(*, user: Any, search: str = "", ordering: str = "title") -> QuerySet[Note]:
    return Note.objects.filter(owner=user, title__icontains=search).order_by(ordering)


list_notes_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=notes_of,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    reads=Parameters.of(
        Parameter("search", "string", help="Part of the title, in any case."),
        Parameter("ordering", "string", choices=["title", "-title"], default="title"),
    ),
    select_related=["owner"],
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteRow),
)

kind is SelectorKind.LIST or RETRIEVE. A retrieve returns one row: a queryset is read with .first(), a DoesNotExist raised by a selector written with .get() means the same missing row, and a missing row is reported as not-found unless the spec sets allow_none=True, which makes it the value None - the shape of an optional singleton, or of an upsert's target. On a list, allow_none=True says the selector may return None for "no rows": the result is the empty list, its scope check and preconditions are asked of that empty set as they are of an empty queryset, and the shaping is skipped, since there is nothing to shape. Without it, a list selector's None is passed on as it came, and presenting it fails as the author's error.

A selector may also raise Django's Http404, as get_object_or_404 does. On a retrieve that is the same missing row a DoesNotExist is: not-found, or None under allow_none=True. On a list it is the selector saying "not found", usually of a parent row it looked up before listing that parent's children, and the result is not-found whatever allow_none says. A DoesNotExist escaping a list is different: a list has no missing row, so it is a fault inside the selector and raises. An output selector runs after the write, so a list one raising Http404 raises a RuntimeError chained from it, rather than report a write that happened as not found: a bare Http404 would be answered 404 by Django's handler and by DRF's. Only the selector's own raise is read this way: an Http404 from its extend_queryset passes through.

reads is the selector's whole input. There is no Validator in front of a read, so these Parameters are what the closed argument set and the shape check hold the caller to: an argument the spec does not declare is refused before the selector runs.

shapes sits beside reads, for the arguments that shape what the presenter renders rather than which rows are read: which fields, a query over each row. They are Parameters of their own and part of spec.parameters(), after the reads, so the schema, the closed argument set and the shape check cover them as any argument. No shape is in the selector's pool under its own name, so the selector, its extend_queryset and its filter_set never receive one as an argument: what the caller sent for them reaches the presenter on PresentationContext.shapes, and any callable that names the shapes seed, which holds the same mapping. A selector that eager-loads by the query its presenter renders reads it there. A shape a read or a filter also declares is refused when the spec is built, as is one named for a seed dispatch provides and one the kwargs provider is annotated to fill, since no provider's values reach them. A presenter reading them is shown under shaping each row by the call.

select_related, prefetch_related and annotations are applied to the queryset the selector returns, in that order, then extend_queryset, with the shaped queryset as queryset, and filter_set last. Declaring any of them on a selector that returns something other than a queryset is refused at dispatch.

filter_set is a django-filter FilterSet class, installed with the filter extra. One that declares no filters - its base_filters missing, empty or None - is refused with ImproperlyConfigured when the spec is built, unless it is a django-filter FilterSet class: it declares no Parameters, so it would be handed none of the caller's data and never filter. A duck-typed stand-in taking (data, queryset) declares its filters in base_filters, and a step narrowing the queryset by no argument belongs in extend_queryset. A real FilterSet declaring no filters is accepted, and narrows nothing. Its filters are reads: each is read as a Parameter by filter_set_parameters and joins reads after the author's own, named as django-filter reads it - price_min and price_max for a range - so the schema, the closed argument set and the shape check cover every filter, and a filter named like a read declared differently is refused. Every filter is optional. A number filter, and each bound of a numeric range, is a decimal string, which its DecimalField reads exactly: read as a float on the way, a key past 2**53 would match its neighbour's row. A JSON number is still taken. Each such decimal is bounded at minimum=-1e50 and maximum=1e50: django-filter's number filter refuses a value past 1e50 and leaves a range's bounds and every negative value open, while an integer column's conversion builds every digit of a value such as "1E+999999999", which holds a worker for minutes. So the shape check refuses either side of the line before the FilterSet is reached. A CSV number filter is an array of the same bounded decimals: Parameter("pks", "array", items="string", format="decimal", minimum=-1e50, maximum=1e50), whose format and bounds describe each element. ?pks=1,2 still splits, since no decimal holds a comma, each value reaches the filter with every digit it was sent with, a fraction included, and one past the line is refused at its index in the list.

A selector spec also takes kwargs, preconditions and progress_reporter, which a write declares the same way. Its kwargs provider is called from the base pool and its reads, and on a selector nested in a write scopes the lookup. Its preconditions run on what its selector found, never on a missing row. A nested selector declaring preconditions or a progress_reporter, or an output selector declaring kwargs, is refused when the write is built: dispatch never runs them.

permissions is required on a spec that is dispatched or registered, and ignored on a selector nested inside a ServiceSpec: authorization belongs to the spec being dispatched.

docs.title: A write
docs.text:
A ServiceSpec names its service and, at most, one target selector:

  • instance_selector_spec, a RETRIEVE, for a service that acts on one row. It arrives as instance, and a missing row is not-found: the service never runs and the Validator is never asked. With allow_none=True on the selector, a missing row arrives as instance=None instead, which is how an upsert is written.
  • collection_selector_spec, a LIST, for a bulk operation. The rows arrive as collection.
  • Neither, for a create.

output_selector_spec re-reads what the service produced, with its return in the pool as result. It is how a write returns a row with fresh annotations or prefetches, or a list after a bulk change; the relation-write example uses one. Without one, the service's own return is what is presented, and allow_none=True on the spec declares that it may be None, so its output schema admits "null".

atomic=True, the default, runs the service inside transaction.atomic(). metadata holds a project's own per-operation facts, stored as given, for its own checks or audit hooks to read.

reads are the arguments the service, its providers and its preconditions read with no Validator in front of them - the project_pk a create is scoped by - named after a selector spec's. They are checked as a read's are and handed to each callable that declares them, never to the Validator.

shapes are the arguments that shape what the presenter renders, as on a read: never handed to the Validator, a provider, a selector or the service under their own names, and reaching the presenter, whether that is the spec's own or its output selector's. A callable that names the shapes seed is handed them, the output selector included, but not the Validator, an affordance condition, a seed's resolver, a filter_set or the write's target selector, whose lookup is the same on every route and is handed none. A selector nested in a write, its target or its output selector, declaring shapes of its own is refused: the write's call is the one presented, so they are declared on the write.

spec.parameters() is everything the write takes: its target selector's reads, its own, its shapes, then its Validator's parameters. A name two of them declare is refused - two sources claiming one argument is a declaration bug, and a last-wins merge would hide which declaration a transport describes. The selector sees only its own reads, and the Validator only its own parameters.

docs.title: Partial updates
docs.text:
partial=True declares an update that sends only what changes, as an HTTP PATCH does. Dispatch does not refuse an absent Validator parameter of such a call, at any depth, and tells the Validator through ValidationContext.partial. The spec's reads and its target selector's stay required as declared unless a kwargs provider fills or may fill them, so a partial update still names its row, and a value that is sent is checked as on a whole call. parameters() is unchanged: required still says what a whole update needs. spec_input_schema is what a client reads, so it requires none of the Validator's parameters at any depth, and keeps the reads required as dispatch does.

A Validator returns only the fields the caller sent, or refuses the call. FormValidator binds only the sent fields; DataclassValidator and PydanticValidator cannot, because each builds or validates every field, and say so with supports_partial = False. With those, an update a caller may send in part declares each such field optional, as AuthorPatch below does.

Two declarations are refused with ImproperlyConfigured when the spec is built, rather than on every call:

  • partial=True with no validator. Only a Validator's parameters are relaxed, so with none the declaration changes nothing.
  • partial=True over a Validator whose supports_partial is False, such as the dataclass and pydantic adapters. Every call would be refused. The message names the service and the Validator's class; a partial spec needs a Validator that can bind only what was sent, such as a FormValidator, or one of its own.

docs.title: Many rows in one call
docs.text:
many=True declares a call carrying a list of rows under one argument, many_argument, "items" unless it names another, for one run of the service over all of them, inside one transaction under atomic:

@dataclass
class NoteIn:  # one row
    title: str


def add_notes(*, user: Any, data: list[NoteIn], archived: bool = False) -> list[Note]:
    return [Note.objects.create(owner=user, title=row.title, archived=archived) for row in data]


add_notes_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_notes,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=DataclassValidator(NoteIn),  # what each row is
    many=True,  # the rows travel under "items"
    many_min_length=1,  # an empty list is refused rather than run on no rows
    many_max_length=200,  # and so is one past 200, before any row is read
    reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("archived", "boolean")),  # asked once, beside the list
)

Each row is shape-checked and validated by the spec's Validator, which declares what a row is, before the service runs, and every failing row is refused in one InvalidArguments keyed by the row's int index under many_argument, beside the shape check's refusals of the other rows; see the refusal tree. Beside the list the call takes the spec's reads and nothing else, so a value asked once for the whole call - a confirmation - is a read. The service receives the rows' data as a list under data, and their values as a list under many_argument; neither is spread by field.

Dispatch hands the rows to the Validator's validated_many() in one call, each under its index in the caller's list. By default that validates each row on its own through validated(), and refuses a value a row binds, since the service runs once for every row. A Validator whose library validates a list as one - list-level checks, one bound object for the call - overrides it: its refusal is the list's node, each failing row under its index and a message about the whole list under non_field_errors, and what it binds in Validated.pool reaches the service once. A row the shape check refused is not handed to it, so the indices may have gaps.

The list is an array parameter, so it is bounded as one: many_min_length and many_max_length are its min_length and max_length. Neither is declared by default, so an empty list runs the service on no rows, and many_min_length=1 is how a spec refuses one. Where no many_max_length is declared, the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting bounds the list, 1000 rows by default, since every row is a Validator run inside one transaction. A list outside either is refused at many_argument as a whole, {"items": ["Ensure this field has no more than 200 elements."]}, before any row is checked, beside the top level's other refusals. Either is refused on a spec that is not many.

A many spec must declare a Validator and no target selector, since a list of rows resolves no target, and a condition on the row among its affordances is refused. With no output selector its result is kind="list", unless the service returned None.

docs.title: A service returning rows
docs.text:
returns_many=True declares that the service's own return is a list of rows, each presented by the spec's presenter: the output half of many, for a service that takes one set of arguments and hands back rows. The input is left alone, so the call's arguments are declared as they would be without it:

def archive_all(*, user: Any) -> list[Note]:
    notes = list(Note.objects.filter(owner=user, archived=False))
    for note in notes:
        note.archived = True
        note.save(update_fields=["archived"])
    return notes


archive_all_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=archive_all,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteRow),  # what each row is
    returns_many=True,  # the service hands back rows: each is presented
)

Dispatch reports a return that is not None as kind="list", and present renders it row by row. Its output schema is an array of the presenter's item, never paged: the rows are what the service returned, all of them, and a transport that pages a list pages by the spec rather than by the result's kind (see serving a page). A None return stays one value, presented as None, as a many service's is, so allow_none still decides whether the schema admits "null".

It is refused when the spec is built beside an output_selector_spec, whose kind decides what is presented, and beside many, which presents its return as a list already.

docs.title: Providers and preconditions
docs.text:
Four declarations put the author's code between the checks and the run. Each is called with the keywords it declares, like any other callable here, and is sync-only: an async def one is refused when the spec is built.

  • kwargs returns extra pool entries, merged after the caller's arguments, so a key it answers is the author's value whatever the caller sent - a tenant, a scope. A value of UNSET declines a key the provider is annotated as able to decline (or any key of an untyped provider) and leaves the caller's in place; a key it is annotated to fill is the server's, so the caller's value for it is checked and then dropped.
  • input_data, on a write alone, returns values merged over the caller's arguments before the Validator sees them, so a server-owned field - an owner, a status - is the author's. A Validator field it fills or may fill is not demanded of the caller, and dispatch refuses a required one the provider leaves out before the Validator runs. A value the caller sends for a field the provider is annotated to fill is dropped, not used in its place. The Validator is what consumes it, and the service is handed none of it directly, so a spec that declares input_data with no Validator is refused with ImproperlyConfigured when it is built: declare a Validator, or use kwargs for a value the service reads.
  • preconditions are raise-to-abort rules, in declaration order, after the affordances and before the service, outside its transaction. What the first to raise raises reaches the caller as it is. One answering with a coroutine or an async generator is refused with ImproperlyConfigured rather than read as a pass.
  • progress_reporter returns a ProgressReporter the run reports to beside the transport's - a task record, an audit trail - called only for a run that takes progress, once its keywords are bound: on the run's first report, or before the await of an async def run. A call refused before its run never calls it; a selector spec's selector is its run, so one refused at its object check, its scope check or a precondition may already have. Nothing but the run reports to it: a selector spec's extend_queryset, its preconditions and the affordance conditions answered for its rows read progress from the pool, the transport's reporter, as a service spec's conditions do.

Both providers are called from the base pool, the reads and the resolved target, and never see the Validator's values. A provider returning a name dispatch seeds itself is refused, so a provider can outrank an argument and never a seed.

A provider annotated to return a TypedDict says which keys it fills before it runs, and provider_keys reads them: filled, and declinable for a key whose value admits UnsetType. A key a provider fills or may decline, and every key an untyped provider's values reach, is not demanded of the caller: dispatch checks it once the provider has answered, after the class-level permission check and, for a Validator field, before the Validator runs, and refuses a required one nobody filled, a declined one included. bind_arguments runs no provider, so it leaves that check to the Validator. So a permission check reading such a key from its arguments uses .get. The caller's value for a filled key is dropped, and for a declinable one it stands beneath the provider's answer. The provider's values reach these: a selector's kwargs fills that selector's reads, a service spec's kwargs its reads, and input_data its Validator's fields. A provider annotated to fill a parameter declared anywhere else - input_data naming a read, kwargs naming a Validator field or the target selector's read - is refused with ImproperlyConfigured when the spec is built or, for a Validator field, when parameters() is assembled. server_owned_keys gathers what every provider of a spec fills, with the seeds' names. None of them is a parameter dispatch demands, so a transport building an input schema of its own subtracts the set from what parameters() lists:

class Owned(TypedDict):  # the keys the provider fills, readable before it runs
    owner_id: int


def the_owner(*, user: Any) -> Owned:
    return {"owner_id": user.pk}


@dataclass
class NoteCreate:
    title: str
    owner_id: int


def create_note(*, data: NoteCreate) -> Note:
    return Note.objects.create(title=data.title, owner_id=data.owner_id)


create_note_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=create_note,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=DataclassValidator(NoteCreate),
    # Merged over the caller's arguments before the Validator sees them, so
    # the owner is the signed-in user whatever the caller sends.
    input_data=the_owner,
)
# server_owned_keys(create_note_spec) names "owner_id": a transport's schema
# need not ask for it, and dispatch does not demand it of the caller.

On a many spec, the keys an input_data provider fills are fields inside each row, merged over every row, so a transport subtracting the set from the top-level parameters() - the list and the reads - removes nothing: it hides them from the list's items instead.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter is one thing an operation takes, and every transport describes itself from it rather than from whichever validation library the spec happens to use: a JSON Schema, argv options, the closed argument set and the shape check are all derived from the same declaration.

  • type is a JSON type: string, integer, number, boolean, array or object. JSON's own, because that is what crosses every wire the kernel serves: a JSON-RPC call, a queue row, and argv once it has been read.
