A refusal a transport defines itself, such as django-spec-html's UnsupportedMediaType, is not in REFUSALS: that transport maps it and tests it. Its row is still read for the precedence trap, since a row nothing reaches is dead whoever's refusal it names.

docs.title: The forms adapter
docs.text:
FormValidator makes a Django form class a Validator. The form you already have - its fields, their validators, clean_<field>(), clean() and, on a ModelForm, the model's own validation and uniqueness checks - is what validates the arguments, and the adapter reads its fields into the Parameters every transport describes itself from.

It needs nothing beyond Django, so like the dataclass adapters it is exported from the package root:

from django_service_specs import FormValidator

There is no presenter: a form describes what goes in, not what comes out.

To serve the form as a page, django-spec-html's SpecFormView renders it, dispatches the post and re-renders it with what dispatch refused. A host's own view does the same with a refusal, placed on a form.

docs.title: A form as a Validator
docs.text:
from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any

from django import forms
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model

from django_service_specs import (
    FormValidator,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    PermissionCheck,
    PoolSeeds,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    ServiceSpec,
    Unrestricted,
    ValidationContext,
    update_from_input,
)
from tests.adapter_app.models import Author, Book, Status


class BookForm(forms.Form):
    title = forms.CharField(max_length=100, help_text="As printed on the cover.")
    price = forms.DecimalField(max_digits=6, decimal_places=2)
    status = forms.ChoiceField(choices=Status.choices)
    published_on = forms.DateField(required=False)
    author = forms.ModelChoiceField(queryset=Author.objects.all())
    shelves = forms.MultipleChoiceField(
        choices=[("fiction", "Fiction"), ("poetry", "Poetry")], required=False
    )

    def clean(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        cleaned = super().clean() or {}
        if cleaned.get("status") == Status.PUBLISHED and not cleaned.get("published_on"):
            raise forms.ValidationError("A published book needs its publication date.")
        return cleaned


# The form is read here, once: a field with no JSON type fails on this line.
book_validator = FormValidator(BookForm)

What book_validator.parameters() declares, then, in the form's own order: title, a required string with the help text as its help; price, a required string in the decimal format; status, a required string with the choices draft and published; published_on, an optional, nullable string in the date format; author, a required integer, because authors are matched on their primary key; and shelves, an optional array of strings whose every element is one of fiction and poetry.

validate() binds the arguments to a new BookForm and returns its cleaned_data: a Decimal for the price, a date, the Author row itself for author. The rule clean() states is the form's to enforce, and its message comes back about the whole call: {"non_field_errors": ["A published book needs its publication date."]}.

The form is read when FormValidator is built, so a field it cannot describe fails on that line, naming the form, the field and the field's class. Nothing in the reading queries: a ModelChoiceField's rows are never listed. The one thing read later is help_text, on each parameters() call, so a lazily translated help text is in the caller's language rather than whichever was active at import.

docs.title: What each field declares
docs.text:
The first match wins, so a subclass is read as the most specific field it extends.

Field Declares BooleanField, NullBooleanField A boolean. DecimalField A string in the decimal format. It takes a JSON number too, and an integer whatever its digits. FloatField A number. An integer past a float's range is refused as the field refuses an infinity: invalid, in its own words. IntegerField An integer. DateTimeField, DateField A string in the date-time or date format. TimeField, DurationField A string. ChoiceField A string with the choices as strings, since a plain choice field cleans with str and compares against each choice's str. The empty choice is dropped and option groups are flattened. TypedChoiceField Choices, of the JSON type every value shares. Values of mixed types, or of a type JSON does not have, are refused. MultipleChoiceField, TypedMultipleChoiceField An array of the same, whose choices constrain each element. No choice field declares a length, so the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting bounds every list one takes. ModelChoiceField The JSON type of the model field rows are matched on - to_field_name, or the primary key - and no choices: they are rows, and listing them would query. It validates to the row. ModelMultipleChoiceField An array of the same, so one matching rows on a DecimalField declares the decimal format for each element and ?rows=12.50,9.99 is two of them. Django matches each against the column's own spelling, "12.50" and not 12.5. It validates to a queryset. FileField, ImageField A file, which a multipart request carries and a Python caller hands as a Django File. The form is bound with it as its files, where a file field reads, and its own checks run on it. An optional one also declares its clear checkbox. any other CharField (EmailField, URLField, SlugField, UUIDField, RegexField, GenericIPAddressField) A string.

A key past the range of the integer column rows are matched on names no row, so either field refuses it as it refuses a key no row holds: invalid_choice, in its own words, beside the form's other refusals. The adapter answers it before the form queries, because Django hands a ModelMultipleChoiceField's keys to the database driver in an __in lookup, and SQLite's raises OverflowError for one past 64 bits on every Django version, as it does for a ModelChoiceField's on Django 4.2. The range is the database's own for the column, as Django reads it to answer an exact lookup past it with no rows, and a key sent as a string of digits is the integer it spells.

A ModelForm value past the range of its model's integer column is refused in the words, and with the code, of the validator Django's model field carries from 5.0: max_value past its top, min_value past its bottom. Django 4.2 states no range for SQLite, so there the form took such a value, and a uniqueness check or a constraint querying with it raised the driver's OverflowError. The value is judged where Django 5.0 and later judge it: after the form field, its clean_<field>() and the form's clean(), on what they hand back, read as the model reads it, so digits a text field cleans to are the integer they spell. So a value the field refuses is refused in the field's words, its own bounds included, a clean_<field>() refusing it is reported in its own words, and one that brings the value inside the range has it taken. Only a column Django validates is judged, the ones it does not leave out of the model's checks: a value clean() sets in cleaned_data for a column the form has no field for, and a field the form declares over a column Meta.fields leaves out or Meta.exclude names, are never written onto the row by the form, and are the form's to use, whatever their size.

Every choice field's choices carry their labels as choice_labels, the label Django displays keyed by the value as the caller sends it, so a schema states each as a title. A choice set given as a callable is computed per form and may query, so it is not read: the field is declared as a string with no choices, which every choice field accepts, and the form checks the choice when it validates.

Refused, with ImproperlyConfigured:

  • JSONField: it takes any JSON value, and a parameter declares one type.
  • MultiValueField, such as SplitDateTimeField: it is cleaned from several widget values at once, which only an HTML form sends. Declare a field per value.
  • ComboField: it has no JSON type of its own.
  • A ModelChoiceField with no queryset, since there is no model to read its key from, or one matching rows on a model field with no JSON type.
  • Any field class the table does not cover, a project's own included.

docs.title: Presence, null and defaults
docs.text:
The Parameters say what the form does about presence and null, so on those the shape check in front of it never refuses what the form would take.

  • required is the field's own. For a BooleanField that is a statement about presence too: an absent checkbox cleans to False, which a required one refuses exactly as it refuses false. A NullBooleanField is never required, whatever it says: its validation is empty, and it takes an absent value as None.
  • nullable is not required, and always true for a NullBooleanField. A form reads None as an empty value for every field, so an optional field takes null and cleans it to its empty value - "" for a string, None for a number or a row, [] for a multiple choice - and a required one refuses it. The shape check and the form agree on it field for field.
  • There is no default. A field's initial is what an unbound form displays; a bound form cleans an absent optional field to its empty value, never to its initial.

The types are JSON's, and do not cross. A form reads its data as an HTML post's strings, so it also takes a value of another type through str - a number for a CharField, 1 for the choice "1". The shape check refuses one, as it does for any declaration: a caller sends the declared type. The empty choice is the other case. An optional choice field reads "" as no value, and a caller says that with null.

docs.title: Declare the fields on the class
docs.text:
The adapter reads base_fields: the fields the class declares. A field the form adds or changes in its own __init__ is not described, and under UnknownArguments.REJECT, the default, the closed argument set refuses its key before the form is ever built. A field declared disabled is not a parameter either: a form ignores what a caller sends for it and cleans its initial, which validate() returns with the rest.

That holds for a form built with keywords of its own, too: a field its __init__ adds from them is still not a parameter. Declare the field on the class and narrow it in __init__, as the form in A form with keywords of its own does.

docs.title: Partial updates
docs.text: On a partial spec's call, every field the arguments do not name is taken off the bound form before it validates, so it is neither required nor cleaned, and validate() returns no key for it: an absent BooleanField does not come back False, nor an absent CharField '', which an update would write over the row. A value that is sent is checked exactly as on a whole call, so a required field may be left out but not sent empty. On a ModelForm the fields left out keep the target's values, and each one's own model check skips them. Its uniqueness checks and constraints do not: they run over the row as it would be saved, what was sent on top of the target's values, and leave out only the model fields the form never declares, as a whole call does. An update that sends one field of a unique_together pair or a UniqueConstraint and collides is refused as the whole call would be, under non_field_errors, rather than failing with an IntegrityError when the row is saved. That needs a target row: a partial call with none checks only what was sent. clean() sees only what was sent, so it reads cleaned_data with get. The parameters are the same for both calls: required says what a whole call needs.

docs.title: Clearing a file
docs.text:
Django clears an optional file through its widget's clear checkbox, which a ClearableFileInput - the default widget of a FileField and an ImageField - posts beside the file as <name>-clear. The adapter declares that checkbox as a parameter of its own, a boolean right after the file, so the closed argument set, the shape check and the schema all know it. A ModelForm over title, an attachment declared blank=True and a required scan declares title, attachment, attachment-clear and scan, in that order.

It is the only way a caller clears a file: null keeps the file the row holds, as a form reads no data beside an initial value, and false is refused as not a file.

  • Checked with no upload, the form cleans the field to False, its own value for a cleared file. validate() returns it under the field's name, {"attachment": False}, and nothing under the checkbox's. A ModelForm writes it as no file through the model field's save_form_data, and so do the mutation helpers: a service handing the validated values to update_from_input(row, data) clears the file with no more code.
  • Unchecked, or absent, the file is kept.
  • Checked beside an upload, the form refuses the pair under the field's name, in its own words.
  • On a partial call, a checked checkbox sends its file field, so {"attachment-clear": true} alone clears the file; an unchecked one is what an absent one is, and leaves the field out.

A required file field has no checkbox, since its widget never reads one, and neither has a file field whose widget is not a ClearableFileInput. A form field already named as a checkbox would read the same argument, so it is refused when the Validator is built.

docs.title: A ModelForm behind an update
docs.text:
User = get_user_model()


class UsernameForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = User
        fields = ["username"]  # unique on the model


class IsThemselves(PermissionCheck):
    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any) -> bool:
        return principal.is_authenticated

    def has_object_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any, target: Any) -> bool:
        return target.pk == principal.pk


def rename_user(*, instance: Any, data: dict[str, Any]) -> Any:
    # Saves only the fields whose value changed, which is why the form never
    # writes to ``instance`` itself: it validates against a copy.
    return update_from_input(instance, data).instance


rename_user_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=rename_user,
    permissions=[IsThemselves()],
    validator=FormValidator(UsernameForm),
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=lambda *, pk: User.objects.filter(pk=pk),
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)),
    ),
)

Dispatch resolves the row before it validates, and hands it to the Validator in the ValidationContext. When the target is a row of the form's model, the form is built with instance= set to a copy of it, so its uniqueness check excludes the row being updated: renaming ada to ada is not a clash, and renaming her to bob is refused in the form's own words, {"username": ["A user with that username already exists."]}.

It is a copy because a ModelForm writes the cleaned values onto its instance as it validates. Handed the target itself, it would change the row the service receives before the service runs, and update_from_input, which saves only the fields whose value changed, would find nothing to save. Any other target - the queryset a collection selector resolves, or none for a create - builds the form as a create.

docs.title: A form with keywords of its own
docs.text:
The adapter builds the form from data= and files=, with instance= for a ModelForm. A form whose __init__ takes anything more, such as a queryset scoped to the caller's tenant, is handed it by form_kwargs, a callable returning those keywords:

class FeatureForm(forms.Form):
    # Declared on the class, so the parameter is described; the rows it may
    # name are narrowed per form, to the caller's tenant.
    book = forms.ModelChoiceField(queryset=Book.objects.none())

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, author: Author, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.fields["book"].queryset = Book.objects.filter(author=author)


# Each signed-in user's tenant: here, the author of their name.
tenant_seeds = PoolSeeds().extend(tenant=lambda *, user: Author.objects.get(name=user.username))

feature_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=lambda *, book: book,
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
    # Named from the pool, as every spec callable is: a seed, ``user``, or the
    # row as ``instance`` or ``collection``.
    validator=FormValidator(FeatureForm, form_kwargs=lambda *, tenant: {"author": tenant}),
)

The callable binds through the pool, as a selector or a service does, naming what it wants:

  • user, the principal, on every path;
  • progress, the call's reporter, or null_progress where there is none;
  • every seed the call's PoolSeeds register;
  • call_context, the call's context, the one dict every stage of the call shares (the call's context);
  • the target, under the name the service receives it by: instance for a spec with an instance selector, None when one declaring allow_none finds no row, collection for one with a collection selector, and neither for a create. It is the target itself, never the copy a ModelForm edits. The context carries it as ValidationContext.resolved.

So a caller of feature_spec names a book of their own tenant's and is refused one of another's in the field's own words, invalid_choice, though the row exists: the queryset the form narrowed is what matches it.

Off dispatch - in bind_arguments, or with a ValidationContext built by hand - there are no seeds, so a callable naming one gives it a default or fails with Python's own TypeError; user and progress are there still. bind_arguments names the target= it is passed as dispatch would, from the spec's selectors, and a context built by hand names none. Under adispatch it runs on the thread the call's synchronous phases share, so it may query. It is called on every validation, and a many call validates each row, so it runs once per row: a query every row shares belongs in a seed, which resolves once per call.

The bind sets data, files and instance itself, so a callable returning one of them - naming instance to read the row is another matter - for a plain form as for a ModelForm, is refused with ImproperlyConfigured naming the key, as is one returning anything but a mapping. FormValidator(form_class, form_kwargs=...) refuses a form_kwargs that is not callable when it is built, and keeps the callable as its form_kwargs attribute, so a transport building the form itself, for a page, builds it the same way.

docs.title: The call's context
docs.text:
FormValidator hands the call's context to form_kwargs when it names it, and reads nothing of it otherwise. A Validator built on the adapter reads it, and writes to it, from the ValidationContext its validate() is handed, as call_context: the one dict the stages of a call share, so a later stage reuses what the Validator put there (the call's context).

class RememberingBookValidator(FormValidator):
    """``BookForm``, leaving each author it matched in the call's context."""

    def validate(self, arguments: Mapping[str, Any], context: ValidationContext) -> dict[str, Any]:
        cleaned = super().validate(arguments, context)
        # One key of this Validator's own, made by the first validation of the
        # call and added to by each after it: every row of a ``many`` call.
        matched = context.call_context.setdefault("forms_adapter.authors", {})
        matched[cleaned["author"].pk] = cleaned["author"]
        return cleaned


remembering_validator = RememberingBookValidator(BookForm)

setdefault hands back the dict an earlier validation of the same call made, or makes it, so every validation of the call adds to one mapping: two calls of validate() handed one context leave both authors there. The key is the Validator's own, since every stage shares the dict. A context built by hand has an empty dict of its own, so validate() called off dispatch writes to that and needs no guard.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text: A refusal is one InvalidArguments carrying the form's own errors and messages, {field: [messages]}. The messages about the whole form, which Django keeps under "__all__", are moved to non_field_errors: the key every other refusal in the kernel uses, so a transport reads a form's refusal as it reads any other. See Arguments and refusals for the tree.

docs.title: Serving over HTTP
docs.text:
The plain-Django HTTP transport, which serves a spec from a Django view with no API framework between the request and dispatch, is django-spec-html, a distribution of its own:

pip install django-spec-html

Its JSON views and the functions they are built from keep their names, and are imported from django_spec_html rather than from this package:

from django_spec_html import AsyncSpecView, SpecView, adispatch_request, dispatch_request

The same holds for request_arguments, request_principal, route_arguments, error_response, add_argument_errors and UnsupportedMediaType. Each runs the operation through dispatch as every other transport does, and its documentation covers the views, the arguments read off a request, the principal, the refusals and their statuses, and CSRF. It also serves a spec whose Validator is a Django form as a page. This package no longer ships an HTTP view.

docs.title: A refusal, placed on a form
docs.text: django-spec-html's, in its documentation.

docs.title: Paging and projection
docs.text:
A transport that serves an operation to an agent does two things to its output that an HTTP response does not. It serves a long list a page at a time, so one call cannot pour a whole table into a model's context. And it shapes each row for its reader: an identifier is passed to the next tool rather than read out, a choice is spoken by its display rather than its stored value, and plumbing is not shown at all.

Both are functions a transport calls between dispatch and the wire. Neither is applied by dispatch, present, so a caller that names no audience is not projected: no marking applies to it, so it is served every field, each value as presented, and a list as a bare array.

euros = ValueFormatter(
    lambda amount: f"EUR {amount}",
    produces="string",
    schema={"examples": ["EUR 9.99"]},
)


@dataclass
class BookRow:
    id: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()]
    title: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]
    status: Status
    price: Annotated[Decimal, FieldMarking.formatted(euros)]
    published_on: Annotated[date | None, FieldMarking.timestamp("%d %B %Y")]
    author_id: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.hidden()]


def catalogue(*, user: Any) -> QuerySet[Book]:
    return Book.objects.order_by("pk")


list_books_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=catalogue,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookRow),
)

The output says who each field is for, with the FieldMarkings described under declaring an operation: id is a handle, title names the record, author_id is plumbing, status is content whose choices have displays, and price and published_on are content rendered through a formatter.

docs.title: Built once, where the transport registers
docs.text:
# The transport's own wording and bound, not the spec's.
HANDLE_DESCRIPTION = "An identifier to pass to other tools. Never read it out."
MAX_PAGE_SIZE = 50

# Built once, where the transport registers the spec: the projection a payload
# is shaped by and the schema it is advertised under, from one declaration.
projection = audience_projection_for_spec(list_books_spec, name="Tool 'list_books'")
output_schema = spec_output_schema(
    list_books_spec,
    paginate=True,
    projection=projection,
    handle_description=HANDLE_DESCRIPTION,
)

audience_projection_for_spec reads the spec's Output into an AudienceProjection: each field's marking, the one field marked as the label, each choice field's displays, and the same again for every nested output that has anything to project. A second field marked as the label is refused here, naming both: a record has one name.

spec_output_schema takes that projection and describes what the projected payload will carry, and paginate=True wraps the list in the page envelope. This is output_schema above:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "items": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "id": {
            "type": "integer",
            "description": "An identifier to pass to other tools. Never read it out."
          },
          "title": {"type": "string"},
          "status": {
            "type": "string",
            "oneOf": [{"const": "Draft"}, {"const": "Published"}]
          },
          "price": {"type": "string", "examples": ["EUR 9.99"]},
          "published_on": {"type": ["string", "null"], "examples": ["31 January 2026"]}
        },
        "required": ["id", "title", "status", "price", "published_on"]
      }
    },
    "page": {"type": "integer"},
    "totalPages": {"type": "integer"},
    "hasNext": {"type": "boolean"}
  },
  "required": ["items", "page", "totalPages", "hasNext"]
}

Each change to the item is the mirror of one the payload undergoes:

  • author_id is gone from the properties and from required.
  • status is described in its displays, because that is what the payload carries. The title that annotated each stored value is dropped, since the value now equals it, and a stated "type" is restated as the type of the displays, so an integer choice spoken as "Low" is never described as an integer. "null" is named last where the stated type admitted it and a null is still served: a None the choices give a display, as Django's (None, "Unknown") does, is served as "Unknown", so no null is named for it. Beside a oneOf entry that admits more than its constants the type is left as written, because narrowing it would refuse what that entry admits. Two values sharing one display list it once, so a row served it matches one entry of the oneOf rather than two, and an array of such choices stops claiming uniqueItems: two values selected together are served as that display twice.
  • price and published_on are described as what their formatters produce, and nothing they said about the value before survives: the "format" of a decimal and a date is gone, since "EUR 9.99" is neither. "null" stays in published_on's type, because a null is never formatted. It stays however the property stated it - in a type list, as a {"type": "null"} member of an anyOf (how a dataclass field typed X | None is described), as None among an enum's values (a nullable choice), or as a {"const": null} entry of a oneOf (a labelled one) - and is always written as the formatter's type followed by "null"; an enum in the formatter's own fragment lists None too, and a const becomes an enum of that value and None, so the two never disagree.
  • id keeps its values on both sides - a handle is passed to other tools, which take the stored value - and carries handle_description, the transport's sentence for a handle whose marking declares no description of its own. It defaults to nothing: what to do with an identifier is advice for one kind of reader, and only the transport knows which kind is reading.

The projection applies to the item, never to the array or the envelope around it, whose keys belong to no Output.

docs.title: Formatting a value
docs.text:
A ValueFormatter is a transform and the JSON type it produces, declared together, and a FieldMarking carries it. euros above is the generic form: render turns the presented value - the decimal's string - into the string a reader is told, produces is the type the schema states, and schema adds what the produced value looks like. A fragment naming type is refused, so a formatter cannot advertise one type and declare another.

FieldMarking.timestamp is a formatter already written: a date-time as a local string, strftime's fmt defaulting to day-first and 24-hour, with the example in the schema rendered from that same format. A date-time is converted to Django's active time zone, which is the only zone it can be rendered in: the projection is built once, before any request, so a zone chosen per call would describe one payload and serve another. A date, like published_on, is read as midnight, which is why its format names no time. A string that is not a date-time, and one shaped like a date-time that names no real moment (the thirtieth of February), is served as stored: one row's bad data does not fail the page it is on.

Both sides of the projection read one formatter, so the payload and the schema change together, and a formatter decides over the rest of the field's declaration:

  • it wins over a choice's display, being the transform an author wrote by hand;
  • it is never applied to a HANDLE, which another tool takes as input, so a marking that declares both is honoured as the handle;
  • a null passes through it unformatted.

docs.title: Serving a page
docs.text:
def list_books_tool(
    user: Any, *, page: int | None = None, limit: int | None = None, **arguments: Any
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    # page and limit are this tool's arguments, not the spec's: they never
    # reach dispatch, whose argument set is closed.
    result = dispatch(list_books_spec, principal=user, arguments=arguments)
    shaped = paginate_output(result.value, page=page, limit=limit, max_page_size=MAX_PAGE_SIZE)
    rows = present_for_audience(
        list_books_spec, replace(result, value=shaped.items), projection=projection
    )
    return shaped.envelope(rows)

paginate_output slices a list result's value into one OutputPage. page defaults to 1 and limit to DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE. Both are clamped at both ends - limit to between 1 and max_page_size, page to between 1 and the last page that exists - and the clamp is reported rather than silent: the envelope's page is the page actually served, and totalPages and hasNext are counted at the limit actually used. A queryset is counted with one COUNT before it is sliced, so a page past the end is never an unbounded OFFSET, and no page is longer than the rows counted, so a limit no max_page_size bounds, however large, still serves every row where a LIMIT past 64 bits would be refused by the database. The envelope reports the limit asked for.

Whether to page is read off the spec, never off the result's kind. A LIST selector spec is paged, as is a write whose output selector is a LIST, and spec_output_schema describes either as the envelope under paginate=True. A many write, and one declaring returns_many, come back as kind="list" too, but their rows are what the service returned, all of them, and they are never paged: their schema is a bare array whatever paginate says, so a transport paging every "list" result would serve an envelope its schema does not describe.

The names a caller pages by, and the ceiling, are the transport's. They are not arguments of the spec, whose argument set is closed, so the tool takes them off the call before dispatch sees the rest; and two mounts of one spec may well allow different page sizes.

present_for_audience is present followed by the projection, and the page's rows are what it presents. envelope then wraps them. With three books, page 2 at a limit of 2 is:

{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 3,
      "title": "A Wizard of Earthsea",
      "status": "Published",
      "price": "EUR 9.99",
      "published_on": "01 November 1968"
    }
  ],
  "page": 2,
  "totalPages": 2,
  "hasNext": false
}

The order matters. Paging first means only the page's rows are read and presented. Projecting before wrapping means the projection never walks the envelope's keys.

A selector spec declaring affordances pages the same way. Dispatch answers them on the queryset before paginate_output slices it, so each page's rows carry the affordances object the whole list would have, and the projection passes that object through whole, reason included. spec_output_schema puts it on the item inside the envelope, with or without paginate=True and projection=.

From async code, present with apresent, which runs the queries in the executor, and project what it returns with project_payload: projecting reads only the presented data and the declaration, so it is safe on the event loop.

docs.title: One spec, two mounts
docs.text:
# A second mount whose callers do need the author, as a handle to pass on.
with_authors = audience_projection_for_spec(
    list_books_spec,
    overrides={"author_id": FieldMarking.handle()},
    name="Tool 'books_with_authors'",
)


def books_with_authors_tool(user: Any) -> Any:
    result = dispatch(list_books_spec, principal=user, arguments={})
    return present_for_audience(list_books_spec, result, projection=with_authors)

overrides replaces the declared marking of the fields it names, for this mount only. Here a tool whose callers go on to look up the author keeps author_id, as a handle:

{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "The Dispossessed",
  "status": "Published",
  "price": "EUR 9.99",
  "published_on": "01 May 1974",
  "author_id": 1
}

An override that leaves two fields marked as the label is refused in the mount's name.

docs.title: A caller naming no audience
docs.text:
def books_over_http(user: Any) -> Any:
    # A caller naming no audience is presented every field, unprojected.
    return present(list_books_spec, dispatch(list_books_spec, principal=user, arguments={}))

present applies no marking, so the same spec over HTTP still serves every field, each choice as its stored value and each formatted field as it was presented:

{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "The Dispossessed",
  "status": "published",
  "price": "9.99",
  "published_on": "1974-05-01",
  "author_id": 1
}

Render an agent's answer with the projection. A pipeline that feeds one spec's output into the next keeps presenting with present, or the handles the next step reads by will have been projected away.

docs.title: Shaping each row by the call
docs.text:
Paging and projection are the transport's. What a caller may ask of the rows themselves - which fields, a query over each - is the spec's, declared as its shapes: Parameters beside its reads that no callable receives by name.

class ChosenFields(Presenter):
    """Each book with its handle and the fields the caller chose, or every field."""

    def output(self) -> Output:
        return Output(
            (
                OutputField("id", "integer"),
                # Left out of a row whose caller did not choose them. The
                # schema of a spec declaring shapes requires no field of a row
                # anyway, since a selection can leave out any of them.
                OutputField("title", "string", always_present=False),
                OutputField("price", "string", always_present=False),
            )
        )

    def present(self, value: Book) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {"id": value.pk, "title": value.title, "price": str(value.price)}

    def presented(self, value: Book, context: PresentationContext | None) -> dict[str, Any]:
        row = self.present(value)
        chosen = context.shapes.get("fields") if context is not None else None
        if chosen is None:  # not sent: every field
            return row
        return {name: row[name] for name in ("id", *chosen)}


pick_books_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=catalogue,  # never handed "fields"
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    presenter=ChosenFields(),
    shapes=Parameters.of(
        Parameter(
            "fields",
            "array",
            items="string",
            choices=["title", "price"],
            required=False,
            json_schema_extra={"uniqueItems": True},
        )
    ),
)

fields is an argument like any other to the caller: it is in spec_input_schema, with its uniqueItems from json_schema_extra, it is shape-checked, so a field not among its choices is refused before the selector runs, and an undeclared argument beside it is still refused. It never reaches the selector, which declares no fields and would fail if handed one. What the caller sent reaches the presenter on the PresentationContext as shapes, by name and read-only, with an argument left out absent rather than None, so ChosenFields renders every field unless the call chose some. Every row of a list is handed the same context, and so the same shapes.

A selector that should load what the presenter will render reads the same mapping by declaring the shapes seed, never the shape by its own name. Here the author's row is joined only when the caller chose author, or chose nothing, so each page is one query whichever fields were asked for:

class ChosenFieldsAndAuthor(Presenter):
    """Each book with its handle and the fields the caller chose, its author among them."""

    def output(self) -> Output:
        return Output(
            (
                OutputField("id", "integer"),
                OutputField("title", "string", always_present=False),
                OutputField("price", "string", always_present=False),
                OutputField("author", "string", always_present=False),
            )
        )

    def present(self, value: Book) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return self.presented(value, None)

    def presented(self, value: Book, context: PresentationContext | None) -> dict[str, Any]:
        chosen = context.shapes.get("fields") if context is not None else None
        fields = {
            "title": lambda: value.title,
            "price": lambda: str(value.price),
            # Read only when chosen: the author is a row of its own.
            "author": lambda: value.author.name,
        }
        names = fields if chosen is None else chosen  # not sent: every field
        return {"id": value.pk, **{name: fields[name]() for name in names}}


def catalogue_for(*, user: Any, shapes: Mapping[str, Any]) -> QuerySet[Book]:
    books = Book.objects.order_by("pk")
    # What the presenter will render decides what is worth joining: the
    # author's row only when the caller chose it, or chose nothing.
    if "author" in shapes.get("fields", ["author"]):
        books = books.select_related("author")
    return books


pick_books_and_authors_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=catalogue_for,  # handed the "shapes" seed, never "fields"
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    presenter=ChosenFieldsAndAuthor(),
    shapes=Parameters.of(
        Parameter(
            "fields",
            "array",
            items="string",
            choices=["title", "price", "author"],
            required=False,
            json_schema_extra={"uniqueItems": True},
        )
    ),
)

A spec declaring shapes promises no field of a row. A shape is the presenter's to apply, and the kernel cannot see which keys it leaves out: an adapter's always_present follows its library's rendering rule, not the call. So spec_output_schema lists no presenter field in any required, at any depth, wherever the item sits: the item itself, an array's items, or a page's. Here even id, which every row carries, is not required, and a client is never promised a key a row may not carry. What the kernel writes around the item keeps its own: the affordances object dispatch adds to each row, and a page's envelope. A spec declaring no shapes keeps the required its presenter's always_present states.

A shape is refused by its declaration, before the call runs, never by its presenter: the choices on fields are what turns away a field the presenter cannot render, and a presenter that raised on one would fail after the selector had read the rows. The schema advertises the same choices, so a client is told the line before it crosses it.

docs.title: The pieces on their own
docs.text: A transport with a schema or a payload that did not come from a spec uses the two halves directly: annotate_output_schema applies a projection to an item schema, or to an array of them, and project_payload applies it to a presented value. Both return their input unchanged for an empty projection, and neither modifies what it is given.

docs.title: The pydantic adapter
docs.text: PydanticValidator and PydanticPresenter let a pydantic model declare an operation's input and its output. The model does what it does for any other caller - builds the instance, runs its own validators, dumps itself as JSON - and the adapter reads the model's fields into the kernel's Parameters and Output, so a transport describes the operation exactly as it describes one declared with the dataclass adapter.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
pydantic is an optional extra:

pip install "django-service-specs[pydantic]"

The package root never imports pydantic, so nothing changes for a project that does not install it. The adapter is imported from its own subpackage, and is the only thing that needs the extra:

from django_service_specs.adapters.pydantic import PydanticPresenter, PydanticValidator

docs.title: Declaring with models
docs.text:
The nested write from Relations, declared as models:

from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Annotated, Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, model_validator

from django_service_specs import (
    ChangeResult,
    ChildSpec,
    FieldMarking,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    ServiceSpec,
    create_from_input,
)
from django_service_specs.adapters.pydantic import PydanticPresenter, PydanticValidator
from docs.examples.declaring import IsSignedIn
from tests.adapter_app.models import Author, Book, Status


class BookIn(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(max_length=100)
    price: Decimal = Field(gt=0, description="In euros.")
    status: Status = Status.DRAFT
    published_on: date | None = None
    # The key a relation write matches an incoming row by.
    pk: int | None = None

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def _dated_when_published(self) -> BookIn:
        if self.status == Status.PUBLISHED and self.published_on is None:
            raise ValueError("A published book has a publication date.")
        return self


class AuthorIn(BaseModel):
    name: str
    books: list[BookIn] = Field(default_factory=list)


class BookOut(BaseModel):
    id: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()]
    title: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]
    price: Decimal
    status: Status


class AuthorOut(BaseModel):
    id: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()]
    name: str
    books: list[BookOut]


def create_author(*, data: dict[str, Any]) -> ChangeResult[Author]:
    return create_from_input(Author, data, relations={"books": ChildSpec(model=Book, fk="author")})


create_author_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=create_author,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=PydanticValidator(AuthorIn),
    output_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=lambda *, result: Author.objects.filter(pk=result.instance.pk),
        prefetch_related=["books"],
        presenter=PydanticPresenter(AuthorOut),
    ),
)

validate() returns the values keyed by field name, with nested values left as model instances, which is what create_from_input reads a row from. The presenter reads the author and its prefetched books through the related manager, validates what it read with AuthorOut, and returns model_dump(mode="json", by_alias=True).

docs.title: What a model declares
docs.text:
A model's fields are read as the dataclass adapter reads a dataclass's, from the same table, so a model and a dataclass declaring the same field declare the same parameter:

Annotation Declares str, int, float, bool Their JSON types. Decimal, datetime, date A string with the format it decodes from. X \| None Nullable. Inside a list, list[X \| None], the element is: items_nullable. Literal[...], an Enum (Django's TextChoices and IntegerChoices included) Choices. A Django Choices enum's labels are its choice_labels; a plain Enum and a Literal label nothing. list[X] An array. list[SomeModel] is an array of rows, each declared as nested Parameters. list[Decimal] declares the decimal format for each element, as list[Decimal] on a dataclass does. The list's length is declared: see below. a model An object, with its fields as nested Parameters. dict[str, X] An object with no declared fields. Its values are the model's to validate.

Annotated is looked through, so Annotated[str, Field(max_length=100)] declares a string.

A list's length is declared as the model states it: Field(min_length=, max_length=), conlist(...), annotated_types' Len, MinLen and MaxLen, whether on the field or inside an Annotated in its annotation, become the parameter's min_length and max_length, and a schema's "minItems" and "maxItems". So tags: list[str] = Field(max_length=5000) takes 5000 tags where an undeclared list is held to the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting, 1000 by default, and a list the model allows 5 of is refused at 6 by the shape check before the model runs. Where a field states a length twice, the declaration takes the one pydantic enforces: the last it applies, the annotation's innermost first and the field's own last. A length on a string or a dict is the model's alone, since a parameter's length counts an array's elements. Anything else - Any, a union of two types, UnsetType, a RootModel, set, tuple, a dict not keyed by str - is refused with ImproperlyConfigured naming the model and the field, when the validator or presenter is constructed.

A field is required when pydantic says so. Its default is declared when JSON carries it as itself: 3, "draft", None, []. A default_factory, or a default such as a Decimal or a date, is not declared, and the field is optional all the same. The field's description is the parameter's help.

What PydanticValidator(AuthorIn) declares, then, is what DataclassValidator declares for the dataclass AuthorIn in Declaring an operation, with the price's description as its help: name, and an optional array of books whose rows take a title, a price in the decimal format, a status with its choices and default, a nullable published_on in the date format, and the nullable pk that lets an update match a row. The rule stated there holds here too: a row that updates must declare its key. The title's max_length and the price's gt are not declared; see the last section for why.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
A parameter is named for the key pydantic validates by: the field's validation_alias when it is a string, else its alias, else its name. An output field is named for the key model_dump(by_alias=True) emits: the serialization_alias, else the alias, else the name.

class Contact(BaseModel):
    # Validated from "fullName" and dumped as "fullName".
    full_name: str = Field(alias="fullName")
    # Validated from "mail" and dumped as "email".
    email: str = Field(validation_alias="mail", serialization_alias="email")


contact_validator = PydanticValidator(Contact)
contact_presenter = PydanticPresenter(Contact)

Contact takes fullName and mail, and outputs fullName and email. validate() returns {"full_name": ..., "email": ...}: the field names, whatever the wire called them, because those are the keywords the service is called with. A model that sets validate_by_alias=False takes its field names.

An AliasPath or AliasChoices is refused: a parameter has one name, and a transport must be able to say which.

docs.title: A model that contains itself
docs.text:
Category.children is a list of Category, which has no end. The adapter describes a model at most four times on one path, the top counting as the first, and the level past that as an object with no declared fields:

class Category(BaseModel):
    name: str
    children: list[Category] = []


category_validator = PydanticValidator(Category)

The bound is on the description, not on the data. The shape check stops looking at the fourth level, and pydantic validates every level below it, so a tree ten levels deep is built in full and a bad name ten levels down is refused at its path. A model that appears twice side by side is described in full both times: the count is per path.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
A refusal keeps pydantic's words, addressed into the kernel's refusal tree, as Arguments and refusals describes it:

  • a field is addressed by its parameter name, and a row by its index as an int: {"books": {0: {"price": ["Input should be greater than 0"]}}};
  • a model refusing itself - a model_validator raising - is addressed at non_field_errors inside that model, or at the top for the model being validated: {"books": {1: {"non_field_errors": ["Value error, A published book has a publication date."]}}}.

The kernel's shape check runs first, so a wrong JSON type, and a list past the length it declares, is refused in the kernel's words and never reaches the model: Ensure this field has no more than 5 elements. where the model would say List should have at most 5 items after validation, not 6, under the same max_length code. pydantic's words are what a caller reads for the model's own rules: bounds, patterns, validators.

The context reaches pydantic's validators as info.context, a dict with "principal", "target" and "call_context", so a field_validator can check a value against the caller or the row being updated, and read or leave something in the dict every stage of the call shares (the call's context).

A partial spec is refused with ImproperlyConfigured when it is built, as one over the dataclass adapter is, and so is a partial call made to the Validator directly. pydantic validates a model whole, and a model_validator is written against every field being there, so validating only the fields sent would skip the model's own rules. A spec whose calls are partial uses a FormValidator, or a Validator of its own that returns only what was sent.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
PydanticPresenter declares the model's fields in order, then its computed_fields. A field declared exclude=True is not output, and a field with an exclude_if is declared as not always present. A field's title is its label, and a FieldMarking is declared in its Annotated metadata, as BookOut does above.

present(value) takes an instance of the model, a model row, any object carrying the fields' names, or a mapping keyed by them. Anything but an instance is read one field at a time and validated by the model; a related collection is read through .all(), so a prefetch is used, and a field the value does not carry takes the model's default. A value the model refuses raises pydantic's ValidationError as it is: the value is the operation's own, so a mismatch is a defect, not a refusal to report.

docs.title: Where it differs from the dataclass adapter
docs.text:
• Nothing is omittable. validate() returns every field, a left-out one at its default, and UnsetType is refused, because a pydantic model has no value that means "not sent". An update whose fields may be left out is declared with the dataclass adapter's X | UnsetType = UNSET, as AuthorPatch is.
  • Time zones are pydantic's. An offset-less date-time stays naive, where the dataclass adapter makes it aware as Django's forms do. Declare the offset, or convert in the service.

docs.title: What model_json_schema() is not used for
docs.text:
A transport describes an operation's input from parameters(), whichever adapter declared it, and the model's own JSON Schema is not consulted. There is one dialect: a Decimal is a string in the decimal format for a model as for a dataclass, where pydantic's schema describes it as a number or a patterned string. The price of that is that what Parameters cannot carry - a string's max_length, gt, a pattern - is not described. It is still enforced, by the model, in validate(). A list's length is the exception, as Parameters carries one and the kernel bounds every list without it.

A number's bounds are not declared either, although a parameter takes an inclusive minimum and maximum. pydantic's gt and lt are exclusive, which a parameter cannot state, and its bounds may be a Decimal or a date, which a parameter does not take; declaring only ge and le would answer one model's bounds in two dialects, the kernel's words for some and pydantic's for the rest. So every bound stays the model's, in its words.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Everything below is exported from django_service_specs directly, and from the subpackage it is listed under. Import from the package root in application code; the subpackage paths are where each name is defined.

The pydantic adapters are the one exception. pydantic is an optional extra, so they are exported from django_service_specs.adapters.pydantic alone, and importing the package root never imports pydantic.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
One Django setting, read at the call rather than at import, so override_settings reaches a spec built before it. The management command's output format is SPEC_CLI_OUTPUT, read by django-spec-cli.

  • SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH: the most elements an array argument takes where its parameter declares no max_length, and the most rows a many call carries where its spec declares no many_max_length. 1000 when unset; None bounds no array. Anything but a non-negative int or None is refused as ImproperlyConfigured where it is read. See how long a list may be. django-spec-html's request reader bounds a query string's lists by the same key.

docs.title: ServiceSpec dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: AffordanceDeclarer

A write: what it takes, who may run it, what it acts on, what it returns.

Dispatch runs it in a fixed order, once a deactivated principal has been refused: the shape check and the closed argument set, class-level authorization, target resolution, object-level authorization, validation with the target in the Validator's context, the affordances, the preconditions, the service, then the output selector.

Attributes:

Name Type Description service Callable[..., Any]

The operation. Called with the keywords it declares: the principal (user), the validated values (data, and each one spread by name), the resolved target (instance or collection), and any registered pool seed. It may be async def; the kernel bridges it into atomic either way.

permissions Sequence[PermissionCheck] | None

The checks a principal must pass. None means none were declared, which registration and dispatch both refuse; an open operation says [Unrestricted()]. An empty sequence is refused when the spec is built, since no checks would pass everyone.

reads Parameters

The arguments the service, its providers and its preconditions read with no Validator in front of them - the project_pk a create's kwargs provider scopes by - as a selector spec's reads are. Part of parameters(), after the target selector's and before the Validator's, so the schema, the closed argument set and the shape check cover them; never handed to the Validator. A name the target selector also reads is refused at construction, and one the Validator declares when parameters() is assembled.

shapes Parameters

The arguments that shape what the presenter renders rather than what the service does - which fields, a query over the result - as a Parameters group of their own, as a selector spec's shapes are. Part of parameters(), after the reads and before the Validator's (on a many spec, before the list), so the schema, the closed argument set and the shape check cover them as any argument; never handed to the Validator, a provider, a selector or the service. What the caller sent for them reaches the presenter alone, on PresentationContext.shapes, whether the presenter is this spec's or its output selector's. A name a read, the target selector or the many list also declares is refused at construction, and one the Validator declares when parameters() is assembled, as is one dispatch seeds; so is a key a provider is annotated to fill, since no provider's values reach them. A nested selector declaring its own is refused: this spec's call is the one its presenter renders.

partial bool

Whether a call may leave out any of the Validator's parameters, as an HTTP PATCH does: the shape check does not refuse an absent one, at any depth, and the Validator is told through ValidationContext.partial. The spec's reads and its target selector's stay required as declared, so a partial update still names its row, unless a kwargs provider fills them. On a many spec it holds inside every row, and the list itself stays required. Declared with a validator whose supports_partial is true, such as a FormValidator: with no Validator it would relax nothing, and over a Validator that builds every field, as DataclassValidator and PydanticValidator do, every call would be refused, so both are refused when the spec is built.

many bool

Whether the call carries a list of rows, each validated by the validator, under the one argument many_argument names, for one run of the service over all of them. The service receives the validated rows as data, a list, and the validated values as many_argument, a list of their mappings; neither is spread by field. Every row is checked and validated before the service runs, and every failing row is refused in one InvalidArguments, addressed by its int index under many_argument. Declared with a validator, since the rows are the arguments it validates, and with no target selector, since a list of rows resolves no target.

many_argument str

The argument a many spec's list travels under, an ASCII identifier. "items" by default. Beside it a many spec takes its reads and nothing else, so an argument asked once for the whole call - a confirmation - is a read. Naming anything but the default on a spec that is not many is refused, since nothing would read it.

many_min_length int | None

The fewest rows a many call may carry, as the list's own min_length. None by default, so an empty list runs the service on no rows; 1 is how a spec refuses an empty one. A list short of it is refused at many_argument, as a whole, before any row is checked.

many_max_length int | None

The most rows a many call may carry, as the list's own max_length. Where it is None, as by default, the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting bounds the list, 1000 unless the project sets another, since every row is one Validator run inside one transaction. A list past it is refused at many_argument, as a whole, before any row is checked. Each of the two is refused on a spec that is not many, and a pair no list could meet when the spec is built.

validator Validator | None

Validates the arguments its own parameters() declare. A Validator instance; None for an operation that takes no arguments beyond its target.

instance_selector_spec SelectorSpec | None

A RETRIEVE resolving the one row the service acts on, from the arguments its reads declare. A missing row is not-found and the service never runs.

collection_selector_spec SelectorSpec | None

A LIST resolving the rows a bulk operation acts on. At most one of the two target selectors.

output_selector_spec SelectorSpec | None

Re-reads what the service produced, with its return value in the pool as both result and instance - the way to return a row with fresh annotations, or a list after a bulk write. instance there is the return, never the resolved target.

presenter Presenter | None

Renders the dispatch value. When None, the output selector's presenter is used; declaring both is refused.

allow_none bool

Declares that a service with no output selector may present nothing: its return may be None, and spec_output_schema then admits "null". Declaration-only, as on a selector spec's schema: dispatch presents a None the service returned whatever this says, because whether a service may return one is not otherwise in its declaration. Left False, the item stays the strict object its presenter declares. Beside an output selector it changes nothing: a RETRIEVE re-read admits "null" already, and a LIST one presents its rows rather than the service's return.

returns_many bool

Declares that the service's own return is a list of rows, each presented by the presenter, for a service that takes one set of arguments and hands back rows. The output half of many, and it leaves the input alone: the call's arguments are declared as they would be without it. Dispatch presents a return that is not None as a list, row by row, and spec_output_schema describes an array of the item, never paged. A None return stays one value, presented as None, as a many service's is, so allow_none still decides whether the schema admits "null". Refused beside many, which presents its return as a list already, and beside an output_selector_spec, whose kind decides what is presented.

affordances Sequence[Affordance] | None

What must be true for this operation to be possible right now, as a sequence of Affordance declarations, kept as a tuple in declaration order. enforce_affordances answers them at the call: the first one not met refuses it with an ActionUnavailable carrying its code, and the service does not run. Every condition on the row is answered by one query, however many are declared. A condition on the row needs a single resolved row, so it is refused beside a collection_selector_spec. It is a check at the moment of the call, not a lock: the service still re-validates whatever it relies on. None declares nothing and costs nothing - no query, no call. Codes must be unique within a spec, because the code is how a reader tells the conditions apart.

atomic bool

Run the service inside transaction.atomic().

idempotent bool | None

Whether repeating the call with the same arguments leaves the same state as making it once. Declaration-only: nothing in this package reads it, because idempotency is a property of the service the author writes, not something a dispatcher can arrange. It is here so the fact is stated once, on the spec, and every transport reads the same answer - a retry policy, a queue's redelivery handling, an agent tool annotation. None means undeclared and is the default: a transport that turns the signal into a published annotation must be able to tell "nothing was said" from a declared False, or every spec ever written starts claiming it is not idempotent. atomic is a different question: it says a single call is all-or-nothing, not that a second call is a no-op.

preconditions Sequence[Callable[..., None]] | None

Raise-to-abort rules, a sequence of callables each called with the keywords it declares from the service's pool, after the affordances and before the service, outside its transaction. The return value is ignored, unless it is still to be awaited - a coroutine from a decorated async def - which refuses the call with ImproperlyConfigured. Kept as a tuple in declaration order.

kwargs Callable[..., Mapping[str, Any]] | None

A provider of extra pool entries: called with the keywords it declares from the call's pool, it returns a mapping merged into the pool the service is called from after the caller's arguments, so a key it answers is the author's value whatever the caller sent. A value of UNSET declines its key. Annotate its return as a TypedDict and provider_keys reads which keys it fills before it runs: a read it fills is not demanded of the caller, and is the server's even when the provider does not answer it, since the caller's value for it is dropped once checked; and a filled key that a target selector's read or a Validator field declares is refused, since its values never reach either.

input_data Callable[..., Mapping[str, Any]] | None

A provider of server-owned input: called with the keywords it declares from the call's pool, the resolved target among them, it returns a mapping merged onto the caller's arguments before the Validator sees them, after the caller's, so its keys are the author's values. A value of UNSET declines its key. Annotated to return a TypedDict, a field it fills is the server's: the caller's value for it is dropped once checked, in each row of a many call too. A Validator field it fills is not demanded of the caller, and a filled key a read declares is refused, since its values reach only the Validator. Declared with a validator, since the Validator is what consumes it and the service is handed none of it directly; a spec with no Validator is refused when it is built, and kwargs is the provider for a value the service reads.

progress_reporter Callable[..., Any] | None

A provider of a ProgressReporter sink the service reports to beside the transport's - a task record, an audit trail - called with the keywords it declares from the base pool. Resolved on first use, so a call refused before its run never calls it, and a provider returning None declines.

metadata Mapping[str, Any] | None

A project's own per-operation facts, stored as given.

docs.text:
derive(**changes: object) -> Self

A new spec of this class with the named fields replaced, and every other one this spec's.

Built through the constructor, so every check a fresh declaration passes runs again on the result, the combinations included: a change that is valid alone and refused beside the fields it keeps is refused here. The spec it is called on is never changed, and the fields not named are the same objects, not copies.

A field is replaced, never extended: reads= is the new spec's whole reads. Name the base's value to keep it and add to it, reads=base.reads + Parameters.of(...).

The result is another spec, by identity: a Grant minted for this one does not cover it.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

a name in changes is not one of the spec's own fields, such as a method's name or a private field's.

ImproperlyConfigured

the result is refused as a fresh declaration with the same fields would be.

docs.title: parameters
docs.text:
parameters() -> Parameters

Everything this spec takes: its target selector's reads, its own, its shapes, then its Validator's.

On a many spec the Validator's parameters are each row's, so the top level is the spec's reads, its shapes and then the list itself: a required array under many_argument whose rows are the Validator's parameters. A row's field is no top-level argument, so it may share a read's name.

Assembled on every call rather than at construction, because a Validator reading a model-backed declaration may need the app registry, and specs are commonly built at import time. A name two sources declare is refused here, as is one dispatch seeds itself; the three that need no Validator, the target's reads, the spec's and its shapes, were refused at construction already.

docs.title: SelectorSpec dataclass
docs.text:
A read: what it takes, who may run it, how its rows are shaped, what it returns.

Dispatched on its own, it is a list or a retrieve. Nested in a ServiceSpec, it is how that service resolves its target, its collection or its output.

Attributes:

Name Type Description kind SelectorKind

LIST or RETRIEVE; see SelectorKind.

selector Callable[..., Any]

The read itself. Called with the keywords it declares, from the principal (user), any registered pool seed, and the arguments reads declares. It may be async def: the selector is this spec's run, and the run is the one callable allowed to be.

permissions Sequence[PermissionCheck] | None

The checks a principal must pass. None means none were declared, which registration and dispatch both refuse; an open read says [Unrestricted()]. An empty sequence is refused when the spec is built, since no checks would pass everyone. Not read when the spec is nested: authorization belongs to the spec being dispatched.

reads Parameters

The arguments the selector reads with no Validator in front of it - its filters, its ordering, the key of the row it retrieves. With shapes they are the spec's whole Parameters, so the closed argument set and the shape check both apply to them.

shapes Parameters

The arguments that shape what the presenter renders rather than which rows are read - which fields, a query over each row - as a Parameters group of their own. Part of parameters(), after the reads, so the schema, the closed argument set and the shape check cover them as any argument; never in the selector's pool, so the selector, its extend_queryset and its filter_set never see them. What the caller sent for them reaches the presenter alone, on PresentationContext.shapes. A name a read or a filter also declares is refused, as is one dispatch seeds and one the kwargs provider is annotated to fill, since no provider's values reach them. Refused on a nested selector, whose presenter presents no call of its own.

presenter Presenter | None

Renders the rows. Not read on an instance or collection selector, whose rows the service consumes rather than returns.

allow_none bool

On a RETRIEVE, a missing row is the value None rather than not-found - the shape of an optional singleton, or of an upsert's target. On a LIST, a selector returning None has returned the empty list: the shaping is skipped, since there is nothing to shape, and the result is [] wherever the selector runs, so a selector spec's own scope check and preconditions see the empty set, as they see an empty queryset, and its output schema stays an array. Without it, a LIST selector's None is passed on as it came, and presenting it fails as the author's error.

select_related, (prefetch_related, annotations)

Applied to the queryset the selector returns, in that order. Declaring any of them when the selector returns something else is refused at dispatch.

extend_queryset Callable[..., QuerySet[Any]] | None

Applied last, called with the keywords it declares from the same pool plus queryset, the shaped queryset so far. It returns the queryset to use. Sync-only, like filter_set: either one declared async def is refused at construction.

filter_set Any

Applied after extend_queryset: a django-filter FilterSet class, called as filter_set(data=..., queryset=...) and answering .qs. One that declares no filters - its base_filters missing, empty or None - is refused at construction unless it is a django-filter FilterSet class, because it declares no Parameters and so would be handed none of the caller's data: a duck-typed stand-in must declare its filters in base_filters, and a step narrowing the queryset by no argument belongs in extend_queryset. A real FilterSet declaring none is accepted and narrows nothing. Its filters are reads: read as Parameters by filter_set_parameters and added to reads after the author's own, so the schema, the closed argument set and the shape check all cover them, and a filter named like a read declared differently is refused here. Its data is the arguments the call was sent for those names. Needs the [filter] extra to read a real FilterSet.

affordances Mapping[str, AffordanceDeclarer] | None

What can be done to each row right now. A mapping from a name the caller chooses to the ServiceSpec whose affordances are being asked about - the spec objects, not registry names, so the read path takes no registry dependency and the declaration stays the one the operation enforces. Each answer is named affordance__<name>__<code>; a collision with a key of annotations, or between two entries, is refused at construction, because a generated answer silently replacing a project's own annotation is the worst way for this to fail.

kwargs Callable[..., Mapping[str, Any]] | None

A provider of extra pool entries: called with the keywords it declares from the selector's pool, it returns a mapping merged into that pool after the caller's arguments, so a key it answers is the author's value whatever the caller sent - a tenant, a project scope. A value of UNSET declines its key and leaves the caller's in place, unless the key is one its TypedDict return annotation says it fills: the caller's value for that is dropped once checked, so declining or leaving it out leaves it absent. Annotate its return as a TypedDict and provider_keys reads which keys it fills before it runs, and a read it fills is not demanded of the caller. On a target selector it scopes the lookup, and a filled key that the service spec's reads or its Validator declares is refused, since its values reach only the lookup; an output selector's is refused, since nothing would run it.

preconditions Sequence[Callable[..., None]] | None

Raise-to-abort rules, a sequence of callables each called with the keywords it declares from the same pool once the selector has resolved, the row as instance or the rows as collection. The return value is ignored, unless it is still to be awaited, which refuses the call with ImproperlyConfigured. Kept as a tuple in declaration order. Refused on a nested selector, whose run is the enclosing service spec's.

progress_reporter Callable[..., Any] | None

A provider of a ProgressReporter sink the run reports to beside the transport's - a task record, an audit trail - called with the keywords it declares from the base pool. The run is the selector, and the provider is called only for a selector that takes progress, once its keywords are bound: a sync selector calls it on its first report, and an async def one before the await. So a call refused before the run, a read the caller left out included, never calls it, and a provider returning None declines. The object-level and scope checks and the preconditions answer after the selector, so a call they refuse may already have called it. Nothing but the selector reports to it: extend_queryset, the preconditions and the affordance conditions answered for the rows read progress from the pool, which is the transport's reporter. Refused on a nested selector.

metadata Mapping[str, Any] | None

A project's own per-operation facts, stored as given and read back by its own checks or audit hooks.
