docs.title: SpecSource
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

An object that compiles itself to a ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec.

The seam for a library that declares operations in its own vocabulary - djangorestframework-services' spec, compiled from a serializer and permission classes - so its declaration is handed to dispatch, the registry, the schemas and the rest as it is, with no wrapper of this package's around it.

ServiceSpec and SelectorSpec satisfy it too: each compiles to itself, which is how kernel_spec tells a spec from a declaration by that mark rather than by its class.

as_kernel_spec() is called the first time any entry point reads the object, and the compiled spec it answers is the one every later call reads: the object is read as a declaration, and a change to it after that first read is not seen. Two first reads that overlap - concurrent, or a compile that reads its own object - may each compile, and both answer the spec published first. One compiled spec per object is also what lets a Grant, bound to a spec by identity, carry from resolve_target to dispatch when both are handed the same object.

docs.title: as_kernel_spec
docs.text:
as_kernel_spec() -> ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec

This declaration as a spec of this package's.

docs.title: kernel_spec
docs.text:
kernel_spec(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
) -> ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec

spec as a spec of this package's: itself, or what it compiles to.

Everything it takes is a SpecSource, and as_kernel_spec() is what it asks. A ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec compiles to itself, and is returned as it is. Anything else compiles to a spec - an object that in turn compiles to itself - and the compiled spec is cached per object, by identity: the same object answers the same compiled spec on every call, and two objects that compare equal are two declarations, each compiled on its own. The cache holds the object weakly and its compiled spec for as long as the object lives, so a compiled spec that refers back to its object keeps both for the life of the process, as a declaration at module level is kept anyway.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

spec is neither a spec nor an object with as_kernel_spec(); it cannot be weakly referenced, so its compiled spec could not be kept per object without keeping the object forever; or as_kernel_spec() answered something that does not compile to itself, which no ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec fails to do.

docs.title: Parameter dataclass
docs.text:
One thing an operation takes, as a declaration every transport reads.

JSON Schema, argv, the closed argument set and the shape check are all derived from it, so a transport describes itself from the declaration rather than from whichever validation library the spec happens to use.

name and type are positional because every declaration has both; everything else is keyword-only.

items is an array's element: a JSON type name for a flat list, or the Parameters of the object each element is. fields is the same for a parameter whose own type is object. Nesting is what lets a relation write declare its rows: an author with its books says what a book is, where a flat items="object" would say nothing and let a malformed row through.

nullable is the parameter's own: whether the argument may be null. items_nullable is its element's: whether a null may stand in the array where an element would, as in list[int | None]. The two are independent, because a list that may be absent and a list that may hold gaps are different declarations, and an array with no declared items admits a null element already.

type is a JSON type or file, which an array's items may name too. A file is a Django File, an upload included, and has no choices: it is matched by nothing a declaration could list.

type may also be any, for a parameter that declares no type, as an unannotated argument does: 3 and "abc" are both one. Its value is handed on exactly as it arrived, never read as a number or a boolean, so a query string's "3" stays the string "3"; null is accepted only where nullable says so, as for every other type. Having no type, it describes nothing a type would - no choices, format, fields, items or bound - and an array's items never name it, since an array that declares no items takes any element already.

choice_labels names the choices for a reader: a mapping of a choice to its label, or Django's choices spelling, pairs of the two, which keeps apart the 1 and True a mapping's keys would merge. A choice may go unlabelled. The labels constrain nothing, so the shape check reads only choices; the schema carries them as titles. They are stored as a tuple of pairs, and a label may be a lazy translation, rendered when the schema is built.

default is UNSET when none is declared, so a default of None stays a real default. It is reported, not applied: whether an omitted argument arrives as the default, as None or not at all is the validating library's behaviour, and each adapter reports what its library does. It takes no part in the hash, so a declaration with a list or dict default is as hashable as any other, while equality still tells two defaults apart.

minimum and maximum bound a number, inclusively: an integer, a number, or a decimal string, which is compared as the decimal it spells, so "1E+999999999" is past a bound of 1e50 without ever being built as the integer it names. Each is an int or a finite float, a JSON number the schema can state. They exist for the bound a reader needs before any Validator runs: a filter whose form field has none hands the value to the database's integer conversion, which builds every digit. Any other bound - a string's length, a Validator's max_value - is still the Validator's alone.

On an array, format, minimum and maximum describe each element, as choices do: an array of integer or number takes a bound, and an array of string takes format="decimal" and then a bound too, which is what a django-filter CSV number filter declares. A decimal is the one format an element takes: a number element is read as a float on the way, which rounds a fraction past a float's precision, where a decimal string is compared and handed on as it was sent. Any other format on an array, and a format or a bound on an element that cannot carry it, is refused. The list's own count is min_length and max_length's, so an array may carry both pairs.

min_length and max_length bound how many elements an array takes, inclusively, and are refused on anything else: each a non-negative int. They are checked on the list whole, before any element is read, so a list past its maximum costs no per-element work. An array that declares no max_length is still bounded, by the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting, 1000 unless the project sets another count or None: a list a caller controls the length of is a cost the caller controls, and the setting is read at the call, so it applies to a declaration built before settings were configured. A declared max_length outranks it either way, wider or narrower. min_length has no default: an empty list is taken unless one says otherwise.

json_schema_extra carries the JSON Schema keywords no field of a Parameter spells - a pattern, a string's maxLength, uniqueItems - as a mapping of keyword to value, held as a deep copy of its own. It is how an adapter whose library declares more than a Parameter carries keeps it on every route rather than on its own. parameters_schema adds its keys to this parameter's node. A keyword a field states there is refused here, naming the field, whether or not this parameter sets it: type, format (so a custom format is refused too: format is a field), default, the choices' enum, anyOf and const, the bounds, minItems and maxItems, items, description from help, and properties, required and additionalProperties from fields. Either side winning would advertise what the declaration does not say or drop what was written, and refusing the keyword only when one build stated it would make the same declaration valid until the array cap came on or a spec moved to REJECT. A value JSON cannot carry - a Decimal, a lazy translation, at any depth - is refused too, naming its key. It is advertised, not enforced: the shape check never reads it, so what it states holds only where the spec's Validator enforces it (test_it_is_advertised_and_not_enforced_by_the_shape_check). It takes no part in the hash, as default does not, and still in equality.

reflected says the parameter was read off a callable's signature rather than written by an author, as djangorestframework-services reads a selector's, a target lookup's or a spread service's parameters into reads. It counts on a reads parameter alone - a selector spec's, a target selector's or a service spec's - and only at dispatch: a reflected read named like a seed the call's pool_seeds registers leaves that call's argument set, and the seed fills it, where an unmarked one is refused as a configuration error (test_a_reflected_read_a_registered_seed_is_named_like_is_the_seed_s). On a Validator field or a shape it changes nothing. No schema carries it, since it describes where a declaration came from rather than what a caller sends; it takes part in equality and the hash, because two declarations that differ in it dispatch differently (test_reflected_is_compared_and_hashed_and_never_in_the_schema).

docs.title: Parameters dataclass
docs.text:
An ordered set of Parameter.

A spec's Parameters are assembled from several sources - its target selector's reads, its Validator's parameters() - and + is how. A name declared twice is refused, at construction and at + alike: two sources claiming one argument is a spec bug, and a last-wins merge would hide which of the two declarations a transport describes and which one the argument reaches.

Any iterable of parameters is accepted and stored as a tuple, so the declaration stays hashable and ordered.

docs.title: check_arguments
docs.text:
check_arguments(
    parameters: Parameters,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any],
    *,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
    partial: bool = False,
) -> dict[str, Any]

The shape check: what a caller can get wrong that the declaration can see.

Presence, JSON type, format, bounds, length, choices and nullability, at every level of nesting, with no query. It is what runs at enqueue time and in front of an untrusted caller's Validator, so a malformed call is refused before it costs a row lookup, and it is no stricter than the libraries behind it, with three exceptions named below: ASCII digits, a declared bound, and the length of an array. So a decimal accepts a JSON number as well as a string, because every decimal validator does, and a check stricter than the worker refuses what would have run.

  • A required parameter with a declared default is not refused when absent, because the Validator will supply the default. The default is not applied here: whether an omitted argument arrives as its default is the validating library's behaviour, not the shape check's.
  • Under partial=True no absent parameter is refused, at any depth: a partial update sends only what changes, and DRF skips an absent field anywhere below a partial serializer. A value that is present is checked as it would be otherwise, and an unknown key is still refused.
  • A string is read as the number it spells where an integer or a number is declared, wherever the declaration reaches, and the number is handed on: "3" is 3, "3.0" and " 3 " are 3 too, and a number's "1e3" is 1000.0. Django's forms and pydantic's lax mode both read these strings so, and the reading is the one coerce_flat makes, which this shares. Where the two differ it is Django's: an integer's "5." and "5 .0" are 5, which pydantic's int refuses, so this is looser than pydantic there. The exception is a string outside ASCII for an integer or a number, not a decimal: Django's fields read Arabic-Indic or fullwidth digits and Unicode spaces as Python's int does, and this refuses them, as pydantic and JSON do. A string that spells no such number is refused as the type it is not. The number goes on rather than the string because a Validator stricter than those two, the dataclass adapter's, refuses "3" for an int.
  • bool is neither an integer nor a number, although Python makes it an int: a JSON true sent for a count is a caller's mistake, not the number one.
  • A file is a Django File, and nothing else is one: no JSON value can be, so a JSON caller's string for it is refused at its name.
  • An any is handed on as it arrived: no type is declared, so nothing is read as a number, and "3" stays the string "3". A null is still refused unless it is nullable, and NaN and the infinities are still no JSON value. A container is not walked, as an undeclared array element's is not, and a value of no JSON type - a Python caller's, or a multipart upload sent under its name - is handed on too.
  • An integral float is an integer, and is handed on as an int wherever the declaration reaches. JSON Schema counts 5.0 as an integer, so the {"type": "integer"} this kernel advertises admits it, and a Validator never sees 5.0 for an integer: its own type check and its bounds read the int. 5.5 is still refused, and so are NaN and the infinities, which no integer is. A number keeps the float it was sent. DRF reads it differently at an exponent: its IntegerField reads str(value), as Django's form field does, so given 1e16 raw, both read "1e+16" and refuse it, where this check follows JSON Schema and hands on 10000000000000000, which either field then takes.
  • NaN and the infinities are refused wherever the declaration reaches. JSON has no spelling for either, so they are outside the number type, and this is a type rule rather than a stricter check - although pydantic's float and the dataclass adapter's both take one.
  • minimum and maximum bound a number inclusively, in the words Django's MinValueValidator and MaxValueValidator use. The second exception: a bound is the declaration's, and may be stricter than the library behind it. filter_set_parameters draws django-filter's 1e50 below zero and on a range's bounds too, where django-filter draws none, because past it an integer column's conversion builds every digit of the value. A decimal string is compared as the decimal it spells, which reads its exponent and builds none of its digits, so "1E+999999999" is refused as fast as "2" is taken. An array's bounds bound each element, refused at its index.
  • An array's length is read before any of its elements: within its min_length and max_length, and where it declares no maximum, within the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting, 1000 unless the project says otherwise. The third exception, since that default is the kernel's and may be stricter than the library behind it: a list is a cost its caller controls the size of, one Validator run per row of a many call and one query variable per value of an in filter. The refusal is the list's own, at its name, in DRF's words.
  • choices constrain the value, and an array's choices constrain each of its elements, since an array is never one of a list of scalars. So do an array's format and bounds: a decimal array's elements are each read as a decimal is, and handed on as they were sent.
  • An object with no fields is free-form: its type is checked and its contents are not, because nothing is declared inside it to check against. An array with no items takes any element, and each is still one of the array's values: its choices and the finiteness rule reach it, while an element that is itself an object or an array is not walked.

The closed argument set applies at every level, inside each row and each nested object as well as at the top. Closed only at the top, an unknown key in a row would reach the row's constructor and come back as a TypeError naming no row. REJECT refuses the key where it appeared; IGNORE drops it from the returned copy.

Returns a cleaned copy and never modifies arguments. The containers it walks are new - the top-level mapping, each declared object, each array - while a value it does not look inside, such as a free-form object, is passed through as the caller's. The values it replaces are the two it reads as numbers: an integral float declared an integer, and a numeric string declared either.

Raises:

Type Description InvalidArguments

carrying every problem found as one tree addressed by path, rather than the first; the tree's shape is documented on InvalidArguments.

docs.title: NON_FIELD_ERRORS module-attribute
docs.text:
NON_FIELD_ERRORS: Final = 'non_field_errors'

The key a message about a node itself sits under, beside its fields' messages.

A row that is not an object has no field to hang the message on, so it goes here inside the row: {"books": {1: {"non_field_errors": ["..."]}}}. It is Django's and DRF's spelling of the same idea, so a transport rendering either's errors reads the kernel's without a translation table.

docs.title: NON_FIELD_KEYS module-attribute
docs.text:
NON_FIELD_KEYS: Final = (NON_FIELD_ERRORS, DJANGO_NON_FIELD_ERRORS)

The keys a message about the whole input sits under: the kernel's, and Django's.

Django's is here because a service re-raising a model's message_dict as a ServiceValidationError carries its form-wide messages under "__all__". Neither adds a step to the path a message is placed or printed with. Both are held by test_a_refusal_tree_is_read_as_paths_to_messages, which fails with either left out.

docs.title: coerce_flat
docs.text:
coerce_flat(parameters: Parameters, raw: Mapping[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]

Flat strings to the JSON-like primitives a typed caller would have sent.

Every flat-string transport - argv, a query string - needs this, and needs it to agree, so it is the kernel's rather than each transport's: validation libraries read strings differently from one another, and after this every Validator sees an argv call exactly as it would see typed JSON. It is directed by the declaration: an integer or a number is parsed, a boolean is parsed from exactly four spellings, and everything else is left as the string it arrived as. A decimal, a date-time, a date and a UUID stay strings, for the Validator to decode, exactly as they would arrive off a JSON wire, and the shape check reads each format after this: "null" for a uuid is refused there, on every route alike. So does an any: it declares no type to read the string as, so a query string's "3" reaches the shape check and the Validator as "3".

  • An integer is read as Django's IntegerField reads one: "5.0" and "5." are 5, and "5.5" is refused. An array's integer elements are read the same way, a repeated query-string key's included. A string outside ASCII spells no integer or number, Arabic-Indic or fullwidth digits included, although Django's fields read them: see parse_number.
  • An array longer than it takes is refused whole, at its name, before any element is read: the shape check's own length rule, which this shares, so a flat list of a million malformed values costs one message.
  • An array's elements are each coerced by its items type, and a single value becomes a one-element list, since a flat transport sends a one-element list as a bare value. None is not wrapped: an option argparse never received is absent, not a list holding a null.
  • A parameter with nested Parameters is refused by name: an object, or an array of objects, has no flat spelling, and passing its strings through would leave the refusal to a type error that does not say why.
  • A key the parameters do not declare passes through untouched, so the closed argument set in check_arguments stays the one place that refuses it, under the caller's policy.
  • A value that is not a string passes through untouched: it has already been decoded by someone, and this does not second-guess them.

Raises:

Type Description InvalidArguments

every refusal at once, a parameter's at its name and an array element's at its index: {"ids": {1: ["..."]}}.

docs.title: InvalidArguments
docs.text:
Bases: DispatchError

The arguments were refused: their shape, or the Validator's verdict on them.

Parameters are declared and arguments are supplied, and this refuses the arguments. It is raised by the shape check, the closed argument set, coerce_flat, a Validator and the relation writes, so every refusal of input reaches a transport as one type.

Not a service validation error, and not a subclass of one. A service raising ServiceValidationError is stating a business rule about well-shaped input; this says the input was not well-shaped, or did not validate. An MCP server answers the two differently on purpose.

detail is a tree addressed by path, because nested arguments fail inside rows:

  • a field: {"title": ["..."]}
  • a nested object: {"author": {"name": ["..."]}}
  • rows, keyed by their int index, only the rows that failed: {"books": {1: {"title": ["..."]}}}
  • a message about a row itself, under non_field_errors inside the row
  • a message about a many call's list as a whole, under non_field_errors beside the failing rows' indices, after them

Every leaf is a list of str, so the whole tree is JSON-serializable once the integer keys are written as strings, which is what json.dumps does. A many call's node that carries the list's own message mixes int indices with non_field_errors, so json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True) over it raises TypeError: it is already in reading order, and is written as it stands.

docs.title: CodedMessage
docs.text:
Bases: str

A message in an InvalidArguments tree, carrying the code of the mistake it names.

The words are for a person and are translated; the code is for a program and is not. Every refusal the kernel and its shipped adapters make carries one - the shape check, coerce_flat, a selector or extend_queryset refusing a read nothing filled, a FilterSet refusing its data, a relation write refusing a row, and DataclassValidator, FormValidator and PydanticValidator - and the code is the one a DRF field gives the same mistake ("required", "null", "invalid", "not_a_list", "max_length" and the rest), so an adapter building DRF's error details maps each one across unchanged. Where Django or pydantic refused, their own code comes through: Django's as it raised it, and pydantic's error type as DRF's code for the same mistake. The arguments page lists them, refusal by refusal.

It is its message to everything that reads a string. Equality, hashing, json.dumps, %-formatting and repr all see the plain str, and the code takes no part in any of them: a tree with codes compares equal to the same tree written with plain strings, the body a transport writes is unchanged by them, and so is the text str makes of a tree, which a log line or Django's BadRequest carries. That is the difference from DRF's ErrorDetail, whose equality reads the code too, and why this is not one. Read the code with getattr(message, "code", None), since a Validator's own messages reach the same tree as it raised them, a plain str among them.

A copy, a deep copy and a pickle each keep the code.

docs.title: code instance-attribute
docs.text:
code: str

The mistake, as DRF's codes name it. Never translated.

docs.title: refusal_messages
docs.text:
refusal_messages(value: Any) -> Iterator[tuple[tuple[str, ...], str]]

Every message in the refusal tree value, each with its path from the root: books.1.title.

The tree InvalidArguments carries: a key is a step of the path, a row's index included, and a NON_FIELD_KEYS key adds none. A list is the tree's leaf, so its messages share the path, and only a list: anything else is one message whatever its type, a lazy translation (which is not a str) included, so it is never taken apart into characters. Each message is rendered as a str, in the tree's order. A message at the root has the empty path. Read by every transport that prints or places a refusal, so each reads one tree one way.

docs.title: expected_type_refusal
docs.text:
expected_type_refusal(kind: str) -> CodedMessage

The refusal of a value that is not of kind, as one sentence a translator sees whole.

kind is one of a closed set of eight keys: the six JSON types, "string", "integer", "number", "boolean", "array" and "object", and two that are not JSON types, "decimal" and "file". A decimal arrives as a string or a number, so its refusal names both, and a file is a parameter's type that no JSON value is.

Raises:

Type Description KeyError

kind is none of those keys.

One sentence per type rather than "Expected %(type)s", because an interpolated JSON type name would reach a translated sentence untranslated. The shape check and the Validators the adapters build share this one table, so a caller reads the same refusal whichever of them answered, and a transport refusing a value it read itself, such as a query string's, says it in the same words. Built on each call, because a translation looked up at import time needs configured settings before the package can be imported at all.

Its code is the one DRF gives the same mistake: "not_a_list" for an array, as its ListField and ListSerializer both do, and "invalid" for everything else, as each of its scalar fields, its FileField and a nested Serializer handed something other than a mapping do. A free-form object is "invalid" too, where DRF's DictField would say "not_a_dict": one type here stands for both of its fields, and the nested serializer is the one a declared object becomes.

docs.title: max_length_in_force
docs.text:
max_length_in_force(param: Parameter) -> int | None

The most elements the array param takes: its own max_length, or the setting's.

One reading for every place that bounds or describes a list - the shape check, coerce_flat, the split of a flat value, a many call's rows and the schema, and a transport reading a list itself - so the bound a client is told is the bound it meets. None where the setting is None and nothing is declared.

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

a min_length past the setting's maximum on a parameter that declares no maximum of its own, which no call could meet: at the call, and when the parameter's schema is built, so a transport listing every schema fails on it too. Found here because the setting is read only then, so the declaration cannot be refused where it is written.

docs.title: clean_held_to_their_columns
docs.text:
clean_held_to_their_columns(form: BaseForm) -> None

Validate a bound form as its full_clean() does, refusing a number no integer column holds.

Django's own validation hands such a number to the database driver in two places, and SQLite's raises OverflowError for one past 64 bits: a model choice field matching its key, and a ModelForm's uniqueness checks and constraints querying with a value. Each is answered first, in the words of the check Django would have made:

  • a model choice field sent a key its column cannot hold is taken off the form while it validates and given the field's own invalid_choice refusal after, so the form's clean() and its other errors are found as Django finds them with the field refused;
  • a ModelForm's value its integer column cannot hold is refused as the model's validation step starts, before its uniqueness checks and constraints query with it, with the min_value or max_value refusal of Django's model integer field.

Shared by FormValidator, which validates its form so, and by django-spec-html's add_argument_errors, which finds a form's own errors so before it places a refusal beside them.

The form is left as it was found, whether its validation returned or raised: every field it had, in its order, and its own _post_clean, the class's or one the form carried itself. Only its errors and what it cleaned are new.

Public so that a transport in a distribution of its own, validating a project's form, holds it to the same columns with the same words.

docs.title: Validator
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

The kernel's validation contract.

parameters() declares what the Validator takes, and validate() turns JSON-like primitives into validated values or raises InvalidArguments. An adapter reads its library's own declaration into parameters(), and must not query doing it: a transport describes a spec before any call.

Nominal on purpose. An adapter subclasses this, and subclassing is the opt-in. A structural check on a method name is the gate that lets stock classes through by accident: an is_valid protocol matches a Django form and a DRF serializer, and a validate protocol matches a DRF serializer and a pydantic model class, none of which was written to this contract.

No instance and no many keyword: the row a call acts on is target resolution, and a many spec's list is handed to validated_many(), a method of its own. partial arrives in the ValidationContext rather than as a keyword, because it is the spec's statement about the call, not the Validator's: a partial call may leave out any field, and a Validator returns only the fields the caller sent, or refuses a partial call with ImproperlyConfigured when what it builds needs every field. Ignoring the flag is the one wrong answer, since the omitted fields would come back cleaned to blanks and an update would write them.

supports_partial says which of the two a Validator does, so a spec learns it when it is declared rather than on its first call: a ServiceSpec declaring partial=True over a Validator whose supports_partial is False is refused when it is built. True by default; DataclassValidator and PydanticValidator set it False as a class attribute, since each builds every field, and a subclass of either that does handle a partial call sets it back. An adapter whose answer depends on what it was built over sets it on the instance in __init__ instead, and the spec reads the instance. The refusal at the call stays, for a Validator called directly.

Sync-only. A Validator may query - a uniqueness check does - so dispatch runs it in the executor on the async path, and it must not be async def.

validate() receives only the arguments its own parameters() declare: the caller's, through the shape check, with the spec's input_data merged over them. Through dispatch every required field is among them, whoever filled it, since one nobody filled is refused in the shape check's words before validate() runs (test_a_required_field_nobody_filled_is_refused_before_the_validator_runs). bind_arguments runs no provider, so there a field input_data fills or may fill can arrive absent, and is the Validator's to refuse (test_a_field_input_data_fills_is_left_to_the_validator_which_runs_no_provider). It returns the values the operation receives, keyed by name; a nested row may come back as whatever the library builds (a dataclass instance, a model instance), since the mutation helpers read either.

validated() is the call's whole result, and what dispatch asks for: the values, the call's data, and any value the Validator binds for the call. An adapter overrides it where its data is not the mapping validate() returns, as the dataclass adapter's is its instance, or where the library leaves an object the service may want; the rest need not touch it.

validated_many() is what dispatch asks of a many spec instead: the whole list at once. By default it is validated() on each row, which serves a Validator whose library validates one row at a time. An adapter whose library validates a list as one, running list-level checks and binding one object for the call, overrides it.

docs.title: parameters abstractmethod
docs.text:
parameters() -> Parameters

What this Validator takes, as a declaration. Never queries.

docs.title: validate abstractmethod
docs.text:
validate(arguments: Mapping[str, Any], context: ValidationContext) -> dict[str, Any]

Validated values, or InvalidArguments. May query; never async def.

docs.title: validated
docs.text:
validated(arguments: Mapping[str, Any], context: ValidationContext) -> Validated

validate()'s values, as the call's data too, with nothing else bound.

One validate() call, so a Validator that queries queries once. An override returns the same values its validate() would, and may hand an object as data and bind values in pool.

docs.title: validated_many
docs.text:
validated_many(
    rows: Mapping[int, Mapping[str, Any]],
    context: ValidationContext,
    *,
    many_argument: str,
) -> Validated

A many call's rows, validated as one call: what dispatch asks of a many spec.

rows maps each row's index in the caller's list to its arguments, already through the shape check, with the spec's input_data merged over each and only the keys parameters() declares, as on a single call. A row the shape check refused, or one dispatch refused for a required field nobody filled, is not among them, so the indices may have gaps: an override validating a list maps its library's positions back through list(rows), and a list-level verdict it reaches sees only the rows handed to it.

Returns the call's Validated: values holds the rows' values as a list under many_argument and nothing else, since a row's fields are never spread into the service's keywords; data is the list a service declaring data receives; pool is what the Validator binds once for the whole call.

Refuses with InvalidArguments whose detail is the list's own node: each failing row's tree under its int index, and a message about the list as a whole under non_field_errors. Dispatch puts the shape check's refusals beside it and raises the whole under many_argument, so every failing row is reported at once.

By default, validated() on each row in order, every refusal collected before any is raised, and each row's data and values in a list. A value a row binds is refused with ImproperlyConfigured: the service runs once for every row, so a value bound for one has nowhere to go. An override that binds for the call binds once.

docs.title: Validated dataclass
docs.text:
The values a call's service is called with, its data, and what else it binds.

Validator.validated() returns one, and dispatch builds the call's pool from it: values spread by name, data under its own name, and pool beside both.

  • values is what validate() returns: the validated values keyed by the name the service takes each under.
  • data is the validated object as a whole, which a service declaring data receives. For a mapping Validator it is values itself; for DataclassValidator it is the instance, whose fields values holds.
  • pool is any other value the Validator binds for this one call, such as the bound object a library validated through, so a service can ask for it by name. Empty unless the Validator says otherwise.

Three fields rather than one mapping, because data need not be a mapping at all, and a value bound for the call is not one the caller sent: neither belongs among the values a caller's argument names.

docs.title: ValidationContext dataclass
docs.text:
The principal, the target, whether the call is partial, its seeds, and the call's context.

target is here, rather than a constructor keyword the way DRF takes instance=, because the kernel is what resolves it: target resolution runs before validation, so an update's uniqueness check can exclude the row being updated. It is the resolved row for a spec with an instance selector, the resolved queryset for one with a collection selector, and None for a create.

partial is true for a call that may leave out any parameter, an update of only what it names: the shape check in front of the Validator has not refused an absent required one. A Validator then returns only the fields the caller sent, or refuses the call with ImproperlyConfigured if it cannot. It trails the other two with a default, so a context built from a principal and a target is a whole call.

ambient is the call's base pool as dispatch resolved it: user, progress and every registered seed - an HTTP adapter's request, a view it registers, a tenant - read-only at its top level. Its values are the call's own live objects - the principal itself, for one - so a Validator must not mutate them (test_the_validator_reads_the_registered_seeds_and_the_user holds both halves). A library whose validation reads what its caller registered, as a serializer reads its context's request, finds it here rather than in an argument. It never holds an argument, a validated value or the target, which have seats of their own. Empty for a context built by hand, and in bind_arguments, which is handed no seeds; it trails the others, so neither changes.

resolved is the target under the pool name dispatch hands it to the service as, read-only: {"instance": row} for a spec with an instance selector - {"instance": None} when one that allows none finds no row - {"collection": rows} for one with a collection selector, and empty for a create. target is the same object with the role taken off, so a callable a Validator resolves through the pool, as FormValidator's form_kwargs is, names it as a selector or a service does. Dispatch fills it from the target it resolved, and bind_arguments from the target its caller passes and the spec's selectors, by the one rule both share. Empty for a context built by hand; it trails the rest, so no existing construction changes.

call_context is the call's context: one plain dict the transport creates for its natural scope - a request, an agent run - and hands to dispatch, which every stage that declares it receives as the same object. A Validator reads it and writes to it directly, as a DRF serializer does its context, and a later stage of the call reuses what it put there rather than computing it again. Unlike ambient it is the transport's and the stages' to change; the kernel writes nothing to it. A context built by hand gets an empty dict of its own, never one shared with another, so a Validator that writes to it needs no guard for a call that was handed none. It trails every other field, so no existing construction changes. One key is the family's rather than any one transport's: "transport" names the transport serving the call ("agent", "http", "mcp"), set by that transport, by convention only - the kernel neither sets nor checks it, so read it with .get.

docs.title: Presenter
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Turns one value an operation produced into JSON-like data.

output() declares the result and present() renders one value. They are separate because describing the result is not optional where rendering is: an HTML transport hands the object to a template and never renders it, but its confirmation page still reads what the result declares.

present takes one value. A list result is handed to presented_rows() whole, which by default presents it item by item, so a Presenter never has to guess whether it was handed a row or a collection of them.

presented() is what dispatch's present asks for a single value: one value and the call's PresentationContext. By default it is present(value), so a Presenter that reads nothing of the call overrides present() alone. One whose library renders under a context - the principal, a request a transport registered as a seed - overrides presented() and reads it there. A method of its own rather than a keyword on present(), so every Presenter written against present(value) is still one, and nothing reads a signature to decide whether to pass the context.

presented_rows() is what it asks for a list: every row it presents at once - a transport serving one page has already sliced the result, so the page's rows - and the same context. By default it is presented() per row, so only a Presenter that batches something over the rows overrides it: one lookup for every row on the page rather than one per row, or a library whose list rendering takes the collection.

Sync-only. Presenting a row that reads a relation is a query, and the kernel cannot tell in advance whether the row was prefetched, so the async path runs every Presenter in the executor. An async def present, presented or presented_rows is refused when the spec is built, and an answer from any of the three that is still to be awaited is refused where it is read.

docs.title: output abstractmethod
docs.text:
output() -> Output

What present returns, as a declaration. Never queries.

docs.title: present abstractmethod
docs.text:
present(value: Any) -> Any

One value to JSON-like data. May query; never async def.

docs.title: presented
docs.text:
presented(value: Any, context: PresentationContext | None) -> Any

One value to JSON-like data, for the call context describes: present(value).

context is None for a result dispatch did not build, such as a DispatchResult a transport constructed itself.

docs.title: presented_rows
docs.text:
presented_rows(values: Sequence[Any], context: PresentationContext | None) -> list[Any]

Every row of a list to JSON-like data, in one call: presented() per row.

values is a tuple of the rows being presented, already evaluated, so it can be walked as often as a batched lookup needs. Return a list with one presented value per row, in the order given: a selector spec's affordances are added to each presented row by its position, so dispatch's present refuses an answer that is not a list or whose length differs from values. context is the one every row of the result shares, as presented() receives it.

docs.title: PresentationContext dataclass
docs.text:
The principal a call ran for, its target, its seeds, its context and its shapes.

The output-side counterpart of ValidationContext. Dispatch builds one per call and carries it on the DispatchResult, and present hands it to Presenter.presented() with every value it presents, so a library that renders under a context - a field defaulting to the current user, a link built from the request - can read the call it is rendering for.

  • principal is who the call ran for.
  • target is the row or the queryset a service spec resolved, None for a create and for a selector spec, whose rows are the value itself.
  • ambient is the call's base pool, read-only at its top level: user, progress and every registered seed, such as an HTTP adapter's request. Its values are the call's own live objects, so a presenter must not mutate them (test_a_selector_spec_s_rows_are_each_presented_with_the_call_s_context holds both halves). Never an argument, a validated value or a provider's key.
  • call_context is the call's context, the one plain dict the transport created for its scope and every stage that declares it received, as on ValidationContext: the Validator, the service and the presenter share one object, so a presenter - and a nested one handed the same context - reuses what an earlier stage put there. It is the presenter's to read and write; the kernel writes nothing to it. A context built by hand gets an empty dict of its own. Its "transport" key, where set, names the transport serving the call ("agent", "http", "mcp"): a family convention the kernel neither sets nor checks, so read it with .get.
  • shapes is what the caller sent for the spec's declared shapes, the arguments that shape the output - which fields, a query over the rows - by name, read-only. An argument the caller left out is absent rather than None. Empty for a spec that declares none and for a context built by hand; no other argument is ever here. Under dispatch it is also the pool's shapes seed, so a selector naming shapes reads what the presenter reads.

docs.title: Output dataclass
docs.text:
The ordered fields of an operation's output, read without rendering anything.

Readers that never render: an agent tool's output schema, a capability manifest, a command's table header when there are no rows, a confirmation page's target display. Ordered, because a table's columns are, and the order is declaration order.

Paired with Parameters: that is what goes in, this is what comes out.

docs.title: names
docs.text:
names() -> tuple[str, ...]

Every field name, in declaration order.

docs.title: get
docs.text:
get(name: str) -> OutputField | None

The field declared as name, or None.

docs.title: OutputField dataclass
docs.text:
One field of an operation's output, declared without rendering anything.

The output-side counterpart of Parameter, carrying what a reader needs that names and types alone do not give:

  • label: a readable header. Libraries disagree here (one invents Id from id, others give nothing), so the adapter supplies what its library has and None means it has none.
  • choices: value-and-display pairs, because a table shows the display and a schema states it as a title, and a bare value list gives neither.
  • always_present: whether the key is in every rendered row. A rendering rule rather than a type - one library drops a read-only key it cannot read where another always emits it - so the adapter supplies it, and a schema lists only always-present keys as required. The schema of a spec declaring shapes requires none of a row's keys, whatever this says.
  • marking: how an agent audience is shown the field.

fields and items describe a nested object and an array's element, and items_nullable whether a null may stand in for an element, as on Parameter.

type is one of the JSON types, or any for a value whose JSON type is open - a computed field, a JSON column - which a schema then describes with no type at all rather than as a string it may not be. As on Parameter, any lists no choices, since a list of values says what type they are, and an array of any element declares no items rather than items="any".

json_schema_extra carries the JSON Schema keywords no field of an OutputField spells, as on Parameter: a mapping of keyword to value, held as a deep copy of its own, which output_schema adds to this field's node. A keyword a field states there is refused here, naming the field, whether or not this field sets it: type, format, items, the choices' enum, oneOf and const, title from label, and properties and required from fields; so is a value JSON cannot carry. It describes what the presenter renders and constrains nothing. Out of the hash and in equality, as on Parameter.

docs.title: FieldMarking dataclass
docs.text:
How one output field is presented to an agent audience.

Carried on the OutputField it marks, so it belongs to the declaration of what an operation returns rather than to whichever library rendered it. That is what lets a transport's projection for an audience work over a dataclass, a pydantic model and a DRF serializer alike: each adapter reads its own library's declaration into Output, marking included, and the projection reads only Output.

Applied only for a caller that names an audience: audience_projection_for_spec reads the markings into an AudienceProjection, which present_for_audience applies to the presented value and spec_output_schema to the schema. A caller that names none, which is every HTTP response, is presented every field whatever its marking.

The marking lives on the field, not in a list beside the output. That is what lets it travel into a nested output with no hoisting rule, and what stops a rename from silently desyncing it from a name the parent maintains.

docs.title: description class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
description: str | None = None

Audience-facing description, replacing the field's help text for this audience only.

Help text is shared with every human reader, so it cannot say "opaque handle, never read this out". This can, without changing a word of what a human reader sees.

docs.title: formatter class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
formatter: ValueFormatter | None = None

How this field's value is rendered for an agent audience, if not verbatim.

A ValueFormatter transforms the value and declares the JSON type it produces, so the payload and the schema move together. Unset, the default, changes nothing.

An explicit formatter wins over the substitution of a choice's display, which is a real collision: a status field can have choices and still be something an author wants spelled their own way. Only one transform can apply, and the one written by hand is the one that was asked for; a derived default losing to an explicit declaration is the ordinary direction.

HANDLE suppresses it, exactly as it suppresses choice substitution: a handle is another tool's input, and a formatted machine identifier is a broken one. Declaring both is honoured as HANDLE and the formatter never runs. A field a second tool takes as input therefore wants handle, or that tool receives a display string its own input schema rejects.

docs.title: handle classmethod
docs.text:
handle(description: str | None = None) -> FieldMarking

An opaque identifier: passed to other tools, never spoken to a user.

docs.title: hidden classmethod
docs.text:
hidden() -> FieldMarking

Plumbing: dropped from the projected payload and the projected schema.

docs.title: label classmethod
docs.text:
label(description: str | None = None) -> FieldMarking

The field that names this record for a human.

docs.title: formatted classmethod
docs.text:
formatted(formatter: ValueFormatter, description: str | None = None) -> FieldMarking

Ordinary content, rendered through formatter.

The generic constructor: any transform that declares what it produces. timestamp is one of these with the formatter filled in, and a field that is both formatted and something else - a formatted label, say - is written as FieldMarking(FieldAudience.LABEL, formatter=...).

docs.title: timestamp classmethod
docs.text:
timestamp(fmt: str | None = None, description: str | None = None) -> FieldMarking

A date-time read as a formatted local string rather than raw ISO-8601.

due_at: Annotated[datetime, FieldMarking.timestamp()]

The zone is Django's active one and cannot be passed here; fmt is a strftime string and defaults to a day-first, 24-hour rendering. ValueFormatter.timestamp holds the transform and the reasoning behind both of those.

docs.title: AudienceProjection dataclass
docs.text:
How one operation's output is shaped for an agent audience.

Read off the FieldMarkings and the choices an Output declares, by audience_projection_for_spec. Nothing here depends on the value being presented, so a transport builds it once, where it registers the spec, and passes it to every present_for_audience and spec_output_schema rather than reading the declaration again per call.

One projection drives both project_payload and annotate_output_schema, which is what keeps the advertised schema describing the payload sent.

docs.title: fields class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
fields: Mapping[str, FieldMarking] = field(default_factory=dict)

Every explicitly marked field, by name. Unmarked fields are absent.

docs.title: label class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
label: str | None = None

The field naming this record for a human, if one is marked.

docs.title: choice_labels class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
choice_labels: Mapping[str, Mapping[Any, str]] = field(default_factory=dict)

Per field with choices, the {value: display} pairs whose display differs from the value. Absent for a field whose displays only repeat its values.

docs.title: nested class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
nested: Mapping[str, AudienceProjection] = field(default_factory=dict)

Child projections, by field name, for a nested object and for the objects of an array.

docs.title: is_empty
docs.text:
is_empty() -> bool

True when applying this projection would change nothing.

The fast path: an unmarked output with no labelled choices anywhere costs a caller one boolean rather than a walk of the payload.

A value formatter needs no term of its own: it is carried by a marking, so an output that declares one has a non-empty fields already. A term that can never be the deciding one goes stale without failing.

One or-chain, so each term is held by its own case of test_each_term_alone_makes_it_non_empty.

docs.title: audience
docs.text:
audience(name: str) -> FieldAudience

The audience declared for name, defaulting to CONTENT.

docs.title: formatter
docs.text:
formatter(name: str) -> ValueFormatter | None

The formatter that applies to name, or None.

None for a HANDLE however the two were declared together: a handle is another tool's input and a formatted machine identifier is a broken one. The suppression lives here rather than in each walk, so the payload and the schema cannot end up formatting different fields, which is the one failure the projection exists to make impossible.

docs.title: audience_projection_for_spec
docs.text:
audience_projection_for_spec(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    *,
    overrides: Mapping[str, FieldMarking] | None = None,
    name: str | None = None,
) -> AudienceProjection

Resolve the markings on the Output spec presents.

The output is spec.output(): a selector spec's presenter's, or a service spec's own presenter's, or its output selector's when it declares none. A transport that registers its tools up front calls this once per spec and hands the result to present_for_audience and spec_output_schema, so the payload it sends and the schema it advertises are projected by one declaration.

Each OutputField contributes its marking, its choices whose display differs from the value, and, for an object's fields or an array's items declared as an Output, a child projection when the child has anything to project. A spec with no output yields an empty projection rather than an error: there is nothing to mark up.

overrides layers a mount's own markings over the declaration's, for the one case the declaration cannot express: a mount that needs what its sibling hides. The declaration stays authoritative, and an override is the exception rather than a second place to declare an audience. Only the top-level markings and the label move; the choices and the children come from the declaration. name identifies the mount in the refusal below.

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

Two fields of one output are both marked LABEL, whether the declaration says so or an override does. A record has one name, and picking one silently would name it by whichever came first.

docs.title: project_payload
docs.text:
project_payload(payload: Any, projection: AudienceProjection) -> Any

Drop plumbing, speak choice displays and format values, at any depth.

Three changes, each driven by the declaration that shapes the schema in annotate_output_schema, so the two cannot disagree:

  • fields marked HIDDEN are removed. Removed rather than moved under some reserved key: a payload a model reads is read in full either way, so moving a field costs its keys again and hides nothing. What an agent must never use should not be there.
  • a field's choice value is replaced by its display, so a person is not read PENDING_REVIEW. Not on a HANDLE, which another tool takes as input. An array of choices is substituted member by member rather than looked up whole.
  • a field whose marking carries a ValueFormatter is rendered through it: a date-time read as a local date-time rather than raw ISO-8601, an amount with its currency. It wins over the choice display, being the transform an author wrote by hand, and over a nested output's projection. Also not on a HANDLE, for the same reason, and a null is never formatted.

A payload that is neither an object nor a list of them is returned as it is, and so is every key the projection has nothing to say about, including one a transport added beside the declared fields.

Apply this where a payload becomes an agent's answer, not where it feeds the next step of a chain, which still needs the handles. Returns a new payload and never modifies payload.

docs.title: annotate_output_schema
docs.text:
annotate_output_schema(
    schema: dict[str, Any] | None,
    projection: AudienceProjection,
    *,
    handle_description: str | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any] | None

Apply to a schema the projection project_payload applies to the payload.

Four changes, each the mirror of one the payload undergoes:

  • hidden properties are removed, and dropped from required, which is left out when nothing in it remains;
  • a marking's description becomes the property's "description", so a handle says what it is for in the schema a model reads without that wording reaching any other reader;
  • a field with labelled choices is restated in its displays, because that is what the projected payload carries: an enum's values are replaced, and a oneOf's consts are, each losing the title that annotated the value it now equals. A "type" stated beside them is restated as the types of the values now listed, so a display string is never described as the integer it replaced, with "null" named last where the stated type admitted it and a null is still served - not where the choices give None a display, which is served in its place - and left as written beside a oneOf entry that admits more than its constants. A display two values share is listed once, so a row served it matches one oneOf entry rather than two, and an array of such choices no longer claims uniqueItems. Not on a HANDLE, which keeps its values on both sides: a field another tool takes as input should be marked one.
  • a formatted field is restated as the type its ValueFormatter says it produces, plus whatever that declaration adds about the shape of the produced value, in place of everything the property said about the value before, choices included. Its title and description are kept, and so is a null the property admitted - however it stated one, as a type, an anyOf member, None in an enum or a oneOf entry for a labelled choice - since a null is never formatted. The type is written from produces rather than taken from the fragment, so a renderer cannot contradict its own advertisement, and a fragment's enum lists the null too, and its const becomes an enum of that value and a null, where the property admitted one. Not on a HANDLE either.

Generating both sides from one declaration is the point: a schema that advertises a field the payload no longer carries is worse than either behaviour on its own.

handle_description is the wording for a HANDLE whose marking declares none, and defaults to nothing. Telling a reader what to do with an identifier is advice for one kind of reader, and the kernel does not know which kind is reading. The transport that knows its audience supplies the sentence.

Takes the item schema; an array's items are annotated and the array kept. A caller wrapping items in an envelope of its own annotates the item and wraps it afterwards, as spec_output_schema does. None, or a projection with nothing in it, returns schema itself; anything else returns a new schema and never modifies schema.

docs.title: spec_input_schema
docs.text:
spec_input_schema(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    *,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
) -> dict[str, Any]

parameters_schema over spec.parameters().

The whole argument set dispatch checks: a selector spec's reads and shapes, or a service spec's target selector's reads, its own, its shapes, then its Validator's parameters. A many service spec's is its reads, its shapes and the one list its many_argument names, each row an object of the Validator's parameters. A shape is an argument like any other here, closed set included, though only the presenter reads it. Pass the unknown_arguments the transport dispatches with, because the schema closes the argument set exactly when dispatch does.

A partial spec's Validator parameters are required nowhere, at any depth - an object's fields and an array's rows included - because dispatch refuses none of them absent: a client reading required would otherwise never send the partial call the spec exists for. Its reads and its target selector's keep their required, as dispatch keeps them, so the schema still says which row a partial update names. On a many spec the list stays required and its rows' fields are not. parameters() itself is unchanged and still says what a whole call needs. Nothing else is relaxed: a read a kwargs provider fills or may fill is listed as declared, required meaning the call needs the value from someone - the caller, or a provider that may fill it - and server_owned_keys is how a transport finds the keys a provider fills; provider_keys gives the ones it may decline, or None for a provider that names none. A reflected read and a Validator field named like a registered seed are listed as declared too. Nor is anything a transport binds or withholds: this takes no ServerArguments, and a transport subtracts its names() in the schema it builds, as it subtracts server_owned_keys.

Read on every call, as parameters() is, so a Validator reading a model-backed declaration is asked only once the app registry is ready.

docs.title: spec_output_schema
docs.text:
spec_output_schema(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    *,
    paginate: bool = False,
    projection: AudienceProjection | None = None,
    handle_description: str | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any] | None

The JSON Schema of what present returns for spec.

None when spec.output() is None: a spec with no presenter declares nothing about what it returns, and a shape invented for it would be a guess every client then trusts. A SpecSource is described as the spec it compiles to.

Otherwise the item's output_schema, shaped by what dispatch returns for this kind of spec:

  • A LIST selector spec, or a service spec whose output selector is a LIST, presents every row: {"type": "array", "items": <item>}.
  • A RETRIEVE selector spec with allow_none presents None for a missing row, so the item's type gains "null". Without allow_none a missing row is not-found, which a transport answers in its own terms and never presents, so the item stays as it is.
  • A service spec whose output selector is a RETRIEVE gains "null" whatever its allow_none says: once the service has run, a re-read that finds nothing is None rather than not-found, because reporting not-found would tell the caller a committed write did not happen.
  • A many service spec with no output selector, or a returns_many one, which never has one, presents the rows its service returned as {"type": "array", "items": <item>}, never paged, which gains "null" when the spec declares allow_none.
  • A service spec with no output selector presents what the service returned, described by its presenter as the item, which gains "null" when the spec declares allow_none. Undeclared, a None is not stated and the item stays strict: whether a service may return one is not otherwise in its declaration.

Where "null" is admitted is can_present_nothing's answer, which a transport writing a schema of its own asks too.

paginate describes a list served one page at a time, as paginate_output and OutputPage.envelope shape it: {"items": [...], "page": n, "totalPages": n, "hasNext": b}, every key required. It changes only a list's schema, since one row has no pages, so a transport may pass it for every spec it serves paged.

projection describes what present_for_audience hands back rather than what present does, through annotate_output_schema: hidden fields left out, labelled choices restated in their displays, and a marking's wording as a field's "description". It lands on the item, wherever the item sits, because the array and the paging envelope are this function's own shapes and belong to no Output. Omit it, as every caller naming no audience does, and the schema is the full declaration. handle_description is the wording for a handle whose marking declares none, and defaults to none: what a reader should do with an identifier depends on the reader, and the transport is what knows.

A spec declaring shapes promises no field of a row. A shape reaches the presenter alone, and a fields selection there leaves keys out, which nothing in the presenter's declaration can say for every value a caller may send. So the item lists no required at any depth, wherever it sits, while the affordances object dispatch adds to each row and the paging envelope keep theirs. A spec declaring none is described with the required its presenter's always_present states.

docs.title: parameters_schema
docs.text:
parameters_schema(
    parameters: Parameters,
    *,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
) -> dict[str, Any]

The JSON Schema object an argument set must satisfy, read from parameters.

One dialect whichever library declared the parameters, because every adapter reads its library into Parameters and this reads only that. The policy is precise: never false, and not incomplete where the declaration knows. What it still leaves out is what a Parameter does not carry.

  • An object is {"type": "object", "properties": {...}}, with "required" listing, in declaration order, the names the shape check refuses when absent - a required parameter with no declared default, since one with a default is not refused - and left out when there are none.
  • "additionalProperties": false is emitted under REJECT only, and at exactly the levels check_arguments closes: the top, every object parameter that declares fields, and every row of an array whose items are Parameters - an empty declaration included, since it refuses every key. Under IGNORE an undeclared key is accepted and dropped, so stating false there would refuse a call that runs.
  • An object parameter with no fields is {"type": "object"}: what is still known, constraining nothing a valid call could fail. It is also the node an adapter truncates a recursive declaration to.
  • An array is {"type": "array", "items": ...}: a type name's {"type": t}, the object schema of its rows, or {} for an array that declares no items and accepts any element. The array's format and bounds describe each element, so they go on items, as its choices do: a CSV number filter's are {"type": "string", "format": "decimal", "minimum": -1e+50, "maximum": 1e+50}.
  • A file is {}. No JSON value is one, so any JSON type stated here would be false, and JSON Schema has no keyword for a multipart part. What is still known is the rest: whether it is required, its "description". An array of files has {} for its items.
  • An any is {} too, since every JSON value is one; its "default" and "description" are stated as on any other node.
  • A scalar is {"type": t} with its "format" when it declares one. A decimal is therefore {"type": "string", "format": "decimal"}: the form every decimal validator reads without a binary float's rounding. The shape check also accepts a JSON number, which this does not advertise. An identifier is {"type": "string", "format": "uuid"}, JSON Schema's own format name, and the shape check refuses a string that spells no UUID.
  • An array's length is "minItems" as declared, and "maxItems" as in force: the declared max_length, or where none is declared the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting's, 1000 unless the project sets another. The shape check refuses past it either way, so a client told nothing would send a call that cannot run; under a setting of None an array that declares no maximum states none.
  • Bounds are "minimum" and "maximum", inclusive, as declared. JSON Schema applies them to a number instance only, so on a decimal string a validating client enforces neither; the shape check does, and they tell a reader where the line is.
  • Nullable makes the type [t, "null"], on objects and arrays too, and items_nullable does the same to an array's items. A file's node and an any's state no type, so they admit null already and gain nothing; a non-nullable one's null is refused by the shape check alone.
  • Choices are an "enum" beside the "type" the parameter declares. On an array they go on items, because the shape check applies them to each element. A nullable parameter's enum gains None when its choices do not list it, since an enum claims the whole set of accepted values. An array's items do so by items_nullable alone, whether or not the array itself may be null.
  • Labelled choices are an "anyOf" of {"const": value, "title": label} in its place, where some label says more than its value does; labels that only repeat their values keep the "enum". A choice with no label is a bare {"const": value}. A None is {"type": "null"} instead, titled when it is labelled, and so is the None a nullable parameter gains. A choice declared twice is listed once, so the entries are disjoint and each value has one title; True and 1 are two values to JSON, although Python finds them equal. anyOf rather than oneOf, which admits the same values over disjoint entries: an OpenAI strict schema refuses oneOf, and Gemini refuses it too, where pydantic-ai rewrites it only on a node with no "type". And {"type": "null"} rather than {"const": null}, which Google's transform empties into {}, a schema every value matches. A title is str() of the label, so a lazy one is rendered in the language active now, and it constrains nothing.
  • A default is emitted when one is declared and survives JSON encoding; a Decimal, a date or a callable is left out rather than misstated. So is a choice set holding such a value, since listing only some of the accepted values would be false.
  • help becomes "description".
  • json_schema_extra joins the parameter's node last, at any depth: the keywords the declaration has no field for, such as a pattern or a string's maxLength. The Parameter refused every keyword a field states here when it was declared, a custom format included, so the extra never restates or contradicts the declaration. What it states is advertised and not enforced by the shape check; it holds where the spec's Validator enforces it.

Nothing else, deliberately. No title on a property, because a Parameter has no label of its own; a title is only ever a choice's. No $defs or $ref ever: most MCP clients refuse a schema with a reference in it, so every schema is flat and self-contained, however deep the declaration nests. No $schema key, which a transport adds if its wire wants one. And no bound the shape check does not enforce (maxLength, a Validator's max_value) unless a json_schema_extra states it, for a Validator that enforces it. The one stated without being declared is an array's default maximum, because the shape check enforces it.

Every call builds a new schema, so a transport may add its own keys to the result without reaching the declaration or another transport's copy. Defaults, choice values and json_schema_extra values are placed in it as declared, not copied.

unknown_arguments accepts the policy's plain value as well, and a value that is neither, or the kept PASSTHROUGH member, raises ValueError here rather than quietly describing one policy or the other.

docs.title: output_schema
docs.text:
output_schema(output: Output) -> dict[str, Any]

The JSON Schema object of one presented item, read from output.

One item: whether the operation returns a list of them, or may return None instead, is the spec's to say, and spec_output_schema wraps this accordingly. The dialect is the input side's, with the differences a description of what came back needs:

  • An object is {"type": "object", "properties": {...}}, with "required" listing the fields whose always_present is true, in declaration order, and left out when there are none. required says the key is there, not that its value is non-null.
  • No additionalProperties. Output is not a closed set a caller can get wrong, and a transport may add keys of its own to what it sends.
  • A field states its type, [t, "null"] when nullable, its "format" when it declares one, and "title" from its label when it has one. Adapters set a label only where the author wrote one, so a title is never a field name restated in worse English. Its json_schema_extra joins the node last, holding only keywords no field states, since the field refused the rest when it was declared. An any field states no type, nullable or not, since {} admits every value and the null with it.
  • Nesting is as on input: fields make an object schema, an object with none is {"type": "object"}, and an array's items are {"type": t}, a nested item's object schema, or {} when undeclared. items_nullable makes the item's type [t, "null"].
  • Choices are (value, display) pairs. When every display is just str(value) they are an "enum" of the values, since a title restating the constant teaches nothing. Otherwise they are a "oneOf" of {"const": value, "title": display}, so the human phrasing travels with each value; title constrains nothing, and the accepted set stays exactly the constants. The "type" is stated either way. A nullable field adds None ({"const": None} in a oneOf) when its choices do not list it, because both forms claim the whole set of values. On an array the choices describe each element and go on items, widened by items_nullable rather than the array's own nullability. A choice set holding a value JSON cannot carry is left out whole.

marking is not emitted, and a HIDDEN field is described here like any other: this is the whole declaration, which is what a caller naming no audience is presented. Showing a field to an agent audience, or leaving it out, is a projection over this schema, which annotate_output_schema applies and spec_output_schema composes for a caller that passes one.

As on input: no $defs or $ref, no $schema key, and a new schema on every call.

docs.title: can_present_nothing
docs.text:
can_present_nothing(spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource) -> bool

Whether a successful dispatch of spec may present None as its result.

The question an output schema answers before it admits "null", asked in one place so that spec_output_schema and every transport advertising an output schema of its own give the same answer:

  • A SelectorSpec: a RETRIEVE declaring allow_none, which presents None for a missing row. Without allow_none a missing row is not-found, which a transport answers in its own terms and never presents. A LIST presents its rows, [] for none, and never None, whatever allow_none says.
  • A ServiceSpec with an output_selector_spec: a RETRIEVE re-read, whatever allow_none says, because once the service has run a re-read that finds nothing is None rather than not-found, and reporting not-found would tell the caller a committed write did not happen. A LIST re-read presents rows and never None.
  • Any other ServiceSpec presents the service's own return, and answers its own allow_none. That is a declaration rather than an observation: an undeclared None is still presented, against a schema that does not admit it.

many and returns_many are not read. Each decides whether the result is a list of what the service returned, not whether it may be None: a None return from either is presented as None too, so its allow_none answers as any other service's, and a many spec's re-read answers by its kind as above. returns_many is refused beside a re-read, so it never has one.

It answers whether None may come back, not whether a schema exists: a spec with no presenter has no output schema to widen, whatever this says.

A SpecSource answers as the spec it compiles to, never by attributes of its own that share these names: its kinds are another library's, and none of them is this one's RETRIEVE.

docs.title: DataclassValidator
docs.text:
Bases: Validator

A Validator whose declaration is a standard-library dataclass.

The reference adapter: what any adapter owes the kernel, done with nothing but the standard library and Django. parameters() reads the fields and their annotations; validate() decodes JSON-like arguments into those types and builds the instance, nested dataclasses included.

The annotations it reads, and what each declares:

  • str, int, float, bool: their JSON types. float takes an integer as well, since JSON writes 2.0 as 2; nothing else crosses types, so true is not an int. An integer past a float's range is refused as no number, in the words the shape check refuses a non-finite one in, since no finite float stands for it.
  • Decimal, datetime, date: a string, with the format it decodes from. A decimal takes a JSON number too, as every decimal validator does, and an integer exactly, whatever its digits.
  • X | None: nullable. Inside a list, list[X | None], it is the element that is, declared as items_nullable and not as the array's own nullability.
  • Literal[...] and an Enum (Django's TextChoices and IntegerChoices included): choices, of the JSON type the values share. An Enum decodes to the member.
  • list[X]: an array; list[SomeDataclass] is an array of rows, each declared as nested Parameters. For any other element, Parameter.items holds its JSON type, and what else describes the element is declared on the array, where it constrains each element: a list of choices declares them there, and list[Decimal] the decimal format, so each element is read as a scalar decimal is, a JSON number included, and a query string's ?prices=1.5,2.25 is two of them. A list of dates or date-times is an array of strings, since an element takes no other format, and is decoded here.
  • A list declares no length, since a dataclass has no way to state one, so the shape check in front of this Validator holds it to the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting, 1000 by default. A list a caller may send more of is declared with a Validator that states its length, such as a pydantic model's Field(max_length=...), or under a larger setting.
  • a dataclass: an object, with its own fields as nested Parameters.
  • X | UnsetType: the argument may be left out, with or without a default, and the field then holds UNSET rather than a value a service would act on. It adds no JSON type, since no wire can send it.

A field with a default, or a default_factory, is optional, and one with neither is required. Only a plain default is reported as the Parameter's default: a factory's value is computed per instance, so it is not a declaration a transport could print. A field declared init=False is the dataclass's to compute, so it is neither taken nor returned. Annotated is looked through, and an annotation outside this list is refused with ImproperlyConfigured naming the field, never read as a string.

A row that updates must declare its key. A relation write matches an incoming row to an existing one by its primary key, so a row dataclass used for an update needs pk: int | None = None: present for a row that exists, absent for a new one. Without it no incoming row matches an existing one, and every update replaces every row. Nothing fails when that happens, which is why it is written down here.

Time zones follow Django's forms, not pydantic: an offset-less date-time is made aware in the current time zone when USE_TZ is on, so a date-time means the same thing whichever library validated it.

Every failure is reported, not the first, as one InvalidArguments whose detail is addressed by path: {"books": {1: {"title": [...]}}} for a field inside the second row, only the rows that failed, and a message about a row itself under non_field_errors inside it. A ValueError or Django ValidationError raised by the dataclass's own __post_init__ is a message about that object, and lands there too.

It is correct without the shape check in front of it, for a caller that uses it directly: a wrong JSON type is a refusal, not a crash, and an argument no field declares is refused as the dataclass's own constructor would refuse it.

The annotations are read on first use rather than at construction, for the reason a spec's parameters are: specs are built at import time, and an annotation may name a class its module cannot resolve yet.

docs.title: parameters
docs.text:
parameters() -> Parameters

The dataclass's __init__ fields, as Parameters. Never queries.

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
