validate(arguments: Mapping[str, Any], context: ValidationContext) -> dict[str, Any]

The built instance's __init__ fields, by name, or InvalidArguments.

Nested values stay dataclass instances, which is what the mutation helpers read a row from. A partial call is refused: see validated().

docs.title: validated
docs.text:
validated(arguments: Mapping[str, Any], context: ValidationContext) -> Validated

The built instance as the call's data, and its __init__ fields as the values.

A service declaring data receives the instance, typed as the dataclass; one declaring the fields by name receives them. The values are the instance's own attributes, so data.title and title are one object.

A partial call is refused with ImproperlyConfigured, because a dataclass instance holds every field and a partial call may leave any out. Building one anyway would mean a value the field's annotation does not admit standing in for each field not sent, or no instance and no __post_init__ at all. A field an update may leave out is declared X | UnsetType, which every call honours; a spec whose calls are partial uses a Validator that can return only what was sent. supports_partial is False, so a ServiceSpec declaring partial=True over this Validator is refused when it is built, and this refusal answers only a caller using it directly.

docs.title: DataclassPresenter
docs.text:
Bases: Presenter

An operation's output declared as a dataclass, rendered from any object.

output() reads the fields and annotations the way DataclassValidator does, so one dataclass declares the same types going in and coming out.

present(value) reads each declared field by attribute, so the value may be an instance of the dataclass or anything carrying the same names: a model row is the case this is for, and it is never converted into the dataclass first. A nested dataclass field is read the same way off the attribute's value, and a list field may be a related manager, read through .all() so a prefetch is used when there is one. Encoding is JSON's: a Decimal as its string, a datetime or date in ISO 8601, an Enum as its value.

A field whose value is UNSET is left out of the rendered object, and only a field whose annotation admits UnsetType is declared as possibly absent (always_present=False). Labels are None: a dataclass has no label of its own, and a reader can title-case a name as well as an adapter.

Choices are (value, display) pairs. A Django Choices enum supplies its label, translated when output() is called; a plain Enum or a Literal has no display of its own, so the value's str stands in.

A FieldMarking is declared on the field it marks, in its annotation: id: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()].

docs.title: output
docs.text:
output() -> Output

The dataclass's fields as an Output, in declaration order. Never queries.

docs.title: present
docs.text:
present(value: Any) -> Any

One value's declared fields, read by attribute and encoded to JSON-like data.

None is presented as None: it is JSON's null, not a row whose every attribute is missing.

docs.title: FormValidator
docs.text:
Bases: Validator

A Validator whose declaration is a Django form class.

parameters() reads the form's class-level fields, base_fields, in declaration order; validate() binds the arguments to a new form and returns what it cleaned. Every rule the form states stays the form's to enforce - its fields' validators, clean_<field>(), clean() and, on a ModelForm, the model's own validation and uniqueness checks - and the shape check in front of it enforces what the declaration can see.

The fields it reads, and what each declares, the first match winning:

  • BooleanField and NullBooleanField: a boolean.
  • DecimalField: a string in the decimal format, which takes a JSON number as well, and an integer whatever its digits. FloatField: a number, and an integer past a float's range is refused as the field refuses an infinity, invalid in its own words. IntegerField: an integer. On a ModelForm, a value the form cleans to an integer past the range of the model's integer column is refused in the words and with the code of the validator Django's model field carries from 5.0, max_value or min_value, before a uniqueness check or a constraint queries with it: Django 4.2 states no range for SQLite, whose driver raises OverflowError for one. It is judged where Django 5.0 and later judge it, after the field, its clean_<field>() and the form's clean(), so each of those answers first, and a value a clean_<field>() brings inside the range is taken. Only a column Django validates is judged: a value clean() sets for a column the form has no field for, and a field declared over a column Meta.fields leaves out or Meta.exclude names, are the form's, as Django never writes them onto the row.
  • DateTimeField and DateField: a string in the date-time or date format. TimeField and DurationField: a string.
  • ChoiceField: choices, with the empty choice dropped and option groups flattened. A plain one cleans with str and matches the string against each choice's str, so it takes a string and its choices are declared as strings, whatever type they were written in. A TypedChoiceField takes the JSON type all of its values share. A choice set given as a callable is computed per form and may query, so it is not read: the field is a string with no choices, which every choice field accepts, and the form checks the choice.
  • MultipleChoiceField and TypedMultipleChoiceField: an array of that, whose choices constrain each element.
  • ModelChoiceField: the JSON type of the model field it matches rows on - its to_field_name, or the primary key - and no choices, since they are rows and reading them would query. ModelMultipleChoiceField: an array of that, so one matching rows on a DecimalField takes an array of decimal strings, and a query string's ?rows=12.50,9.99 is two of them. Django matches each against the column's own spelling, so "12.50" names a row a two-place column holds and 12.5 names none. A date or a date-time key is an array of strings, since an element takes no other format. They validate to the row, and to a queryset of rows. A key past the range of the integer column rows are matched on names no row, and is refused as the field refuses a key no row holds, invalid_choice in its own words, before the form queries: Django hands a ModelMultipleChoiceField's keys to the database driver, which raises OverflowError for one, and so does a ModelChoiceField's on Django 4.2.
  • No choice field declares a length, since Django's have none, so the shape check in front of this Validator holds a list to the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting, 1000 by default.
  • any other CharField (email, URL, slug, UUID, regex, IP address): a string.
  • FileField and ImageField: a file, which no JSON caller can send. A multipart request carries one, and a Python caller hands a Django File; the form is bound with it as its files, where a file field reads, and the form's own checks run on it. A ContentFile built with no name is refused by the form, which needs one.
  • an optional file field whose widget is a ClearableFileInput, as a FileField's and an ImageField's are by default, declares its clear checkbox as well: a boolean named as the widget names it, <name>-clear, right after the file. Checked with no upload, the form cleans the field to False, its own value for a cleared file, which validate() returns under the field's name and a ModelForm writes as no file through the model field's save_form_data; checked beside an upload, the form refuses the pair. It is the only way to clear one, since null keeps the file a row holds and false is not a file. A required file field, or one whose widget has no checkbox, declares none, and a field named as a checkbox is refused.

Every choice field's choices carry their labels, as choice_labels, for a schema to show beside each value: the label Django displays, keyed by the value as the caller sends it, so a plain ChoiceField's are keyed by the string. A lazy label stays lazy until a schema renders it.

Refused with ImproperlyConfigured, naming the form, the field and its class: a JSONField, a MultiValueField such as SplitDateTimeField, a ComboField, any field the list does not cover, and a ModelChoiceField with no queryset or matching rows on a model field with no JSON type. The declaration is read at construction, so a form that cannot be described fails where the spec is written; nothing in it queries or needs a translation, so building a spec at import time is safe. help is the exception, and is read from help_text on each parameters() call, in the language active then.

What the Parameters say about presence is what the form does:

  • required is the field's own required. For a BooleanField that is a statement about presence too: an absent checkbox cleans to False, which a required one refuses, as it refuses false. A NullBooleanField is never required, whatever it says, because its validation is empty and it takes an absent value as None.
  • nullable is not required, and always true for a NullBooleanField. A form reads None as an empty value for every field, so an optional field takes null and cleans it to its empty value, and a required one refuses it. A clear checkbox is no field: it is optional and never null, since unchecked and absent are the one answer the widget reads.
  • default is always UNSET: a field's initial is what an unbound form displays, and a bound form cleans an absent optional field to its empty value, never to its initial.

The types are JSON's, and do not cross. A form reads its data as an HTML post's strings, so it also takes a value of another type through str - a number for a CharField, 1 for the choice "1" - and the shape check refuses one, as it does for every declaration: a caller sends the declared type. The empty choice is the other case: an optional choice field reads "" as no value, and a caller sends null for that instead.

An argument is in its wire form, which no locale touches. A number field reads a string through the active locale when it is localized, and under one whose thousands separator is a dot that reads "1.500" as fifteen hundred. So a string argument for an IntegerField, FloatField or DecimalField is bound as the Decimal it spells, which the field reads as the number it is, localized or not.

Declare the fields on the class. A field a form adds or changes in its own __init__ is not in base_fields, so it is not described, and under UnknownArguments.REJECT the closed argument set refuses its key before the form is built. A field declared disabled is not a parameter either: the form ignores what a caller sends for it and cleans its initial, which validate() returns with the rest on a whole call.

A partial call binds only the fields the caller sent. When the ValidationContext says partial, every field the arguments do not name is taken off the bound form before it validates, so it is neither required nor cleaned, and validate() returns no key for it: an absent BooleanField does not come back False, nor an absent CharField '', which an update would write over the row. A value that is sent is checked exactly as on a whole call, so a required field may be left out but not sent empty. A checked clear checkbox sends its file field, and an unchecked one is what an absent one is. On a ModelForm the fields left out keep the target's values, and each one's own model check skips them, as Django skips any model field a form does not have. Its uniqueness checks and constraints do not: they run over the row as it would be saved, what was sent on top of the target's values, leaving out only the model fields the form never declares, as a whole call does. So an update that sends one field of a unique_together pair or a UniqueConstraint and collides is refused as the whole call would be, under non_field_errors, rather than failing with an IntegrityError when the row is saved. That needs a target row: a partial call bound as a create checks only what was sent, since the rest would be the model's defaults, which nothing writes. clean() sees only what was sent, so it reads cleaned_data with get, as Django advises for a field that failed. parameters() is the same for both calls: required says what a whole call needs.

A ModelForm is bound to a copy of the target. When the ValidationContext carries a row of the form's model, the form is built with instance= a shallow copy of it, so its uniqueness checks exclude the row being updated. It is a copy because a ModelForm writes the cleaned values onto its instance while it validates: handed the target itself, it would change the row the service receives before the service runs, and a helper that saves only what changed, such as update_from_input, would find nothing to save. Any other target - the queryset a collection selector resolves, or none - binds the form as a create.

A form whose __init__ takes more is handed it by form_kwargs. It is a callable returning a mapping of extra constructor keywords, such as a queryset scoped by the caller's tenant, and it binds through the pool as a selector or a service does, naming what it wants: user, progress, every registered seed, and the target under the name the service receives it by, from the context's resolved: instance for a spec with an instance selector, None when one that allows none finds no row, collection for one with a collection selector, and neither for a create. It is the target itself, never the copy the form edits. user is the context's principal on every path, and progress is null_progress wherever the context carries no reporter. Off dispatch - bind_arguments, or a ValidationContext built by hand - the context holds no seeds, so a callable naming one gives it a default or meets Python's own TypeError. It is called on every validate(), on the thread the call runs on, which under adispatch is the one its synchronous phases share, so it may query; on a many call that is once per row, so a query belongs in a seed, which resolves once per call. What it returns is passed beside data, files and instance, and returning one of those three, for a plain form as for a ModelForm, is refused with ImproperlyConfigured naming it, as is returning anything but a mapping. parameters() still reads only the class: a field __init__ adds from those keywords is not a parameter. The callable is kept as form_kwargs, so a transport building the form itself, for a page, builds it the same way.

A refusal is one InvalidArguments carrying the form's own errors and messages, {field: [messages]}, with the form-wide ones Django keeps under "__all__" moved to non_field_errors, the key every other refusal uses. An argument no field declares is ignored by the form, as Django ignores any key it has no field for: the closed argument set in front of it is what refuses one.

docs.title: parameters
docs.text:
parameters() -> Parameters

The form's class-level fields, in declaration order, as Parameters. Never queries.

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
validate(arguments: Mapping[str, Any], context: ValidationContext) -> dict[str, Any]

The form's cleaned_data, or InvalidArguments carrying its errors.

A ModelChoiceField cleans to the row and a ModelMultipleChoiceField to a queryset, which is what the service receives. On a partial call, only the fields the caller sent are bound, and so only those are returned; a ModelForm's uniqueness checks still read the whole row, as the class docstring says.

docs.title: filter_set_parameters
docs.text:
filter_set_parameters(filter_set: Any) -> Parameters

The arguments a FilterSet reads, as the Parameters a caller sends.

This is what lets a filter be a read like any other: the schema describes it, the closed argument set admits it, the shape check judges it and each transport accepts it, all from the declaration rather than from django-filter. SelectorSpec puts these after its own reads.

Named as django-filter reads them, because a Parameter describes what a caller sends and the FilterSet is what receives it. A range filter (RangeFilter, DateFromToRangeFilter and the rest) reads one key per bound - price_min and price_max, joined_after and joined_before - so it is one Parameter per bound, never an object called price that no FilterSet reads. A CSV filter (BaseInFilter, BaseRangeFilter) reads one key holding several values, and is an array; its widget takes a list as it takes "1,2". A choice filter offers its values, flattened out of any group, as integer when every value is an int and otherwise as the strings Django's ChoiceField compares; a choice set built by a callable, and a related row's key, offer only string. Every other filter is its scalar: boolean, a date or date-time string, and string for the rest. A number filter, and each bound of a numeric range, is a decimal string, because its form field is a DecimalField and reads one exactly, where a float read on the way loses a key past 2**53; a JSON number is still taken. So is each value of a CSV number filter: an array whose format and bounds describe each element, as its choices would, so a fraction keeps every digit it was sent with and ?pks=1,2 still splits over HTTP, since no decimal holds a comma. Each decimal is bounded, minimum=-1e50 and maximum=1e50, a CSV filter's values each: the line django-filter's number filter draws above, drawn below too and on a range's bounds, which it leaves open. A value past it is refused by the shape check, at its index in a CSV filter's list, before it reaches the database's integer conversion, which builds every digit of "1E+999999999".

Every one is optional, because a filter narrows a read and never stands between a caller and it. help is the author's help_text when there is one; otherwise it says what the filter matches when the argument's name does not (min_pk is pk with gte), and for a bound, which bound of which field it is.

Two filters that read one key - a range joined and a filter called joined_after - are refused, as any two Parameters of one name are, because django-filter would hand one value to both.

An object whose base_filters is missing, empty or None declares nothing, and is read without django-filter. A SelectorSpec refuses one as its filter_set unless it is a django-filter FilterSet class, since none of the caller's data would be handed to it. Reading any filter needs the [filter] extra.

docs.title: Pydantic adapters
docs.text: Installed with the pydantic extra and imported from django_service_specs.adapters.pydantic.

docs.title: PydanticValidator
docs.text:
Bases: Validator

A Validator whose declaration is a pydantic model.

parameters() reads the model's fields into Parameters, and validate() hands the arguments to the model: pydantic builds the instance, nested models included, and its own validators run as they would for any other caller.

The annotations are read as DataclassValidator reads them, from one shared table, so a model and a dataclass declaring the same field declare the same parameter: str, int, float, bool; Decimal, datetime and date as strings with their format; X | None as nullable; Literal[...] and an Enum as choices; Annotated looked through; and list[X] of any of these, where list[X | None] makes the element nullable and not the array and list[Decimal] declares each element a decimal. On top of those:

  • a list's length, however the model states it - Field(min_length=, max_length=), conlist, annotated_types' Len, MinLen and MaxLen - is the parameter's min_length and max_length, so a list the model allows more of than SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH is not held to it. Where a field states one twice, the last pydantic applies is the one declared, as it is the one pydantic enforces. A number's bounds are not declared: gt and lt are exclusive, which a parameter cannot state, and the model keeps every bound in its own words rather than some in the kernel's;

  • a nested model is an object with its own fields as nested Parameters, and list[SomeModel] an array of rows;

  • dict[str, X] is an object with no declared fields, whose values are pydantic's to validate;
  • a model that contains itself is described four times on one path (MAX_APPEARANCES in the adapter's utils), and deeper levels as an object with no fields. pydantic still validates every level.

Any, a union of two types, UnsetType, a RootModel and anything else without one JSON type is refused with ImproperlyConfigured naming the model and the field, never read as a string.

Names. A parameter is named for the key pydantic validates by: the field's validation_alias when it is a string, else its alias, else its name (the name alone when the model sets validate_by_alias=False). An AliasPath or AliasChoices is not one name, and is refused. validate() returns the values keyed by the field name whatever the wire called them, because that is the keyword the service is called with.

required is pydantic's own is_required(). The default is reported when JSON carries it as itself; a default_factory, or a default such as a Decimal or a date, is not reported, and the field is optional all the same. help is the field's description.

A row that updates must declare its key, as with the dataclass adapter: pk: int | None = None on the row's model, or no incoming row matches an existing one and every update replaces every row.

Refusals keep pydantic's words, addressed by path into the kernel's tree: {"books": {1: {"title": ["..."]}}}, with a row's index as an int. A message about a model itself - its model_validator refusing - sits under non_field_errors inside that model, or at the top for the model being validated. The kernel's shape check runs first and refuses a wrong JSON type, and a list past its declared length, in the kernel's words, under the code pydantic's would carry; pydantic's are what a caller reads for the model's other rules: bounds, patterns, validators.

Each message carries a code, the one a DRF field gives the same mistake where pydantic's error type has one: missing is "required", a None refused by a type is "null", a string or a list too long or too short "max_length" or "min_length", a number past a bound "max_value" or "min_value" (an exclusive bound too, which no DRF field has), a Literal or an Enum "invalid_choice", a list's type "not_a_list", a decimal's digits "max_digits", "max_decimal_places" and "max_whole_digits", and a forbidden extra key the kernel's "unknown". Any other of pydantic's own types is "invalid", DRF's code for a value it cannot take, and a ValueError or an assert in a validator is too, as DRF says for a message raised with no code. A PydanticCustomError's type is the author's code, and is kept, as a Django ValidationError's is.

Time zones are pydantic's: an offset-less date-time stays naive, where DataclassValidator makes it aware as Django's forms do. Declare the offset, or convert in the service.

The declaration is read at construction, so an unmappable field fails where the spec is written. A model whose annotations named a class not yet defined when it was built is completed first, as pydantic completes it on first use.

docs.title: parameters
docs.text:
parameters() -> Parameters

The model's fields as Parameters, named as pydantic validates them. Never queries.

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
validate(arguments: Mapping[str, Any], context: ValidationContext) -> dict[str, Any]

Every field's validated value, keyed by field name, or InvalidArguments.

The context reaches pydantic's validators as info.context, a dict with "principal", "target" and "call_context", the call's context as the very dict the transport passed, so a validator can check a value against the caller or the row being updated, and read or write what the call's other stages share. Nested values stay model instances, which is what the mutation helpers read a row from.

A partial call is refused with ImproperlyConfigured. pydantic validates a model whole: a required field not sent is missing, and a model_validator is written against every field being there, so there is no partial validation to hand the call to. Validating only the fields sent, one by one, would skip the model's own rules; a spec whose calls are partial uses a Validator that can return only what was sent. supports_partial is False, so a ServiceSpec declaring partial=True over this Validator is refused when it is built, and this refusal answers only a caller using it directly. validated() is the default: the values are the call's data.

docs.title: PydanticPresenter
docs.text:
Bases: Presenter

An operation's output declared as a pydantic model, rendered by that model.

output() reads the fields as PydanticValidator does, so one model declares the same types going in and coming out, and adds what only the output side has:

  • each field is named for the key model_dump(by_alias=True) emits: its serialization_alias, else its alias, else its name;
  • fields declared exclude=True are not output, and each computed_field is, after the fields, typed by its return annotation;
  • every field is always_present, because model_dump emits every key, except one with an exclude_if, which may be dropped;
  • label is the field's title when the author set one, and None otherwise: pydantic invents no label, and a reader can title-case a name as well as an adapter;
  • choices are (value, display) pairs: a Django Choices enum supplies its label, translated when output() is called, and a plain Enum or a Literal has no display of its own, so the value's str stands in;
  • a FieldMarking is declared in the field's Annotated metadata: id: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()].

present(value) renders with the model itself, so its serializers and its JSON encoding are what a caller receives. The value may be an instance of the model, a model row, any object carrying the same names, or a mapping keyed by field name. Anything but an instance is read one declared field at a time, by attribute or by key, and the model validates what was read: a related collection may be a manager, read through .all() so a prefetch is used when there is one, where pydantic's own from_attributes would fail on it. A field the value does not carry is left to the model's default.

A value that does not fit the model raises pydantic's ValidationError as it is. What is presented is the operation's own value rather than a caller's, so a mismatch is a defect in the operation, not a refusal to report.

The declaration is read at construction, as the validator's is.

docs.title: output
docs.text:
output() -> Output

The model's output fields, then its computed fields, as an Output. Never queries.

docs.title: present
docs.text:
present(value: Any) -> Any

One value, validated by the model and dumped as JSON data by alias.

None is presented as None: it is JSON's null, not a row whose every attribute is missing.

docs.title: dispatch
docs.text:
dispatch(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    *,
    principal: Any,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any],
    grant: Grant | None = None,
    pool_seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
    progress: ProgressReporter | None = None,
    target: Any = UNSET,
    extra_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> DispatchResult

Run spec for principal with arguments, in a fixed order.

First, a deactivated principal is refused as PrincipalUnavailable: an authenticated one whose is_active is false, with or without a grant. One with no is_active reads as active, and anonymous goes on to the permission check, which decides whether anonymous may act. It is the rule resolve_principal applies and is_deactivated exports for a transport's own entry points, so a principal is refused alike whichever way it reached dispatch.

Then the same seven steps for both kinds of spec, and for adispatch:

  1. check_arguments over spec.parameters() under unknown_arguments: the closed argument set and the shape check. It refuses no absent Validator field under a service spec's partial, at any depth, while a reads argument and the target's read stay required; nor a parameter a provider fills or may fill - a read the kwargs of the spec declaring it reaches, a Validator field input_data reaches, where the provider is annotated to fill the key, may decline it, or names no keys at all. Such a parameter is still required of the call: once the provider has answered, a read declared required that nobody filled is refused where the answer is merged, in the shape check's words (step three for a selector's read, before the affordances for a service spec's), and a Validator field by the Validator. A value the caller sends for a key a typed provider is annotated to fill is checked, then dropped, so it never stands in for the provider's; one for a key the provider may fill is kept beneath its answer. Before that, a parameter a registered seed in pool_seeds is named like is answered by where it is declared: a reflected read leaves the argument set and the seed fills it; a top-level Validator field stays the caller's, and reaches the service in data while the seed keeps the parameter of its name; anything else is refused as a configuration error.
  2. authorize, honouring grant if it covers this spec and principal. Before anything is resolved, so a refused principal learns nothing about which rows exist.
  3. Resolution: a selector spec's own selector, or a service spec's instance or collection selector, called with the base pool plus the arguments its reads declare and what its kwargs provider returns, then shaped, and a RETRIEVE collapsed to its row. A missing row is DispatchResult(kind="not_found"), returned rather than raised, unless the selector says allow_none. A RETRIEVE's missing row is None, a DoesNotExist or an Http404 alike; a LIST raising Http404, as get_object_or_404 does of a parent row, is not found whatever allow_none says, while a DoesNotExist escaping a LIST is a fault and raises.
  4. authorize_target on a retrieved row, and authorize_scope where no row is: on a list, a collection target's set, empty or not, a create's None, and the None a service spec's instance selector lets through under its allow_none. A selector spec's own None under allow_none is asked of neither.
  5. A service spec's Validator, on only the arguments it declares, with its input_data provider's values merged over the caller's, and the resolved target and partial in its context. Its validated() result is the call's: the values, data, and what it binds.
  6. A service spec's affordances, through enforce_affordances: the first one not met refuses the call as ActionUnavailable carrying its code. After the object-level check, so a principal who may not see the row is never told what state it is in, and before the run's transaction opens, so a refusal never opens one. Then its preconditions, in declaration order, from the same pool: the first to raise aborts the call, and what it raises reaches the caller as it is.
  7. The run: the service, called with the principal, data (the Validator's data), instance or collection, each validated value by name, what the Validator binds, the spec's reads, what its kwargs provider returns, progress and every registered seed, through run_service so spec.atomic holds and an async def service is bridged. Then the output selector, if declared, with the service's return as result.

A selector spec stops after step four and its preconditions: its selector is its run, and they run on what it found, never on a missing row. Its affordances are answers about each row, for a list to report, and nothing about reading is refused by them.

A many service spec takes a list of rows under its many_argument, beside its reads and nothing else, and runs the service once for all of them, inside one transaction under atomic. Its steps differ in three places:

  • Step one checks the top level - the list, and the reads - and each row, but raises only the top level's refusal there. A row's refusal is raised in step five, beside the Validator's refusals of the other rows, so a principal refused in step two learns nothing about the rows it sent.
  • Steps three and four resolve nothing: the scope check is asked of None, as for a create, never of the caller's rows.
  • Step five runs the Validator once per row, each with the input_data provider's values merged over it; the provider is called once for the call. Every row is checked and validated before the service runs, and every failing row is refused in one InvalidArguments, addressed by the row's int index under many_argument: a field as {"items": {2: {"title": [...]}}}, a message about the row itself under non_field_errors inside the row, and the list's own refusal as {"items": [...]}. The service receives the rows' data as a list under data, and their values as a list under many_argument; neither is spread by field. The affordances - conditions on no row, since one on the row is refused when the spec is declared - and the preconditions are answered once.

kind is "list" for it, unless an output selector says otherwise or the service returned None, which is presented as None.

progress is the transport's own progress reporter, seeded under the reserved name progress into the pool of whatever is this call's run - the service, or a selector spec's own selector - and into that spec's callable affordance conditions'. With none, the pool carries null_progress, so a callable that declares the parameter runs on every transport. A target or output selector, and its affordance conditions, always get null_progress: a lookup has nothing to report, and one reporting after the service finished would read as the work restarting. The run alone also reports to the spec's progress_reporter, and only a run that takes progress: called on the run's first report, or before an async def run once nothing before the run can refuse the call; either way a call refused before its run never calls it. A selector spec's run is its selector, and its step four and preconditions answer after it, so a selector spec refused there may already have called it: by the selector's first report, or, for an async def selector, before the await.

target is a service spec's target resolved by the caller - the row an HTTP view's get_object() found, or what resolve_target returned - and stands in for step three: no lookup runs, and the call's instance or collection is target. Step four still runs on it, unless grant says target_checked, so with that grant has_object_permission is asked once across both. Without target step four runs whatever the grant says: the grant vouches for the target the caller found, not for what the arguments make the lookup find. So a selector spec, which takes no target, runs it on the row or the list its selector found, whatever the grant says. None is a missing row, not-found unless the instance selector says allow_none; a create takes None and refuses anything else. Dispatch trusts it: the target's reads are still checked as declared, and keeping them and target in agreement is the caller's. A selector spec refuses it.

extra_kwargs is the transport's per-call overlay for the spec's kwargs provider - what an HTTP view's per-request hook adds - merged beneath it, so the spec's own provider wins on a clash. It is treated as the provider's own return is: an UNSET entry is dropped, a key the provider is annotated to fill is the server's and the overlay's value for it is dropped too, so an overlay never fills a key the provider declined to, and a key naming a registered seed is refused. So, before step one, is a key naming a parameter the spec declares - a read, a Validator field, a target read, a many spec's list - unless its value is UNSET or the spec's typed kwargs provider fills it: the caller's value for a parameter is what steps two and three read, so an overlay standing in for it would run the call on a value they never saw. That is the only refusal of a key the spec could own, because it is static: it turns on the spec alone, never on what a request sent. The overlay is the lowest of three tiers: beneath the spec's provider, and beneath what the Validator computed or bound in step five, so a key among those is left to the Validator's value and the overlay's entry is dropped for that call - a Validator computing a key only from some requests makes it the overlay's on the others, and an error on none. It reaches a selector spec's own selector and a service spec's service, never a target or output selector. There is no overlay for the Validator's input: a transport merges such values into arguments, where the checks and the Validator read one value.

call_context is the call's context: one plain dict, created and owned by the transport for its natural scope - an HTTP request, an agent run - and handed to every stage that declares it as the same object, never a copy. A kwargs or input_data provider, a selector of any role, an affordance condition, a precondition, the service and the run's progress_reporter declare it as a parameter named call_context, a name reserved as every seed's is, so no argument may take it. It reaches them by that name alone: one taking **kwargs for the rest of the pool is never handed it, so a catch-all forwarding what it gets runs as it did before the name was reserved (TestACatchAllIsNeverHandedTheCallContext). A permission check's method declares it as a keyword, as it declares arguments; the Validator reads it as ValidationContext.call_context and the presenter, every row of a list and any presenter it hands its context on to, as PresentationContext.call_context. So a later stage reads what an earlier one put there rather than computing it again. With none, a fresh empty dict for this call alone, so a stage writing to it runs unchanged on a transport with nothing to put in it. The kernel writes nothing to it and keeps nothing across calls. Stages of one call run in sequence; calls sharing one dict across threads should write to it by compute-if-absent - get, and on a miss compute the value and store it with call_context.setdefault(key, value) - for a value any of them would compute the same.

A permission check's method may also name a registered seed in pool_seeds as a keyword, and is handed its value at whichever of the three questions declares it. The seeds the checks name, and only those, are resolved before step two, so the class-level check can read them, and every pool after takes those values as they are: each resolves once for the call, and the check, the selectors and the service see one object. Every other seed resolves as before, once per pool and each after step two, as every seed does for a spec whose checks name none. A seed named arguments is never named this way: a check declaring arguments is handed the call's. A parameter a check's method fills by position - principal, spec and the target or scope, whatever it calls them - is never read as an opt-in.

The presenter's context also carries shapes: what the caller sent for the spec's declared shapes, read-only, a shape left out absent. No shape reaches a pool under its own name, nor the Validator at all; the same mapping is in the pool of every callable but a service spec's target selector as the shapes seed, for a callable that names it (the target selector is handed an empty mapping, as under resolve_target; see RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS).

kind is "list" for a LIST selector spec, a service whose output selector is a LIST, or a many or returns_many service with no output selector that returned something, and "instance" otherwise. Nothing is presented here; present does that, so a transport that hands the object to a template never pays for rendering it.

Raises:

Type Description PrincipalUnavailable

a deactivated principal, before step one.

InvalidArguments

step one, or the Validator, or a parameter of a selector, its extend_queryset or the service that has no default, that a caller could have filled and that nothing in the call's pool did - a read declared optional and not sent, a Validator parameter a call that is not partial left out - keyed by that parameter, and the same for a precondition's. One no caller can fill, or one the caller sent and the Validator did not hand back under that name, raises the callable's own TypeError.

NotPermitted

step two or step four.

TypeError

target on a selector spec or a many spec, or anything but None on a service spec that declares no target selector.

ActionUnavailable

step six, an affordance not met.

ServiceNotFound

step six, a condition on the row reached after the row was deleted.

ImproperlyConfigured

a spec that declares no permissions, a parameter, a validated, bound or provided value named after a seed, a bound value named after a validated one, any value bound for a row of a many call, an extra_kwargs key naming a declared parameter, shaping declared on a selector that returned something other than a queryset, a condition on the row with no row to answer it for, or a precondition answering with a coroutine or an async generator.

docs.title: adispatch async
docs.text:
adispatch(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    *,
    principal: Any = None,
    principal_id: Any = None,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any],
    grant: Grant | None = None,
    pool_seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
    progress: ProgressReporter | None = None,
    target: Any = UNSET,
    extra_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> DispatchResult

Run spec from async code: dispatch's steps, order and refusals.

Every concept is sync-only, and so is every spec-carried callable but one. A permission check, a Validator, a selector nested in a service spec, extend_queryset, a seed's resolver, a spec's providers and its preconditions may each query, so each runs in Django's thread-sensitive executor, never on the event loop. Only the run may be async def - the service, or a selector spec's own selector - because it is the one callable no phase shares: a spec is written once for both entry points, and a concept written async def could not be called from dispatch.

So the phases run in one sync_to_async(thread_sensitive=True) hop, and the run's shape decides only what else joins it:

Every refusal before the run is made inside that hop, an affordance and a service spec's precondition included: a condition on the row is a query. A selector spec's preconditions run on what its selector found, so after an async def one they join the hop that shapes its return.

  • A sync run joins the hop, so a sync spec costs exactly one.
  • An atomic async def service joins it too, through the bridge in run_service: transaction.atomic is sync-only, so the transaction is opened on the executor thread and the coroutine is driven from inside it, where its own thread-sensitive ORM calls come back to the connection holding it.
  • A non-atomic async def run is awaited on the loop after the hop. Holding the executor thread while it awaits - a network call, say - would stall every thread-sensitive call queued behind it. What follows it (an output selector; a selector spec's shaping, row and object-level check) takes a second hop, and only when there is such a thing to do.

Exactly one of principal and principal_id. principal_id is resolved with resolve_principal inside the hop, because resolving it is itself a query; taking only the row would push that query into a hop of the caller's. A grant never covers a principal resolved here, since a grant is bound to the principal object it was minted for. A deactivated row is refused there, with its identifier in the message; a deactivated principal is refused by dispatch's own check, which reads the same rule, so the two cannot disagree about who may act.

progress reaches the run as it does under dispatch, including an async def one awaited on the loop, so a reporter must be safe to call from either: the executor thread for a sync run, and an event loop for an async def one, atomic or not. A spec's progress_reporter is never called on the loop: for an async def run it is resolved inside the hop, once nothing before the run can refuse the call.

target is dispatch's: a service spec's target the caller resolved, standing in for the lookup inside the one hop, and checked there unless grant says target_checked; without target, checked whatever the grant says. A selector spec and a many spec refuse it before any hop, and a selector spec's row or list is checked whatever the grant says, as dispatch's is.

extra_kwargs is dispatch's overlay, copied on entry, merged beneath the spec's kwargs provider inside the hop, on every path, and refused there where it names a declared parameter; beneath the Validator's computed and bound values too, as in dispatch, on both hops (test_a_value_the_validator_computed_outranks_the_overlay_on_both_hops). That refusal and the read of whether a check declares arguments both run off the loop (test_the_overlay_refusal_and_a_check_s_signature_are_read_off_the_loop).

call_context is dispatch's: the transport's dict, handed to every stage that declares it as the same object, on every path and across every hop; with none, one fresh dict for the call, made here on entry, so the stages of each hop share it.

A many spec checks, validates and writes its rows as dispatch does, every row inside the one hop.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

both or neither of principal and principal_id; target where dispatch refuses it.

PrincipalUnavailable

principal_id names no principal who may act, or principal is deactivated.

(InvalidArguments, NotPermitted, ImproperlyConfigured)

as dispatch.

(ActionUnavailable, ServiceNotFound)

as dispatch, from its affordances.

docs.title: DispatchResult dataclass
docs.text:
The value an operation produced, and how to read it.

Not-found is reported, not raised: a required row that does not exist comes back as kind="not_found" and the transport decides what that means on its wire - a 404, an exit code, a tool error. Nothing here is a status code, because most transports have none.

Attributes:

Name Type Description kind Literal['instance', 'list', 'not_found']

"instance" (one value, possibly None), "list" (a collection, a queryset when it can be one), or "not_found".

value Any

What to present: the selector's rows, or the service's return, or what its output selector re-read.

service_result Any

The service's own return, before any output selector.

instance Any

The resolved target - the row, or the collection's queryset.

data Any

The Validator's data the service received: the validated mapping, or the instance a dataclass Validator builds.

context PresentationContext | None

The call a presenter renders for: its principal, its target, its resolved seeds, the call's context and the arguments sent for the spec's shapes, which present hands to Presenter.presented(). None on a result dispatch did not build, and on a not-found, which is never presented. It takes no part in equality: two results of one value are one result.

docs.title: present
docs.text:
present(spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource, result: DispatchResult) -> Any

Render result.value as JSON-like data, the way spec declares it.

The presenter is a selector spec's own, or a service spec's presenter_for_output(): its own, or its output selector's when it declares none.

  • kind="list": every item through the presenter's presented_rows() in one call, which presents each in turn unless the presenter batches over them. To serve a page, hand present a result holding the page's rows, and those are the rows it receives. With no presenter the items are returned as they are, but still in a list: a queryset is evaluated here rather than handed back lazily, because apresent's caller is on the event loop, where the first iteration of an unevaluated queryset is a query Django refuses to run.
  • kind="instance": the value through the presenter. With no presenter, or a value of None - an allow_none retrieve that found nothing, a service that returned nothing - the value as it is. None is not a row, and asking a presenter to render one produces either a crash or an object of blank fields indistinguishable from a real row.

Affordances. When the selector spec presented through declares affordances - a selector spec's own, or a service spec's output selector's, never a service spec's own, which are what its call is checked against - each presented object gains an affordances key: per declared name, {"available": true}, or {"available": false, "code": ..., "reason": ...} naming the first condition the row does not meet, or a bare {"available": false} for a row deleted before its answers were asked, which fails no condition and so has no sentence to report. None is not a row and carries none. The answers are read off the rows as the selector's dispatch left them - annotations on a queryset's rows, or the answers it attached to rows a selector returned directly - so presenting them costs no query. A spec declaring none presents what its presenter answers, untouched.

The call's context. Each value is handed to the presenter's presented(), or a list's to its presented_rows(), with result.context, the PresentationContext dispatch built for the call, or None on a result it did not build. presented() is present() unless overridden, so a Presenter that reads nothing of the call needs only present(). Every value of one result is handed the same context, so a list's rows, and a nested presenter a presenter hands it on to, share its call_context - the dict the transport created for the call - and read the arguments that shape the output from its shapes. A spec declaring no shapes and a presenter reading neither present exactly as before.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

kind="not_found". Presenting nothing as a success is the bug this refuses; the transport answers a not-found in its own terms (a 404, an exit code, a tool error) and never presents it.

ImproperlyConfigured

The spec declares affordances and no presenter to present them through; a presented row is not an object, or already has an affordances key; or a row carries no answer, because it did not come through the selector that declares them. Also a presenter answering with a coroutine or an async generator, which is never awaited, so it is refused rather than handed back as the payload; and a presented_rows() answering with anything but a list of one presented value per row.

docs.title: apresent async
docs.text:
apresent(spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource, result: DispatchResult) -> Any

present in one executor hop.

A presenter is sync-only and may query - reading a relation off a row the selector did not prefetch, or evaluating a list's queryset - and the kernel cannot tell in advance which, so the whole of present runs on Django's thread-sensitive executor rather than on the event loop. What comes back is plain data, safe to use on the loop.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

kind="not_found", as present.

docs.title: present_for_audience
docs.text:
present_for_audience(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    result: DispatchResult,
    *,
    projection: AudienceProjection | None = None,
) -> Any

present plus the agent projection.

The one call an agent transport makes instead of present, so an MCP server, an in-process toolset and anything added later shape payloads identically rather than each growing its own post-processor. spec and result mean exactly what they mean to present, which this calls first: the projection applies to the presented value and never to the value it was presented from.

djangorestframework-services' render_for_audience is the same composition over its serializer render, and takes the view, request and many that render reads. This is named apart so that neither package's name means two signatures.

projection is the output's resolved markings. Omit it and one is read off the spec; a transport that registers its tools up front builds it once with audience_projection_for_spec, a mount's overrides included, and passes it in. None is therefore not a way out of projecting: a caller naming no audience calls present, which is what every HTTP response is.

To serve one page, page the result's value first and present the page's rows: present_for_audience(spec, replace(result, value=page.items)), then envelope what comes back. The presenter's presented_rows() is then called once, with the page's rows and no others, so a lookup it batches over them costs the same whatever the size of the whole set. The envelope's keys belong to no Output, so the projection must never walk them. Whether to page is read off the spec, never off the result's kind: a LIST selector spec, or a service spec whose output selector is a LIST, is paged, while a many or returns_many service spec's kind="list" is every row its service returned, which its output schema describes as a bare array.

A selector spec's declared affordances pass through whole: the affordances object present adds to each row is a key no Output declares, so the projection has nothing to say about it, and an agent reads available, the code a client branches on, and the reason - the sentence a model relays when it explains why an action is not possible, written for exactly that reader.

Render an agent's answer with this. A pipeline that feeds one spec's output into the next keeps presenting with present, or the handles the next step reads by will have been projected away.

From async code, project what apresent returns: project_payload(await apresent(spec, result), projection). Presenting may query and runs in the executor; projecting reads only the presented data and the declaration, so it is safe on the event loop.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

kind="not_found", as present.

docs.title: resolve_target
docs.text:
resolve_target(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SpecSource,
    *,
    principal: Any,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any],
    grant: Grant | None = None,
    pool_seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> tuple[Any, Grant] | DispatchResult

Find and check spec's target as dispatch would, without running anything else.

For a page that shows the row before the call acts on it - the form in front of an update, the confirmation in front of a delete - and so must show the row dispatch would find, refused where dispatch would refuse. It runs dispatch's own steps, in dispatch's order, and the walk after them is the very function dispatch runs:

  1. A deactivated principal is refused, as PrincipalUnavailable.
  2. The shape check over the target selector's parameters alone, on only the arguments they name. A Validator field is neither required nor an unknown key here, so a GET carrying the route's arguments and a POST carrying the whole form both resolve; the target's own reads are required as declared, except one its kwargs provider fills or may fill, which the lookup's pool must then hold once the provider has answered, as at dispatch. A reflected target read a registered seed is named like is no argument, and the seed fills it.
  3. Class-level authorization, honouring grant as dispatch does. Like the two steps before it, before any query.
  4. The lookup, and the checks on what it finds: has_object_permission on a row, and has_scope_permission on a collection target's set, empty or not, and on None - a create, which resolves nothing, and a missing row the instance selector's allow_none lets through.

Returns (target, grant): the row, the set, or None, and a grant covering spec and principal with target_checked set, which is what dispatch(spec, ..., target=target, grant=grant) takes. So a call resolved here looks nothing up again and asks no object-level or scope check twice. The grant vouches for that target alone: handed to dispatch without target=, it covers the class-level check and nothing else, and dispatch checks the row its own lookup finds. A target_checked grant handed in here is read the same way, since this function looks its target up itself. A missing row allow_none does not let through returns DispatchResult(kind="not_found"), dispatch's own answer, so it is never mistaken for the None it lets through.

call_context is the call's context, as dispatch takes it: the transport's dict, handed as the same object to the target selector and to every permission check method naming it, or a fresh dict of their own when none is passed. A check naming a registered seed is offered it here as at dispatch, at the class-level check and at the checks on what the lookup finds. A page resolving its row ahead of the call passes the dict it will hand that call, so the two read and write one context.

It is sync, as dispatch's steps are; an async caller hops once, with sync_to_async(resolve_target, thread_sensitive=True).

Raises:

Type Description PrincipalUnavailable

a deactivated principal.

InvalidArguments

a target read the arguments leave out or get wrong.

NotPermitted

the class-level, object-level or scope check.

ImproperlyConfigured

as dispatch, for a spec declaring no permissions or a parameter a registered seed occupies that is neither a reflected read nor a top-level Validator field, though this checks no Validator field's value.

ImproperlyConfigured

also a many spec, which declares no lookup: its rows are the call's arguments, and none is found ahead of it.

TypeError

a SelectorSpec, whose selector is its run rather than a lookup in front of one.

docs.title: paginate_output
docs.text:
paginate_output(
    rows: Any,
    *,
    page: int | None = None,
    limit: int | None = None,
    max_page_size: int | None = None,
) -> OutputPage

Slice rows into the page a transport serves.

A function a transport calls on a paged spec's result value before presenting it, not a paging scheme: the names a caller pages by, and the ceiling a mount allows, are the transport's. A transport takes them off the call before the spec's closed argument set sees them, and bounds legitimately differ between two mounts of one spec.

Whether to page is read off the spec, never off the result's kind: a LIST selector spec, or a service spec whose output selector is a LIST, is paged, and spec_output_schema describes it as the envelope under paginate=True. A many or returns_many service spec's result is kind="list" too, and is never paged: it is every row the service returned, which its output schema describes as a bare array whatever paginate says.

page and limit default to 1 and DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE. Out-of-range values clamp at both ends - limit down to max_page_size and up to 1, page up to 1 and down to the last page that exists - and the clamps are not silent the way truncating an unpaged result would be: totalPages and hasNext are computed from the clamped limit, and the returned page is the one actually served. A caller that asked for 500 rows and got 100, or for page 10 of 3, is told what it received.

Both values are taken already parsed. Turning an untyped argument into an integer is where transports legitimately differ - a public endpoint clamps a malformed value and answers, an in-process toolset can hand a model its mistake back and ask again - and that is a policy about bad input, not about what a page is.

The upper clamp on page is why total is counted before the slice: (page - 1) * limit on an unclamped page is an arbitrarily large SQL OFFSET, which a backend either scans towards or refuses outright with a DatabaseError this does not catch. No slice is longer than total for the same reason, so a limit past any integer a database holds, which no max_page_size bounded, still serves every row; the page reports the limit asked for.

A queryset is counted with COUNT and sliced lazily, so the page's items is still a queryset: present them, as present does a list, and the page is read once. A manager - any BaseManager, so one built with BaseManager.from_queryset too - is paged as its .all(), since it counts and cannot be sliced.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

rows is neither a queryset nor a sized, sliceable sequence, so there is nothing to count and nothing to slice.

docs.title: DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE module-attribute
docs.text:
DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE: Final[int] = 100

Rows per page when the caller asks for a page and names no size.

docs.title: bind_arguments
docs.text:
bind_arguments(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any],
    *,
    principal: Any,
    target: Any = None,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]

Check arguments against the spec's parameters, then validate them.

The bind a transport calls when it binds input itself rather than through dispatch - an MCP server answering a malformed call before it opens a transaction, a queue validating a task in the worker. It is the same two steps dispatch takes, so a transport that binds for itself cannot drift from the gate dispatch applies. spec may be a SpecSource, bound as the spec it compiles to:

  1. check_arguments over spec.parameters(), under unknown_arguments: the closed argument set and the shape check, at every level, relaxing what dispatch relaxes: an absent Validator field when the service spec is partial, one its input_data provider fills or may fill, and a read the kwargs provider of the spec declaring it fills or may fill - a typed provider's filled and declinable keys, and every parameter an untyped provider's values reach.
  2. For a ServiceSpec with a Validator, validated() on only the arguments the Validator's own parameters() declare - never a selector's or the spec's reads - with ValidationContext(principal, target, partial), whose resolved names target as dispatch would: instance for a spec with an instance selector, collection for one with a collection selector, nothing for a create, and whose call_context is call_context, the very dict passed, or a fresh one.

Returns the Validator's values. A service spec with no Validator returns {}, because every argument it takes is a read and none is validated. A SelectorSpec has no Validator and returns the checked arguments, which are what its selector is called with.

It runs no provider. The spec's input_data, which dispatch merges over the caller's arguments before the Validator, is not called here: it reads the resolved target and the call's seeds, which this function is not handed. A spec declaring one is bound on the caller's arguments alone, so a field the provider fills or may fill passes the shape check and is the Validator's to refuse: left out, or sent, since a value the caller sends for a field the server owns is checked and then dropped, as in dispatch. The presence check dispatch makes of such a field before the Validator, once the provider has answered, is not made here (test_a_field_input_data_fills_is_left_to_the_validator_which_runs_no_provider). No kwargs provider is called either: a read one fills or may fill passes the shape check absent, and the presence check dispatch makes once the provider has answered is not made here (test_bind_arguments_relaxes_a_may_fill_read). A read one is annotated to fill is absent from a selector spec's checked arguments whether or not the caller sent it.

It takes no pool_seeds, so it refuses no registered seed's name and splits none: a reflected read is checked as declared, so a required one is demanded of the caller here though a registered seed fills it on dispatch, which refuses the caller's value for it as an unknown argument under REJECT (test_bind_arguments_still_demands_a_required_reflected_read), and a Validator field named like a registered seed is validated and returned among the values, as any field is. Which values a service's pool spreads is dispatch's question.

It does not resolve or authorize. Dispatch runs class-level authorization, target resolution and object-level authorization between these two steps, so the Validator sees the resolved row and a refused principal learns nothing about which rows exist. A caller of this function owns both: it authorizes before binding, and passes the row it resolved as target, or None for a create.

It is the complement of check_call: this validates and does not authorize, and check_call authorizes and does not validate.

Raises:

Type Description InvalidArguments

from either step. The shape check's tree carries every problem at once, and a Validator is only reached with well-shaped arguments. A many spec is the one exception, row by row: the Validator's validated_many() is handed every row that passed the shape check, and a shape refusal and a Validator refusal on different rows come back as one tree keyed by row index.

docs.title: check_requested_input
docs.text:
check_requested_input(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    schema: Mapping[str, Any] | None,
    *,
    pool_seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
) -> None

Refuse an AdditionalInputRequired.schema some route could not ask, or could not hear answered.

schema is what a service raised AdditionalInputRequired with, read against spec: a transport calls this before it renders the question, so a service asks the same question on every route or on none. None, a raise that carries no schema, asks nothing and passes.

It reads the spec's top-level parameters() and the schema, runs no query and returns nothing. Each key is refused, by name, with ImproperlyConfigured, in this order:

  • A key no top-level parameter declares. The answer comes back as an ordinary argument, so a key the closed argument set refuses could never carry it. On a many spec the top level is the list and the spec's reads, so a value asked once for the whole call is a reads parameter, and a key declared only inside a row is refused.
  • A key the server fills: one a provider the dispatch runs is annotated to fill, or a seed pool_seeds registers - a reflected read the seed fills among them - as server_owned_keys reads them. Dispatch drops the caller's value for such a key, so the answer would never reach the service. pool_seeds is the call's, as dispatch takes it. A top-level Validator field named like a registered seed may be asked for, since the answer reaches the Validator and data (test_server_owned_keys_leaves_such_a_field_out_and_a_service_may_ask_for_it), and so may a key a provider may decline or one an untyped provider's values reach, whose caller's value stands when the provider declines.
  • A fragment that is not a schema object: a dict, as JSON carries one.
  • A shape some transport cannot render. The narrowest is an MCP elicitation form, which takes a string, number, integer or boolean, or an array whose items list enum values, untitled (enum) or titled (anyOf). A type list, an object, a fragment naming no type and an array of anything else are refused.
  • A type the declared parameter does not take, since the answering call would fail the shape check whatever was answered. The answer must be of a type the parameter takes: an integer question may fill a number parameter and not the reverse, any question may fill an any, and a number may fill a decimal string, as check_arguments reads one. An array question fills an array whose element takes its values, which are strings unless its items name a type, as both of MCP's multi-select shapes are; the rows of a many list are objects, which no list of values fills. The type is compared and nothing finer: a format, choices or a bound the parameter declares still checks the answer when it arrives.

A SpecSource is read as the spec it compiles to.

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

naming the first key refused, or for a schema that is no mapping at all.

docs.title: check_call
docs.text:
check_call(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    *,
    principal: Any,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any],
    grant: Grant | None = None,
    pool_seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], Grant]

dispatch's prelude, run alone: the checked arguments and the grant, or its refusal.

For a transport that answers a call before it runs - a task queue refusing at enqueue what the worker's dispatch would refuse before it resolves anything. Only that: no lookup runs, so no object or scope check, no Validator, no affordance and no precondition, and a call this passes may still be refused by dispatch at any of those (test_a_scope_check_is_left_to_dispatch). The steps are dispatch's own, in its order, and the same function runs them for both, so the two cannot drift apart:

  1. A deactivated principal is refused as PrincipalUnavailable, with or without a grant.
  2. A parameter a registered seed in pool_seeds is named like is answered as dispatch answers it: a reflected read leaves the argument set, a top-level Validator field stays in it, and anything else is refused as ImproperlyConfigured.
  3. check_arguments under unknown_arguments, relaxed exactly as dispatch relaxes it: a parameter a provider fills or may fill - a typed provider's filled and declinable keys, and every parameter an untyped provider's values reach - and a Validator field under partial. No provider runs here, so a call this passes without such a value may still be refused by dispatch where the provider's answer is merged (test_check_call_relaxes_a_may_fill_read).
  4. authorize, honouring grant if it covers this spec and principal.

The keywords are dispatch's, less what only a run reads. The kernel's own steps run no query; a project's PermissionCheck may.

It returns the checked arguments and the grant the call ran under, which dispatch honours for the same spec and principal, so the class-level check is not asked twice. A many spec's rows come back as a list of checked rows under many_argument, and a refused row is raised here, after step four, in the tree dispatch raises it in - though dispatch reports it beside the Validator's refusals of the other rows, and this runs no Validator.

It is the complement of bind_arguments: this authorizes and does not validate, and bind_arguments validates and does not authorize. Neither resolves a target; for a service spec that acts on a row, resolve_target finds and checks it.

spec may be a declaration with as_kernel_spec(), read as the spec it compiles to, and the grant is for that compiled spec, which the same object answers on every later call.

call_context is offered to the checks as dispatch offers it, the very dict passed, or a fresh one; a check naming a registered seed is handed it, resolved as dispatch resolves it before the class-level check.

Raises:

Type Description PrincipalUnavailable

step one.

ImproperlyConfigured

step two, or a spec that declares no permissions.

InvalidArguments

step three, or a refused row of a many call.

NotPermitted

step four.

ValueError

unknown_arguments is no policy, PASSTHROUGH included.

docs.title: check_server_arguments
docs.text:
check_server_arguments(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    server: ServerArguments,
    *,
    pool_seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
) -> None

Refuse a ServerArguments that cannot mean what it says for spec.

For a transport to call once, when it is built, with the pool_seeds it dispatches with, so a binding that would do nothing or break every call fails at startup rather than on the first call that reaches it. Pure and synchronous, and it runs no query. The checks run in this order, and the first that finds anything raises, naming the spec's kind and callable and every name it found, in order:

  1. A name that is no top-level parameter of the spec, read as django-spec-html's route_arguments reads a route's kwargs: spec.parameters().names(). So a field inside a many spec's rows cannot be bound; a read beside the list can. Held by test_every_undeclared_name_is_refused_in_order and test_a_field_inside_a_many_row_is_not_a_top_level_parameter.
  2. A name both bound and withheld, which asks for a value and for none. Held by test_a_name_both_bound_and_withheld_is_refused.

  3. A name a registered seed occupies, as dispatch reads one. Only a registered seed can reach here, since parameters() refuses the dispatcher's names as it assembles. Two refusals, in this order, each naming only its own:

  4. a parameter dispatch refuses as a configuration error - a read nobody marked reflected, a shape. Held by test_a_parameter_a_registered_seed_occupies_is_refused and test_an_unmarked_read_is_still_refused_as_dispatch_refuses_it;

  5. a reflected read, which the seed fills on every call, so a binding or a withholding would do nothing. Held by test_binding_or_withholding_it_is_refused_as_doing_nothing.

A top-level Validator field named like a registered seed is not refused: it is the caller's argument, so a bound value reaches the Validator and data while the seed keeps the service's parameter of its name (test_check_server_arguments_binds_such_a_field), and withholding it meets rule 5 as any field does. 4. A name a typed provider fills or may fill: the spec's kwargs and, on a service spec, its input_data and its target selector's kwargs, the providers server_owned_keys walks. A key a provider fills is dropped from the caller's arguments and answered by the provider alone, so a binding would do nothing; one it may decline with UNSET is the provider's on every call where it answers, so a binding would hold only when the provider happens not to. Each half is held by its own test: test_a_name_a_typed_provider_fills_is_refused (the filled keys) and test_a_name_a_provider_may_decline_is_refused_too (the declinable ones), and each provider past the spec's own kwargs too: test_a_validator_field_input_data_fills_is_refused (input_data) and test_a_read_the_target_selector_s_provider_fills_is_refused (the target's kwargs). A provider whose return names no keys may fill any name and so names none, as for server_owned_keys. 5. A withheld name no call could then do without. Withheld, the parameter is absent, so it is refused if the shape check demands it - required and declaring no default, read as dispatch relaxes a partial spec, whose Validator parameters it never demands - or, for a read, if the callable that receives it declares it with no default of its own: the selector of a selector spec or of a service spec's target, and the service for a service spec's reads. Dispatch applies no declared default, so the callable's is the only one that answers, and a call without one is refused as missing, a client error no caller can fix. A Validator parameter is the shape check's alone. Each conjunct is held by its own test, named beside the guard. A parameter an untyped provider's values reach is never refused here: that provider may fill it on any call, so a call may do without the caller's value, and dispatch refuses one nobody filled where the provider's answer is merged (test_check_server_arguments_lets_a_read_an_untyped_provider_reaches_be_withheld, test_check_server_arguments_lets_a_field_an_untyped_input_data_reaches_be_withheld). A typed provider's keys, filled or declinable, were refused by rule 4. 6. A bound value its parameter refuses, checked as the shape check checks it, so a server value in its Python form - a uuid.UUID, a date, a Decimal - for a parameter that takes the wire's string fails here rather than on every call. Held by test_a_bound_value_its_parameter_refuses_fails_at_construction.

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

the first check that finds anything.

docs.title: apply_server_arguments
docs.text:
apply_server_arguments(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any],
    server: ServerArguments,
) -> dict[str, Any]

arguments as dispatch should receive them under server: a new dict, the input untouched.

For a transport to call on every call, before dispatch or adispatch, which take the result as their arguments; both run the same prelude over it, so one applied mapping answers the same through either. Dispatch takes no binding of its own: this is the whole of the rule, and a transport path that does not call it is unbound.

  1. The caller's value for every bound or withheld name is dropped, before anything reads it. A value the caller sends for a name it was never offered - "null" for an integer it could not see - therefore never reaches the shape check and cannot refuse the call. Held by test_a_malformed_value_for_a_withheld_name_never_reaches_the_shape_check.
  2. The bound values are laid over what is left, so a bound name holds the server's value whatever the caller sent, and a withheld one is absent. Held by test_a_bound_value_outranks_the_caller_s, which fails if the two steps swap.

Every other key is left as sent, for the shape check to read under the transport's unknown_arguments, so a name nobody declared is still refused under REJECT.

The bound values are checked against their own parameters, as check_server_arguments checked them when the transport was built, and handed on as the shape check reads them: a uuid in its canonical spelling, an integral float declared an integer as the int. One that fails is the server's mistake, raised as ImproperlyConfigured with the refusal as its cause, never as InvalidArguments: a client refusal would ask the caller to fix a value it neither sent nor can see. This is where the rule parts from django-spec-html's route_arguments, whose bad value is a client's 400, because a client chose the URL and nobody but the server chose a bound value. A bound name the spec does not declare, which check_server_arguments refuses when the transport is built, is refused here the same way.

Every refusal names the spec's kind and its callable, so a transport binding many tools can say which one is misconfigured.

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

a bound value that fails its declaration, or a bound name the spec does not declare.

docs.title: REFUSALS module-attribute
docs.text:
REFUSALS: tuple[type[DispatchError] | type[ServiceError], ...] = (
    DispatchError,
    InvalidArguments,
    NotPermitted,
    PrincipalUnavailable,
    ServiceError,
    ServiceNotFound,
    ServiceConflict,
    ActionUnavailable,
    AdditionalInputRequired,
    ServiceValidationError,
)

Every refusal the kernel defines, family by family, each base before what is under it.

Two families: a DispatchError refuses the call before the operation runs, and a ServiceError is the operation's own refusal. Both bases are listed, because either may be raised bare, and so is ServiceConflict, the base of ActionUnavailable.

A refusal a transport defines - django-spec-html's UnsupportedMediaType is one - is not here: that transport maps it and tests it. Read by unanswered_refusals; a test walking the class tree holds it equal to the package's own refusals, so one a later release adds fails there until it is listed.

docs.title: unanswered_refusals
docs.text:
unanswered_refusals(
    answers: Callable[[DispatchError | ServiceError], object]
    | Sequence[tuple[type[BaseException], object]],
    *,
    unanswered: object = None,
) -> tuple[RefusalFinding, ...]

What a transport's map from the kernel's refusals to its outcomes leaves unanswered.

A RefusalFinding per finding, and none for a map that answers every one of REFUSALS, so a transport holds its map from its own test suite with assert unanswered_refusals(...) == (); pytest's failure shows the first finding, and -v lists them all.
