A transport that leaves a gap on purpose filters the findings by refusal or kind, never by their words, which str() gives and which are free to change. Each transport keeps its own vocabulary - an exit code, a status, a run state - and this checks only that the vocabulary is total.

answers is the map in one of two shapes:

  • An ordered table of (refusal class, outcome) rows, read top to bottom by isinstance with the first match winning, which is how the kernel's own maps are written. A refusal is answered with the outcome of the first row whose class it is an instance of, so a row for a base answers every refusal under it, and a catch-all row of Exception answers them all. A row whose outcome is unanswered is no answer: a refusal it catches first stays unanswered whatever a later row says, as for the callable below. Pass the table itself.
  • A callable, given one instance of each refusal and answering with its outcome, for a map written as branches. A refusal is unanswered when the callable returns unanswered (compared with ==, so a falsy outcome such as 0 is still an answer). Whatever it raises propagates: a map that cannot answer a refusal without raising is broken in a way this should not hide. A mapping looked up by the error's exact class passes lambda error: table.get(type(error)), since reading it as ordered rows would let a base's key answer for a subclass the lookup never reaches.

Three kinds of finding, each a RefusalFindingKind, shown here as str() words them:

  • UNANSWERED, nothing in the map answers NotPermitted: a refusal no row, or no call, answers.
  • BARE_BASE, nothing in the map answers DispatchError itself, though it answers every refusal under it, and DispatchError may be raised bare: the map looks complete and is not. Either family base may be raised bare: the kernel raises neither itself, but a project's own code may, and ServiceConflict is a base too.
  • SHADOWED_ROW, the row for ServiceConflict never answers: the row for ServiceError above it answers every ServiceConflict first: the precedence trap of an ordered table, a subclass's row below its base's. Its refusal is the dead row's class and its shadowed_by the earlier row's. Reported for every row, a transport's own refusal's included, since a row nothing reaches is dead whoever's refusal it names.

The precedence trap is reported for a table only. A callable written as branches orders them in code, and a branch for a subclass below its base's is a body that never runs, which the transport's own branch coverage reports; a table's order is data, which coverage reads as one expression.

docs.title: relax_partial
docs.text:
relax_partial(spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec, parameters: Parameters) -> Parameters

parameters as a call of spec is checked under partial: every Validator parameter optional.

The one reading of what a partial call may leave out, for the shape check and for spec_input_schema's required, so the schema never asks for a field dispatch would not refuse absent, nor leaves one out that it would. Made optional at every depth - an object's fields and an array's rows included - as djangorestframework-services relaxes only its serializer. The spec's reads and its target selector's keep their required: a partial update still names the row it updates (test_a_partial_call_omitting_the_target_s_pk_is_refused_at_the_shape_check). So do its shapes, which say what is presented rather than what is written, as on a many spec, where only the list's rows are walked. On a many spec the Validator's parameters are each row's, so the list stays required and only its rows are walked, since a read may share a row field's name (test_a_partial_many_spec_requires_the_list_and_its_reads_and_nothing_in_a_row).

parameters as they are for a selector spec, which has no partial, and for a service spec that is not partial. One branch to coverage, so each condition is held by its own test: test_a_selector_specs_schema_is_its_reads (the type: without it, a selector spec's missing attribute raises) and test_a_spec_that_is_not_partial_requires_every_required_parameter (the flag). The Validator's are told apart by what they are not, the spec's reads and its target's, so the Validator is not asked for its parameters again; a read and a Validator parameter of one name are refused when parameters() is assembled. Of the names kept, the spec's reads are held by test_a_partial_spec_with_no_target_keeps_its_reads_required, the shapes by test_a_partial_spec_keeps_a_required_shape_required, and the target's by test_a_partial_spec_requires_none_of_its_validators_parameters_at_any_depth.

A copy, so the declaration every other reader sees - parameters() itself, which still says what a whole call needs - is untouched.

Public so that a transport building an input surface of its own - a command's options, a form - asks a partial call for what dispatch asks, rather than restating the rule and drifting from it.

docs.title: enforce_affordances
docs.text:
enforce_affordances(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SpecSource,
    pool: dict[str, Any],
    *,
    instance: Any,
    reserved: frozenset[str] = RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> None

Refuse the call if one of the spec's affordances is not met.

dispatch and adispatch call this themselves for a service spec, with the pool the service is about to receive and the pool seeds' reserved set. A transport that runs a service without them - a chain that owns the transaction and hands each step its own pool, say - must call it too, exactly as it calls authorize, or a condition the direct path refuses is skipped on that one. Neither entry point calls it for a selector spec, whose affordances are answers about each row rather than a refusal of the read.

pool is the keyword pool the service is about to receive and instance its resolved target, None for an operation with none. It raises ActionUnavailable carrying the unmet affordance's reason and code.

Callers must invoke this after object-level authorization and validation, and before the service: class-level authorization -> target resolution -> object-level authorization -> validation -> affordances -> service. After access because a refusal describes the row's state, and telling a caller who may not see the row what state it is in is a disclosure. Dispatch calls it before an atomic service's transaction opens, so a refusal never opens one.

Declaration order decides which refusal a caller sees, and nothing past the first unmet condition runs. Every condition on the row is answered together by one query the first time one is reached. A callable condition sees the seeds of pool - never the call's target, input or client arguments - so a **kwargs catch-all is held to the same rule the declaration enforces on a named parameter. reserved is this call's seed set, registered seeds included: seeds.reserved for the PoolSeeds the pool was built with. A callable's result is read for truth, so one that returns nothing refuses rather than allows.

spec may be a declaration with as_kernel_spec(), read as the service spec it compiles to.

call_context is the call's context, handed to a callable condition that names it and never to one taking **kwargs for the rest: the dict passed, else the one pool carries, else a fresh one the conditions of this call share. A call_context passed beside a different one in pool raises ImproperlyConfigured (with_call_context).

Raises:

Type Description ActionUnavailable

An affordance is not met.

ServiceNotFound

A condition on the row was reached and the row is gone: resolved a moment ago, and there is now nothing to do it to.

ImproperlyConfigured

A condition on the row was reached and instance is not a model instance.

TypeError

spec is, or compiles to, a SelectorSpec, whose affordances name other operations rather than conditions on this one.

docs.title: unmet_operation_affordance
docs.text:
unmet_operation_affordance(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    pool: dict[str, Any],
    *,
    reserved: frozenset[str] = RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> Affordance | None

The first of the spec's operation-scope affordances not met now, or None.

For a transport deciding whether to offer an operation at all, before anyone attempts it: an MCP server building its tool list, an agent assembling the toolset for its next step. An operation whose answer is an Affordance cannot be called right now whatever it is called with, so offering it only invites a refusal.

Only the callable conditions are asked - the ones answered without a row. A condition on the row is skipped without being evaluated, because at list time there is no row: it runs no query and needs no instance, and it goes on being answered per object where it always is, at the call. The callables are asked in declaration order and the first unmet one is returned, which is the one a call would be refused with when no row condition before it answers first. A callable's result is read for truth, so one that returns nothing is unmet here as it is refused at the call. An exception it raises propagates: this answers the question, and a condition that cannot be answered is not a no.

Build pool the way the call's would be. A condition sees the seeds of it, never a client argument, through the same definition the call is refused by, so the two see the same names only if they are handed the same seeds: base_pool with the same seeds=, and reserved=seeds.reserved here, or a condition reading a registered seed is asked without it.

The answer is advisory. Enforcement at the call (enforce_affordances) remains the authority, so a list built a moment before a condition flips is answered, when the stale entry is called, by an ActionUnavailable carrying the code this would return if asked again then (or a row condition's, where one declared earlier refuses first). A condition driven by a clock has no event: it is answered when asked, and nothing announces the moment it flips. A transport that can push list changes to its client needs something else to tell it when to ask again.

A SelectorSpec is accepted and answers None: its affordances maps names to other operations, to be answered for its rows, and is never a condition on the selector itself - so a transport passes whatever spec it holds rather than branching on its type and risking reading that mapping as the selector's own.

call_context is the call's context, handed to a callable condition that names it and never to one taking **kwargs for the rest: the dict passed, else the one pool carries, else a fresh one the conditions of this call share. A call_context passed beside a different one in pool raises ImproperlyConfigured (with_call_context).

docs.title: operation_affordances
docs.text:
operation_affordances(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
) -> tuple[Affordance, ...]

The operation-scope affordances spec declares, in declaration order.

The callable ones: the conditions answered without a row. A condition on the row is left out, and so is anything on a SelectorSpec, which answers (): its affordances maps names to other operations, to be answered for its rows, and reading that mapping as the selector's own conditions would answer a question about some other operation. A spec declaring none answers () too.

A transport uses this to decide cheaply whether there is anything to ask at list time before it builds a pool: most operations declare nothing, and an empty answer means unmet_operation_affordance would return None without running anything. That function selects its conditions here, so a transport's shortcut and the answer it skips cannot disagree about which conditions there are.

docs.title: aenforce_affordances async
docs.text:
aenforce_affordances(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SpecSource,
    pool: dict[str, Any],
    *,
    instance: Any,
    reserved: frozenset[str] = RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> None

enforce_affordances for an async caller.

For a transport that runs a service without adispatch, which answers a spec's affordances inside its own hop. It refuses and lets through exactly as the sync function does, with the same arguments.

A condition on the row is a query and a callable condition is user code that may query, and neither can run on the event loop. So every condition is answered in one sync_to_async(thread_sensitive=True) hop, as dispatch's async path runs every sync concept: not one hop per condition. A spec declaring none returns before the hop, so declaring nothing costs the async path nothing. spec may be a SpecSource, read as the spec it compiles to, and a SelectorSpec is refused with the sync function's TypeError whatever it declares.

Raises:

Type Description ActionUnavailable

An affordance is not met.

TypeError

spec is, or compiles to, a SelectorSpec.

ServiceNotFound

A condition on the row was reached and the row is gone.

ImproperlyConfigured

A condition on the row was reached and instance is not a model instance.

docs.title: aunmet_operation_affordance async
docs.text:
aunmet_operation_affordance(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    pool: dict[str, Any],
    *,
    reserved: frozenset[str] = RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> Affordance | None

unmet_operation_affordance for an async caller.

For a transport building its list of operations on an event loop: an MCP server answering a tool list, an agent assembling its next step's tools. It gives the sync function's answer for the same arguments.

A callable condition is user code and may query, so the conditions are answered in one sync_to_async(thread_sensitive=True) hop, as dispatch's async path runs every sync concept. A spec with nothing to ask at list time - nothing in operation_affordances, which is every SelectorSpec and every spec declaring only conditions on the row - returns None before the hop: a transport asks this for every operation it lists, and most declare nothing. spec may be a SpecSource, read as the spec it compiles to.

A caller that must release a connection a condition opens - a long-lived agent run, a worker with its own event loop - makes its own hop instead, calls unmet_operation_affordance inside it, and releases the connection in that same hop.

docs.title: PermissionCheck
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Whether a principal may run a spec, and whether they may act on a row.

A principal and a spec, and nothing else: no request and no view, because most transports have neither. Instances rather than classes, so a check can carry its own configuration (a codename, a group) and a spec reads as the list of checks it applies.

has_permission is the class-level check, run before any row is resolved, so a principal refused here learns nothing about which rows exist. has_object_permission runs against the resolved target of a retrieve or an update; it allows by default, because most checks are class-level only.

has_scope_permission is the same question for a call that resolves no single row: it is asked of the set a bulk call acts on or a collection reads, and of None where the call acts on no existing row (a create). It is a separate method rather than has_object_permission handed a set or None, because a check written for a row would read an attribute off it and fail on neither; it allows by default for the same reason.

A method may ask for the call's arguments by declaring a keyword arguments: dispatch then hands it the call's shape-checked arguments, as a read-only mapping, at each of the three questions - a route's captured pk, a filter the caller sent - and a method that does not declare it is asked without them. The base methods do not declare it, so every check written without it stays a valid override; a many call's rows are not among them, as they are validated after every check. Opt-in is by name, read layer by layer down the __wrapped__ chain functools.wraps leaves: a layer spreading **kwargs passes the keyword to the one beneath, so it is handed only where a layer names it before any layer without **kwargs, and a forwarding decorator keeps a check opted in. arguments is None where a transport calls authorize() without them, and a check that needs them decides for itself what that means; reading it as an allow fails open. Only the mapping is read-only: its values are the call's own objects, the ones the run receives, so a check must not mutate them.

A method may ask for the call's context and for a registered seed the same way: a keyword call_context is handed the one dict every stage of the call shares, a fresh one where the transport passed none, and a keyword named after a seed in the call's PoolSeeds is handed that seed's value. Only the seeds a spec's checks name are resolved before the class-level check, and the run reuses those values, so each resolves once per call and the check and the service see one object; a seed raising PrincipalUnavailable there ends the call as a refusal does. A parameter the call fills by position - the principal, the spec, the target or scope, whatever a method calls them - is never read as an opt-in, so a DRF-style has_permission(self, request, spec) under a transport registering a request seed is asked as before. A seed named arguments is never handed this way: arguments is always the call's arguments.

message is what NotPermitted says when this check refuses; None keeps the generic wording.

Sync-only, like every concept: a check may query, so the async path runs it in the executor. An async def method would answer with a coroutine, which is truthy and would allow every call, so a spec refuses a check declaring one when it is built, with ImproperlyConfigured naming the method; and an answer that is still to be awaited - from a plain def wrapping an async def - is refused where it is read, failing closed.

spec is typed Any in each method, and is always the ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec being run. The spec modules import this one to declare their permissions field, so naming either class here would make the package that declares specs and the one that judges them import each other. A subclass may annotate it ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec.

docs.title: has_permission abstractmethod
docs.text:
has_permission(principal: Any, spec: Any) -> bool

Whether principal may run spec at all.

spec is the ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec being run.

docs.title: has_object_permission
docs.text:
has_object_permission(principal: Any, spec: Any, target: Any) -> bool

Whether principal may act on target. Allows unless overridden.

spec is the ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec being run.

docs.title: has_scope_permission
docs.text:
has_scope_permission(principal: Any, spec: Any, scope: Any) -> bool

Whether principal may act on scope. Allows unless overridden.

spec is the ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec being run. scope is the resolved set of a bulk or collection call, or None for a call that acts on no existing row.

docs.title: Unrestricted
docs.text:
Bases: PermissionCheck

Anyone may run this spec: permissions=[Unrestricted()].

A spec that declares no permissions is refused at registration and at dispatch, because off HTTP there is no view whose policy it could inherit, and running it anyway is how an off-HTTP runner skips authorization with nothing warning. An operation that is genuinely open says so with this.

A named class rather than an empty list, so every open operation in a project is one search away, and an empty list computed by accident is not read as a decision: a spec handed one is refused when it is built.

docs.title: Grant dataclass
docs.text:
Proof that the class-level check already ran, for one spec and one principal.

Dispatch enforces permissions by default. A transport that authorized through its own machinery first - an HTTP view running its framework's permission classes - passes a grant instead, rather than skipping the check by omission, and pays one class-level evaluation per call instead of two.

Bound to one spec and one principal, by identity: a grant carried to another operation or another user covers nothing, and dispatch refuses it.

target_checked says the target-level checks ran too - has_object_permission on a row, has_scope_permission on a set or on nothing - which a transport can only claim once it has resolved the target itself. It covers the target handed to dispatch as target=, and nothing else: dispatch skips the checks only on that target. When dispatch looks the target up itself, from the arguments, it runs them whatever the grant says, since the row it finds may not be the one the grant was minted for. resolve_target mints such a grant for the target it returns, to be handed on with it. A selector spec takes no target=, so on one the flag covers nothing: its selector finds the row or the list from the arguments, and the checks run on what it found.

Without it, dispatch runs those checks on what it resolves.

Not serializable. Pickling one raises TypeError, so a grant cannot ride a queue into a worker: a task runs minutes later against state that may have moved, and it re-authorizes by construction.

docs.title: covers
docs.text:
covers(spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource, principal: Any) -> bool

Whether this grant is for exactly this spec and this principal.

The spec is compared as compiled: a grant minted for a SpecSource covers that object and the spec it compiles to, and a grant minted for the compiled spec covers the object, since each compiles once. Any other object is covered exactly when it compiles to that very spec: objects are compiled each on its own, so where a library compiles each declaration afresh, as djangorestframework-services does, a grant covers one declaration and not another that compares equal to it.

docs.title: authorize
docs.text:
authorize(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    principal: Any,
    *,
    grant: Grant | None = None,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    seeds: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> Grant

Run spec's class-level permission checks for principal.

Dispatch enforces this by default. A transport that already authorized through its own machinery - an HTTP view running its framework's permission classes - passes the Grant it produced instead of paying for a second evaluation; the grant is honoured only if it covers this exact spec and principal, by identity, so a grant carried over from another operation or another user is refused rather than trusted.

spec may be a SpecSource: each check is asked about the spec it compiles to, the object dispatch hands it for the same declaration, and the grant returned covers both.

Without a grant, spec.permissions is None is a configuration error, not the principal's fault: off HTTP there is no view whose policy an undeclared spec could inherit, so an operation that means to be open says so with permissions=[Unrestricted()].

Otherwise every check's has_permission must pass, in order; the first refusal raises NotPermitted with that check's own message, or the generic one when it declares none. An answer still to be awaited - a coroutine from a check that is not sync - raises ImproperlyConfigured rather than being read as a pass.

arguments is handed to each check's method that declares a keyword of that name, and to no other, so a check that declares none is asked without it. Dispatch passes the call's shape-checked arguments as a read-only mapping, whose values are the call's own and must not be mutated; None when the caller has none to hand.

call_context and seeds are offered the same way, by name: a method declaring call_context is handed the call's context - the dict the transport handed dispatch, a fresh one when it handed none or this is called without one - and a method naming a registered seed is handed that seed's value from seeds, which dispatch resolves for the call only when one of the spec's checks names one. A parameter the call fills by position is never read as an opt-in, whatever its name.

Returns:

Type Description Grant

The grant that was honoured, or a freshly minted one covering this

Grant

spec and principal.

docs.title: authorize_scope
docs.text:
authorize_scope(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    principal: Any,
    scope: Any,
    *,
    grant: Grant,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    seeds: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> None

Run spec's scope-level permission checks against scope.

The counterpart of authorize_target for a call that resolves no single row: scope is the resolved set of a bulk or collection call, or None for a create. Every check's has_scope_permission must pass, in order, and the first refusal raises NotPermitted with that check's own message. An answer still to be awaited raises ImproperlyConfigured rather than being read as a pass. A SpecSource is checked as the spec it compiles to.

grant.target_checked skips the checks here as it does there: a transport that already ran the target-level checks has claimed them. Dispatch honours it, as there, only for a service spec's target handed in as target=, so never on the list a selector spec reads.

arguments is handed to each check's method that declares a keyword of that name, and to no other, so a check that declares none is asked without it. Dispatch passes the call's shape-checked arguments as a read-only mapping, whose values are the call's own and must not be mutated; None when the caller has none to hand.

call_context and seeds are offered the same way, by name: a method declaring call_context is handed the call's context - the dict the transport handed dispatch, a fresh one when it handed none or this is called without one - and a method naming a registered seed is handed that seed's value from seeds, which dispatch resolves for the call only when one of the spec's checks names one. A parameter the call fills by position is never read as an opt-in, whatever its name.

docs.title: authorize_target
docs.text:
authorize_target(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    principal: Any,
    target: Any,
    *,
    grant: Grant,
    arguments: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    call_context: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    seeds: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> None

Run spec's object-level permission checks against a resolved target.

Dispatch calls this on a retrieved row, never on a list: a collection has no single object to check against, and a member-level rule belongs to the presenter or the query that shaped it.

grant.target_checked lets a transport that resolved the row itself and already ran the object-level check claim it once, so dispatch does not pay for it twice; dispatch honours it only for a service spec's target handed in as target=, and never on a selector spec's row (see Grant); otherwise every check's has_object_permission must pass, in order, and the first refusal raises NotPermitted with that check's own message. An answer still to be awaited raises ImproperlyConfigured rather than being read as a pass. A SpecSource is checked as the spec it compiles to.

spec.permissions is None means nothing to check here rather than a configuration error: authorize already refused an undeclared spec before any target could be resolved, so this function is never reached with one - iterating an empty tuple in its place is simpler than asserting an invariant this module cannot enforce.

arguments is handed to each check's method that declares a keyword of that name, and to no other, so a check that declares none is asked without it. Dispatch passes the call's shape-checked arguments as a read-only mapping, whose values are the call's own and must not be mutated; None when the caller has none to hand.

call_context and seeds are offered the same way, by name: a method declaring call_context is handed the call's context - the dict the transport handed dispatch, a fresh one when it handed none or this is called without one - and a method naming a registered seed is handed that seed's value from seeds, which dispatch resolves for the call only when one of the spec's checks names one. A parameter the call fills by position is never read as an opt-in, whatever its name.

docs.title: resolve_principal
docs.text:
resolve_principal(identifier: Any) -> Any

Look up the user who is to act, from an identifier a transport carries.

HTTP has a session or a token to resolve a principal from; most transports this kernel dispatches for do not, so a caller hands the primary key it already has (a queue payload, a management command argument, an agent's own notion of who is asking) and this is the one place that becomes a user row.

Every way an identifier can fail to name someone who may act becomes PrincipalUnavailable, terminal and never a fallback:

  • no row with that primary key (DoesNotExist), including a key past the range of an integer key's column, an infinite one among them, which no row can hold;
  • a malformed primary key (ValueError, TypeError, or Django's own ValidationError - a non-UUID string against a UUID primary key raises that one instead of ValueError);
  • the row is deactivated, by the rule dispatch applies to a principal it is handed (is_active false, and a model with no such field reads as active). So adispatch(principal_id=...) refuses here, with the identifier in the message, and dispatch's own check never disagrees.

Never AnonymousUser: an operation dispatched with no resolvable principal has no principal, not an anonymous one.

docs.title: is_deactivated
docs.text:
is_deactivated(principal: Any) -> bool

True for an authenticated principal whose is_active is false.

ModelBackend never logs a deactivated account in, but AllowAllUsersModelBackend and a project's own backend may, and a transport that holds a user object of its own may hand one over long after it was deactivated. The kernel's rule is that a deactivated principal never acts, whichever way it arrived.

The kernel reads the rule in two places: dispatch, refusing the principal it was handed, first and whether or not a Grant came with it; and resolve_principal, refusing the row an identifier named. It is public so that a transport in a distribution of its own refuses exactly the principals dispatch refuses, by calling this rather than restating it, as django-spec-html's entry points do with request.user before the request is read. It imports nothing that imports dispatch, so each reader can read it without a cycle.

Both attributes are read with getattr rather than assumed, because a principal is whatever a transport hands over:

  • No is_active reads as active, as ModelBackend reads it: a custom user model is not required to declare the field.
  • Anonymous is not deactivated. AnonymousUser.is_active is false, so the rule asks about authenticated principals alone, and anonymous goes on to the permission check, which is what decides whether anonymous may act. A principal with no is_authenticated is not anonymous, so it is read as authenticated and refused only when it says it is inactive.

Each condition is held by its own test in tests/authorization/test_is_deactivated.py: test_anonymous_is_not_deactivated fails without the first and test_an_active_user_is_not_deactivated without the second.

docs.title: NotPermitted
docs.text:
Bases: DispatchError

A permission check refused the principal, or a grant did not cover the call.

Named for what a failed has_permission means, literally. Not PermissionDenied, which Django and DRF both own for their own exceptions, and not a service error: a model that reads a denial as a refusal to route around keeps trying, where a denial should end the attempt.

docs.title: PrincipalUnavailable
docs.text:
Bases: DispatchError

The principal cannot act: an identifier naming nobody, or a deactivated account.

Raised by resolve_principal for an identifier that is missing, malformed or names a deactivated row, and by dispatch for a deactivated principal it was handed. Either way it comes before any permission check, which is about what a principal may do, not whether there is one.

Terminal. Never a fallback to AnonymousUser, which would run the operation as somebody the caller did not name, and never a retry: a deleted row does not come back, and a deactivated account is deactivated on purpose.

docs.title: run_service
docs.text:
run_service(fn: Callable[..., Any], kwargs: dict[str, Any], *, atomic: bool) -> Any

Call fn(**kwargs) from sync code, optionally inside transaction.atomic().

An async def service is bridged transparently via async_to_sync. The bridge is not optional politeness: without it an async service returns its coroutine object to the caller un-awaited — no exception, and under atomic=True the transaction commits before the body would have run.

Async services under atomic=True route through arun_service, which owns the thread-sensitivity rule that keeps the ORM connection holding the open transaction the same one the inner async DB calls use.

docs.title: arun_service async
docs.text:
arun_service(
    fn: Callable[..., Awaitable[Any]], kwargs: dict[str, Any], *, atomic: bool
) -> Any

Await fn(**kwargs), optionally inside transaction.atomic().

docs.title: ServiceError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

Raised by services to signal a business-rule failure.

Carries a message and nothing else, so a transport can surface it without the service depending on that transport. A structured payload belongs to a member that declares one: ServiceValidationError carries a field-keyed detail.

docs.title: ServiceValidationError
docs.text:
Bases: ServiceError

Raised by services to signal invalid input or invalid state.

Distinct from ServiceError so a transport can tell "the arguments were fine but the business rule refused" from "the input itself is invalid" and map the two differently. detail may be a string, a dict (field → error(s)), or a list of errors.

docs.title: ServiceConflict
docs.text:
Bases: ServiceError

The operation collides with the resource's current state.

A slot already taken, a row someone else moved first, a name already used. The resource is there and the request is well-formed; the two are simply incompatible right now, and a caller can often resolve it by re-reading and trying again — distinct from a plain ServiceError, which says "understood, and still not doing it" with no such implication.

def slot_is_free(*, user, data):
    if Event.objects.filter(owner=user, day=data["day"], hour=data["hour"]).exists():
        raise ServiceConflict(f"{data['day']} at {data['hour']}:00 is taken.")

A transport that has never heard of this type still handles a ServiceError, and one that wants to do better matches on the class. It must match before its generic ServiceError handler, or the subclass check swallows it.

docs.title: ServiceNotFound
docs.text:
Bases: ServiceError

The operation's target does not exist, or is not this caller's to see.

The distinction from a plain ServiceError is which thing is wrong: the resource is absent rather than in the wrong state, so a client should stop asking rather than try again differently.

def move_event(*, user, data):
    event = Event.objects.filter(owner=user, pk=data["event_id"]).first()
    if event is None:
        raise ServiceNotFound(f"No event {data['event_id']}.")

Say the same thing for "absent" and "not yours." Answering a permission refusal for a row the caller cannot see confirms that it exists, which is why the owner-scoped lookup above raises this either way.

A transport that has never heard of this type still handles a ServiceError, and one that wants to do better matches on the class. It must match before its generic ServiceError handler, or the subclass check swallows it.

docs.title: ActionUnavailable
docs.text:
Bases: ServiceConflict

The operation is not possible right now, for a reason with a stable name.

Raised when one of a spec's Affordance conditions is not met, carrying that affordance's code and its reason as the message. django-spec-html's error_response answers it over HTTP as a 409 whose body is {"detail": <reason>, "code": <code>}.

A ServiceConflict subclass rather than a code= argument on its parent, for three reasons. The 409 answer needs no new status, because a subclass is matched by its parent's arm. A transport that wants the code matches this class ahead of its generic conflict handler, and one that has never heard of it still reports a conflict. And a ServiceConflict a service raises by hand genuinely has no code and never will, so a nullable code on the parent would be a field that lies at every other call site.

code names the rule and is what a transport or client branches on; the message is the affordance's reason, the sentence a person or a model is shown when the call is refused. A transport serving an agent should pass on both: the model can say the sentence, and the code is what stays stable when the sentence is reworded.

Like every member, it must be matched before a generic ServiceConflict or ServiceError handler, or the subclass check swallows it.

docs.title: AdditionalInputRequired
docs.text:
Bases: ServiceError

A service cannot proceed without a value it was not given.

Not "what you sent is wrong" - that is ServiceValidationError - but "I got far enough to discover I need something else", usually conditional on what the service found, so it cannot be expressed as a required parameter:

def delete_rows(*, data, confirmed: bool = False):
    doomed = rows_matching(data)
    if len(doomed) > 100 and not confirmed:
        raise AdditionalInputRequired(
            f"{len(doomed)} rows match. Confirm to proceed.",
            schema={"confirmed": {"type": "boolean"}},
        )
    ...

schema describes what is missing, keyed by the argument name the service expects it back under: a transport that can ask renders it, one that cannot still has a message worth showing. The answer comes back as an ordinary argument on every transport - an HTTP client re-submits with confirmed in the body, an MCP client is asked and its answer is merged into the tool arguments before dispatch - so raising is the whole of the service's involvement; there is no callback to hold and no session to resume. The operation declares that argument like any other, so the closed argument set admits it on the second call.

A ServiceError subclass deliberately, so a transport that has never heard of it still reports that the operation could not be completed and why. One that wants to do better must catch it before its generic ServiceError handler.

docs.title: CreateService
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[InputT, ResultT]

The structural shape of a service that takes validated input and no target.

data is what the spec's Validator returned, under the pool's reserved data seed. **extras absorbs whatever else the keyword pool delivers - user, a registered seed, the spec's kwargs - without the service declaring each key. It is typed Any so a service conforms under every type checker.

Nothing reads the Protocol at run time: dispatch binds a service from the keywords it declares whatever it is annotated with, so conforming is a claim checked by a type checker, through implements.

Strictly typed extras stay possible on the service's own signature: declare them as a TypedDict whose keys are all NotRequired and annotate **extras: Unpack[YourExtras], so extras["tenant"] is typed in the body. NotRequired because the Protocol's caller may not supply them. The Protocol carries no type argument for the extras, since that cross-check is not portable across type checkers.

docs.title: UpdateService
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[InputT, InstanceT, ResultT]

The structural shape of a service that acts on a resolved row with validated input.

instance is the row the spec's instance_selector_spec resolved, under the pool's reserved instance seed, and data what the spec's Validator returned.

See CreateService for **extras and strictly typed extras.

docs.title: DeleteService
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[InputT, InstanceT, ResultT]

The structural shape of a service that acts on a resolved row, input optional.

instance is the row the spec's instance_selector_spec resolved. Most deletes return None.

data has a default in the Protocol, so a service that reads no input conforms without declaring it: bind InputT to NoInput and leave data out. A delete that does take input - a reason, a confirmation - binds InputT to its input type and declares data with a default of its own, data: ReasonInput | None = None: declared without one it does not conform, since the Protocol's caller may leave data out.

See CreateService for **extras and strictly typed extras.

docs.title: implements
docs.text:
implements(proto: type[F]) -> Callable[[F], F]

Return the decorated callable unchanged, typed as conforming to proto.

proto is a parameterised service or selector Protocol:

@implements(CreateService[NoteInput, Note])
def create_note(*, data: NoteInput, **extras: Any) -> Note: ...

A type checker reports a callable that does not conform - a keyword the Protocol passes and the callable does not take, a return of the wrong type - at the decorator line, as ty does.

It lives in services/ beside the service Protocols, and decorates a selector the same way, with ListSelector or RetrieveSelector. Nothing changes at run time: dispatch binds a callable from the keywords it declares, annotated or not.

docs.title: PoolSeeds dataclass
docs.text:
Names a project adds to every dispatched callable's kwargs pool.

The names in RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS are the dispatcher's own. Everything else a service legitimately needs — a tenant, a correlation id, a locale, a clock, a feature-flag reader — has no channel, because off HTTP there is no request for it to hang off. This is that channel.

A registration contributes two things:

  • the value, resolved into every pool base_pool builds;
  • reservation: dispatch refuses a spec whose Parameters declare the name, and a Validator that returns a value under it, so an argument never meets a seed in one pool. A caller sending the name is then refused as an unknown argument, or dropped under UnknownArguments.IGNORE, like any other name the spec does not declare.

The reason the two travel together is that either alone is a trap. A seed with a value and no reservation shares the pool with an argument of the same name, and which of the two a callable receives would depend on spreading order; a reserved name with no value makes a callable that declares it fail with a TypeError instead.

Immutable, and extend returns a new registry rather than mutating, so there is no shared global state to leak between mounts or across tests. Pass one per dispatch rather than installing it process-wide: a project that mounts two operations with different ambient context needs them to differ, and a module-level default cannot.

seeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS.extend(tenant=lambda *, user: user.tenant)
dispatch(spec, principal=user, arguments=arguments, pool_seeds=seeds)

A resolver is called through the same declare-to-receive rule as every other spec callable: it names the pool entries it wants (user, an adapter's own entry) and receives only those, or takes **kwargs for all of them.

A resolver is sync-only. A seed is a resolver - a callable whose return is the value - and resolvers are called from sync code and never awaited. An async def one would seed a coroutine, which is truthy, so an affordance condition or a precondition reading the seed would read an answer nobody computed. One is refused when the registry is built, with ImproperlyConfigured; a plain def handing back an awaitable is refused where it is resolved, by base_pool.

Attributes:

Name Type Description seeds tuple[_Seed, ...]

The registrations, in registration order.

docs.title: names property
docs.text:
names: frozenset[str]

The registered names, without their resolvers.

docs.title: reserved property
docs.text:
reserved: frozenset[str]

Every name an argument may not occupy: the dispatcher's plus these.

Dispatch reads this rather than RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS directly, which is what makes a registered seed as protected as a built-in one.

docs.title: extend
docs.text:
extend(**seeds: Callable[..., Any]) -> PoolSeeds

Return a new registry with seeds appended.

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

A resolver is async - an async def, an object whose __call__ is one, or an async generator function. A resolver is never awaited.

ValueError

A name is one of the dispatcher's own, or is already registered here. Both are refused at registration rather than at dispatch, because a silent last-wins is the exact failure the reservation exists to prevent — and a collision discovered on the hot path is one a test suite can miss.

docs.title: resolvers
docs.text:
resolvers() -> Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]]

The registrations as a mapping, for a caller that resolves them.

Resolution itself lives in base_pool rather than here: it needs the declare-to-receive helper (resolve_callable_kwargs), and this module stays a plain value carrier so nothing in pool/ depends on it in a cycle.

docs.title: DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS module-attribute
docs.text:
DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS: PoolSeeds = PoolSeeds()

The empty registry every dispatch entry point falls back to.

A project that registers nothing gets the pool dispatch builds on its own: the principal as user, a reporter as progress, and each step's own values (data, instance, collection, result, queryset) where that step has them.

docs.title: RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS module-attribute
docs.text:
RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS: Final[frozenset[str]] = frozenset(
    {
        "user",
        "data",
        "instance",
        "collection",
        "result",
        "queryset",
        "progress",
        "call_context",
        "shapes",
    }
)

The names dispatch seeds into a callable's keyword pool, which no argument may use.

user is the principal, progress the caller's progress reporter, data the validated values, instance and collection the resolved target, result the service's return (in an output selector's pool, where instance is that return too, as djangorestframework-services binds it) and queryset what extend_queryset shapes. call_context is the call's context: the one plain dict the transport handed dispatch, or a fresh one per call when it handed none, which every callable dispatch resolves - a kwargs or input_data provider, a selector and its extend_queryset, an affordance condition, a precondition, the service, the run's progress_reporter - receives as the same object by naming it, and never through **kwargs. Never a copy, and the kernel writes nothing to it. Seed resolvers do not see it: a seed is resolved before anything the call adds. shapes is what the caller sent for the spec's declared shapes, keyed by shape name and read-only: the mapping PresentationContext.shapes holds, so a selector that eager-loads by the query its presenter renders reads the value the presenter reads. It is in the pools dispatch builds for a spec's callables: a selector and its extend_queryset, a kwargs or input_data provider, a precondition, the service, the run's progress_reporter, and a service spec's output selector. A service spec's target selector is handed an empty mapping instead, on every route, because resolve_target checks only the target's own parameters and the lookup must find the same row either way (test_a_target_selector_is_handed_no_shapes_on_any_route). It is an empty mapping on a spec declaring no shapes, and, like call_context, it is handed only to a callable naming it, never through **kwargs. Unlike call_context it is not in an affordance condition's pool, the Validator's (a FormValidator's form_kwargs included) or a mutation helper's nested row services', and like it, not in a seed resolver's or a filter_set's (test_form_kwargs_naming_the_shapes_is_handed_no_seed, test_a_seed_resolver_naming_the_shapes_is_handed_none, test_a_filter_naming_the_shapes_is_handed_none; a helper's row services are handed its **kwargs, which test_a_catch_all_is_never_handed_the_shapes keeps free of the seed). The seven besides those two are the names djangorestframework-services seeds for the same values, so a callable written for it runs under this kernel unchanged.

progress is in every pool, and live only where there is work to report on: a service's run, and a selector spec's own selector. In a target or output selector's pool it is null_progress, because a lookup has nothing to report, and one reporting after the service finished would read to a watching client as the work restarting.

A parameter declaring one of these names is refused, because a spread argument must never be able to outrank the value dispatch seeded - a caller naming itself user is the case that matters. request and view are not here: they are an HTTP adapter's, and it registers them through PoolSeeds, which reserves them the same way.

docs.title: base_pool
docs.text:
base_pool(
    *,
    user: Any,
    progress: ProgressReporter | None = None,
    seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
    **extra: Any,
) -> dict[str, Any]

The seeds a dispatched callable's kwargs pool carries, on every transport.

Every pool dispatch and adispatch build routes through here, so a spec callable that declares a seed behaves the same whichever entry point resolved it.

That is a property of the pools built here, not a rule the kernel can enforce on its callers: this is a builder, not a gate. A transport adapter that assembles a pool as a dict literal of its own carries exactly the keys it wrote there, because resolve_callable_kwargs forwards only keys the pool actually has. A callable declaring a seed the literal omitted then raises TypeError at call time rather than running - progress most often, since it is the seed with a default and so the one nobody remembers.

There is no request entry here: this is the kernel, and off HTTP there is no request to seed. An HTTP adapter that wants one registers it as its own seed through PoolSeeds, the same way any other ambient value is added.

A seed resolving to an awaitable is refused with ImproperlyConfigured and never enters the pool. PoolSeeds refuses an async def resolver when it is registered, but a plain def handing back a coroutine - a decorated async def, a partial over one - looks sync until it answers. Nothing awaits a pool entry, and a coroutine is truthy, so a condition reading it would read an unmet condition as met.

progress is the caller's reporter, and defaults to null_progress rather than to None, so a declared reporter is always callable - see ProgressReporter. Only None is replaced: a reporter that happens to be falsy, such as a list-backed recorder that is empty until its first report, is seeded as it is, where djangorestframework-services' or would swap it for null_progress and drop every report. A seed's resolver sees it like any other entry.

An adapter that dispatches callables through this package must build its pool from this function, with its own entries spread in — base_pool(user=…, **own_entries) — rather than restating the seeds. Routing those entries through **extra is also what makes a name collision loud: an entry called user raises TypeError here, where in a dict literal it would quietly outrank the value the transport authenticated.

seeds is the project's own registry (PoolSeeds), resolved into every pool this builds. It is the supported way to add an entry, and the difference from spreading one through **extra is not convenience: a registered name is also reserved, so dispatch refuses a spec that declares an argument by that name rather than letting the two meet in one pool. An **extra entry has no such protection. Spread an entry that is genuinely per-call; register one that is ambient.

docs.title: null_progress
docs.text:
null_progress(
    progress: float,
    *,
    total: float | None = None,
    message: str | None = None,
    meta: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> None

The ProgressReporter a transport with nowhere to send progress uses.

Seeded by base_pool whenever the caller supplied no reporter, which is every dispatch from a transport with no progress channel of its own, every HTTP request, and every test.

The default is what makes the seed usable. Without it, a service declaring progress would work over one transport and raise a TypeError over the others, so nobody could declare it in code meant to be shared - which is the entire premise of writing a service once. Discarding the report is the honest behaviour for a caller that cannot forward it; refusing the call is not.

docs.title: combine_progress
docs.text:
combine_progress(*reporters: ProgressReporter | None) -> ProgressReporter

One ProgressReporter forwarding to all of reporters.

For a transport with more than one sink of its own to hand dispatch's progress=: the channel back to its client - MCP notifications, a websocket - beside a task record, an audit trail or metrics. Neither displaces the other; each report reaches every sink, in the order given.

Each sink is isolated. A sink that raises neither skips the sinks after it nor reaches the service that reported, because telemetry failing must not take down the run it describes. The failure is swallowed, not logged: a sink that cares about its own errors handles them inside itself, where the context to act on them is. No sink may depend on the order, since none can observe whether an earlier one succeeded.

This is not how dispatch joins a spec's own progress_reporter to the transport's reporter: there, a sink's failure reaches the service, as the transport's own reporter failing does.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default *reporters ProgressReporter | None

The sinks, in call order. None is dropped, so an optional reporter can be passed straight through.

()

Returns:

Type Description ProgressReporter

null_progress

ProgressReporter

when no sink is left, so the result is always callable; the one sink

ProgressReporter

itself, unwrapped, when one is left; otherwise a reporter handing each

ProgressReporter

report to every sink.

docs.title: provider_keys
docs.text:
provider_keys(provider: Callable[..., Any] | None) -> ProviderKeys | None

The names provider fills and those it may decline, or None if it does not say.

The static half of the kwargs= provider contract, whose runtime half is how dispatch calls the provider. ServiceSpec.kwargs and SelectorSpec.kwargs return a mapping, and one annotated to return a TypedDict says, before it runs, which names it fills. A transport reads that here to build a schema that does not ask the caller for them, and to know which calls to refuse before dispatch, rather than keeping a copy of this reader.

Returns a ProviderKeys, (filled, declinable): two disjoint sets that together are every key of the TypedDict, the keys the provider always answers for and the keys whose value admits UnsetType, which it may decline with UNSET. It unpacks as a pair and names each set, so keys.filled reads as well as filled, declinable = keys.

ProviderKeys(frozenset(), frozenset()) for provider=None: a spec with no provider fills nothing. None when the provider says nothing about its keys -- no return annotation, a plain dict, a lambda, or a return annotation that does not resolve -- so it may fill any name, and a transport requires none of them for lacking a default. Held by test_a_spec_without_a_provider_fills_nothing and test_a_provider_whose_return_says_nothing_is_untyped.

Each annotation costs only what it says. The return annotation is resolved on its own, in the globals of the function a decorator wrapped rather than the wrapper's (decorated-elsewhere in test_a_generic_typed_dicts_arguments_decide_which_keys_may_be_declined), so a parameter annotation naming a type imported only under TYPE_CHECKING leaves the keys readable (test_a_parameter_type_imported_only_for_type_checking_leaves_the_keys_readable). The keys are read off the TypedDict without hints, and each value is resolved on its own, so one that does not resolve makes only its own key declinable: whether the provider may decline it cannot be read, and declinable is the reading that neither hides the name from the caller nor requires it (test_a_value_type_that_does_not_resolve_makes_only_its_key_declinable). Python 3.14's lazily evaluated annotations are read the same way, in the format that leaves an unresolvable name as a forward reference rather than raising (test_lazily_evaluated_annotations_are_read_one_at_a_time). That format is why typing-extensions is floored at 4.14: on 3.14, 4.13 hands the standard library's annotationlib a format number it reserves for internal use, which raises, and every typed provider would read as untyped.

A generic TypedDict is read with whatever binds its parameters. Scope[str | UnsetType] does not relay __required_keys__, so the keys come off Scope, where a value annotated T is the bare type variable. What T stands for is substituted wherever it appears in a value, a union included, whether an alias's arguments bind it (test_a_generic_typed_dicts_arguments_decide_which_keys_may_be_declined) or a class statement does, as class Declining(Scope[str | UnsetType]) does, and a subclass handing its own parameter on to Scope (test_a_subclass_binding_decides_which_keys_may_be_declined). An argument that does not admit UNSET still fills the key (test_a_parameterised_typed_dict_is_read_off_its_origin), and one wrapped in Annotated is read as what it wraps (test_annotated_around_a_binding_is_read_as_what_it_annotates). A PEP 695 class Scope[T](TypedDict) is read the same way under postponed annotations, where the "T" a value leaves resolves only beside the class's __type_params__ (test_a_pep_695_type_parameter_is_read_as_the_class_declares_it).

Each key is read with the bindings of the class that declared it, so one T reused at every level reads as each class binds it: class Shadow(Scope[list[T]], Generic[T]) with extra: T, returned as Shadow[str | UnsetType], fills tenant with a list and may decline extra (test_each_key_is_read_with_the_bindings_of_the_class_that_declared_it). A key reached through two bases that bind it differently is filled if either reading fills it.

A type variable nothing binds counts as filled, as in a bare -> Scope (test_a_type_variable_nothing_binds_is_filled). Whether it may be UNSET is written nowhere, and filled keeps the decision with the provider by hiding the key from the caller. Declinable would let a transport whose caller's value wins put that value in a key the provider was meant to decide, such as a tenant.

Three readings stay as they are, each held by a test:

  • A PEP 696 default on a type variable is not consulted (test_a_type_variables_default_is_not_consulted).
  • A base that cannot be substituted makes the provider read as untyped (test_a_base_that_cannot_be_substituted_leaves_the_provider_untyped).
  • A key a subclass redeclares is read with its base's bindings, since no runtime record says which class wrote it (test_a_key_a_subclass_redeclares_is_read_with_its_bases_bindings).

Duck-typed on the keys a TypedDict class carries rather than is_typeddict, because the standard library's answers False for a typing_extensions.TypedDict on the older Pythons this package supports.

docs.title: server_owned_keys
docs.text:
server_owned_keys(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    *,
    pool_seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
) -> frozenset[str]

Every name spec's dispatch fills from the server, whatever the caller sends.

For a transport building an input schema of its own, beside the one parameters() describes: subtract this set from what it lists, so it asks the caller for no key the server answers anyway. The union of:

  • the names the pool seeds carry: the dispatcher's own (user, data, instance and the rest) and every seed pool_seeds registers, but a registered seed's name that the spec's Validator declares as a top-level field. Such a field is the caller's to send: dispatch validates it into data and leaves the service's parameter of its name to the seed, so a transport subtracting this set still asks for it (test_server_owned_keys_leaves_such_a_field_out_and_a_service_may_ask_for_it). A read marked reflected and named like a registered seed is here, since the seed fills it and the call takes no argument of its name;
  • the keys each provider the dispatch runs is annotated to fill, as provider_keys reads them: the spec's kwargs and, on a service spec, its input_data and its target selector's kwargs. Dispatch drops the caller's value for a key a provider fills once it has been checked, so the key holds the author's value whatever the caller sent. When the provider leaves it out or returns UNSET, a parameter declared required is refused where the provider's answer is merged, and one that is not is absent.

No name here is a parameter dispatch demands of the caller, so a key a provider fills is the server's for the whole call. Each provider's values reach one seat - a selector's kwargs that selector's reads, a service spec's kwargs its reads, input_data its Validator's fields - and dispatch does not demand a parameter there that the provider fills. A filled key that a parameter in any other seat declares is refused when the spec is built, or, for a Validator field, when parameters() is assembled. A key no parameter declares is the server's alone.

A key a provider may decline with UNSET is not here, nor is any key of a provider whose return says nothing about its keys, which may fill any name and so names none. Dispatch does not demand either of the caller, since the provider may fill it, and keeps the caller's value beneath the provider's answer, so the caller's is the one the callable receives when the provider declines. A transport that asks the caller for neither reads them off provider_keys: its declinable keys, or every parameter in the seat of a provider it reads as None.

Static per spec. A transport that also answers some declared parameters itself, per mount or per toolset, describes them with a ServerArguments and subtracts its names() beside this set: those are parameters the spec declares and the caller is still not asked for.

A SpecSource owns what the spec it compiles to owns. djangorestframework-services' own reading adds the keys its reflected input markers hide, which this package does not read.

docs.title: resolve_callable_kwargs
docs.text:
resolve_callable_kwargs(fn: Callable[..., Any], pool: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]

Pick the subset of pool matching fn's declared parameters.

Every pool-resolved callable in the kernel — a seed's resolver, a spec's selector, extend_queryset, a service — binds through this one rule, so a callable written for one entry point runs unchanged on another: it names what it wants and gets exactly that, or takes **kwargs for the rest of the pool, which is every entry but the call's context.

If fn declares **kwargs, the entire pool is passed, except a name handed by name only (BY_NAME_ONLY_POOL_NAMES, the call's context), which reaches a catch-all only where it also names it. Otherwise only parameters present in the signature are forwarded.

docs.title: create_from_input
docs.text:
create_from_input(
    model: type[ModelT],
    data: Any,
    *,
    field_map: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    exclude_fields: list[str] | None = None,
    m2m: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    relations: Mapping[str, RelationSpec] | None = None,
    context: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> ChangeResult[ModelT]

Build, save(), and return a fresh instance of model.

Regular fields come from data (a dataclass, dict, or object with __dict__).

A file field is written as a ModelForm writes it, through the model field's save_form_data: a file is stored, None leaves the field to the model, and False, a form's value for a cleared file, stores no file.

m2m maps a many-to-many attribute to the rows it should hold — instances or primary keys of rows that already exist — and set()s them after the save; it creates nothing. A ManyToManySpec in relations does the other job: it writes the target rows from the payload, creating or updating each, and then links them. A relation named by both is refused, since it would be written twice and keep whichever ran last.

relations maps a relation name to the spec for its kind, and is the one map for every kind — a reverse-FK ChildSpec included. The nested payload is read from data[relation] and written in the order the kind dictates, not the order the map is spelled in (see RelationPhase). Keep the whole call inside the service's atomic block.

context is an opaque mapping forwarded verbatim down the tree, into the pool of every row service a relation spec declares and of every scope callable. This helper never reads it — it exists so per-row work downstream can see the acting caller. A service opts in by handing on the pool it was called with, context=kwargs. A catch-all is never handed the call's context, so a service whose nested callables should see it names call_context and hands it on beside the pool, as create_model's service does.

docs.title: update_from_input
docs.text:
update_from_input(
    instance: ModelT,
    data: Any,
    *,
    field_map: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    exclude_fields: list[str] | None = None,
    m2m: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    update_fields: bool | list[str] = True,
    relations: Mapping[str, RelationSpec] | None = None,
    context: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> ChangeResult[ModelT]

Update instance with values from data, persisting only deltas.

By default (update_fields=True), the save call uses update_fields=<changed> to write the minimal set of columns. auto_now=True fields (e.g. updated_at) are automatically added to that list so they are refreshed alongside the mutation, and so are a changed ImageField's width_field and height_field, which setting the image wrote on the instance. Pass False to perform a full save, or an explicit list to control exactly which columns are written (no auto-injection in that case).

A file field is written as a ModelForm writes it, through the model field's save_form_data: a file replaces the one the row holds, None keeps it, and False, a form's value for a cleared file, leaves no file, reported as a change to "". An upload, or any File that is not one a row holds, is always written and reported, even under the name of the file it replaces, since a name says nothing of the content; the held file handed back as itself is no change.

m2m assigns many-to-many rows that already exist, and only where the set of primary keys differs from the current one; ManyToManySpec in relations writes the target rows from the payload instead. A relation named by both is refused rather than written twice.

relations maps a relation name to the spec for its kind, one map for every kind. The nested payload from data[relation] is reconciled with what is already there — create / update / orphan-remove per the spec — and a relation the input omits is left untouched. Kinds are written in the order their class dictates, so a forward foreign key is resolved before this instance is saved and the assignment rides the same diff and update_fields path as any other column. Keep the call inside the service's atomic block.

A relation that was written stays readable off the returned instance. The one-row kinds resolve their row by re-querying, so the parent's cached related object is replaced with the row that was written — and dropped where the write removed it — rather than left holding pre-write values.

context is an opaque mapping forwarded verbatim into the pool of every row service and scope callable the relation specs declare; this helper never reads it. See create_from_input.

docs.title: delete_relations
docs.text:
delete_relations(
    instance: ModelT,
    *,
    relations: Mapping[str, RelationSpec],
    context: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> ChangeResult[ModelT]

Remove the rows instance owns, deepest first, and leave instance.

The cascade for a delete service to run where the database will not: a PROTECT foreign key, a relation whose row services must see each removal, or a soft delete, which Django never cascades through because no row is deleted. The service deletes (or retires) instance itself afterwards, inside the same atomic block.

relations is the same map the write helpers take, so one declaration describes both how a payload is written and what goes when the row does. One rule covers every kind: the rows the instance owns are disposed of, and the rows it merely points at are not.

  • A ChildSpec or GenericRelationSpec collection, and a ReverseOneToOneSpec row, is disposed of after its own declared relations, so a non-nullable grandchild goes first. Each row is deleted, unlinked or handed to the spec's delete_service by the rule a write removing it follows: the spec's orphan setting, or the service when one is declared.
  • A ManyToManySpec loses its membership, and its target rows survive.
  • A ForwardRelationSpec is reported untouched rather than refused: its row is not the instance's, and refusing it would make a map that is right for writing impossible to cascade.

The returned ChangeResult reports the collections under children and the one-row kinds under relations, as a write does, with no field changes. The instance's cached relations are brought in line with the removal, so an instance that outlives its cascade renders without the rows it lost.

context is an opaque mapping forwarded verbatim into the pool of every row service the specs declare; this helper never reads it.

docs.title: adelete_relations async
docs.text:
adelete_relations(
    instance: ModelT,
    *,
    relations: Mapping[str, RelationSpec],
    context: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> ChangeResult[ModelT]

Async variant of delete_relations.

The same rule, the same order and the same report, through Django's async ORM. A row service a spec declares must be async def here, as in every async helper: one the loop cannot await is refused, naming its slot.

docs.title: register_row_error
docs.text:
register_row_error(
    error_class: type[ErrorT], read_detail: Callable[[ErrorT], Any]
) -> None

Re-root error_class under the row that raised it, as the kernel's own refusals are.

A relation write re-addresses a refusal raised inside one row - by a row service, or by the write of a row further down - under that row's place in the arguments, so the caller learns which row was refused. It does that for the two refusals this package raises and for Django's own write failures. A refusal from a library this package cannot name - a framework's validation error, raised by a row service written for that framework - would otherwise escape naming no row. Registering its class puts it in the same tree:

  • read_detail is handed the exception and returns its detail: a mapping of field names to messages, or the row's own messages as a list or a string. It is placed at the row's address as the kernel's refusals are - a collection's row under its int index, a list or string under non_field_errors inside the row - and the messages are kept as they are, codes and all.
  • The re-rooted tree is handed to error_class as its one argument, and that is what is raised. The class is kept because the class says who refused and decides how each transport answers. A subclass raised by a row is caught as the registered class and rebuilt as it, so register the narrowest class whose constructor takes a detail this way.

A grandchild's refusal is re-rooted at each row it passes, so it arrives carrying both addresses. A list form - a list as long as the incoming one, empty against the rows that passed - is a rendering of this tree, and the transport answering in it renders it.

Registering the same class with the same reader again does nothing, so a registration that runs at import or in an AppConfig.ready() may run twice. Pass a module-level function rather than a lambda built per call, which would be a second reader. Raises ImproperlyConfigured for:

  • something that is not an exception class;
  • a class already registered with a different reader, which keeps the first;
  • a class the kernel already re-roots, or one wider than such a class: a ServiceValidationError or InvalidArguments, or Django's ValidationError, ValueError or TypeError. A narrower one would never be asked, and a wider one, Exception at its widest, would read the caller's own bug in a row service as a refusal of the arguments. Each of the five is refused by its own case of test_a_class_the_kernel_already_reads_is_refused, and the wider direction by test_a_class_wider_than_one_the_kernel_reads_is_refused.

Registrations are process-wide, as the relation specs that read them are, and there is no removal: an adapter registers for the life of the process.

docs.title: ChangeResult dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Generic[ModelT]

Outcome of a mutation helper call.

instance is the model instance after the mutation. created is True iff this came from create_from_input / acreate_from_input. changes records every field whose value actually differed from its prior value (or from UNSET for creates).

Every relation declared in relations= reports in one of two fields, chosen by the relation's shape. children carries one ChildCollectionChange per collection: a reverse-FK ChildSpec, a GenericRelationSpec and a ManyToManySpec. relations carries one RelatedObjectChange per one-row relation: a ForwardRelationSpec and a ReverseOneToOneSpec. A collection reports tuples of pks and a one-row relation reports an outcome, so they are different carriers. Both are empty when no relation is declared, and a declared relation the input omits still gets its entry, reporting nothing. A forward relation shows up twice and means two different things — here as what happened to the row it points at, and in changes as the parent's foreign-key column, which only appears if it actually changed.

The class is generic over the concrete model type: callers that pass Author into a mutation helper get back a ChangeResult[Author] whose .instance is typed as Author. The bare name ChangeResult (no parameter) resolves to ChangeResult[Model] and keeps working for callers that don't care.

docs.text:
changed_fields: tuple[str, ...]

Names of every field present in changes.

docs.text:
get_field_change(field_name: str) -> FieldChange | None

Return the FieldChange for field_name, or None.

docs.title: get_child_change
docs.text:
get_child_change(relation: str) -> ChildCollectionChange | None

Return the ChildCollectionChange for relation, or None.

docs.title: get_relation_change
docs.text:
get_relation_change(relation: str) -> RelatedObjectChange | None

Return the RelatedObjectChange for relation, or None.

docs.title: FieldChange dataclass
docs.text:
One field's before/after pair from a mutation.

old will be UNSET for fields populated as part of a create (no prior value existed).

docs.title: ChildCollectionChange dataclass
docs.text:
What a nested write did to one relation that holds a collection.

Carried in ChangeResult.children, one entry per collection declared in relations=: a reverse-FK ChildSpec, a GenericRelationSpec or a ManyToManySpec. A relation holding one row reports a RelatedObjectChange instead. The tuples hold row primary keys:

  • created — rows inserted.
  • updated — rows that already existed, matched by the spec's match_key and written: among the parent's own rows for a child or generic collection, inside scope for a many-to-many.
  • deleted — rows the relation let go and deleted.
  • unlinked — rows the relation let go and kept, with their link to the parent set to None.
  • removed — rows handed to the spec's delete_service. Deliberately a fifth tuple rather than a reuse of deleted: once a service owns the row, the loop no longer knows whether it was deleted, archived, unlinked or left standing, and folding those into deleted would report a guess as fact. What the loop does know is that the row left the relation and a service decided the rest.

Whether a row let go is deleted or unlinked is the spec's orphan (RelationOrphan), not the column alone: "delete" always deletes; "unlink" always unlinks, and is refused where the link cannot hold NULL; "auto", the default, unlinks when it can — both columns, for a generic relation — and deletes when it cannot. A many-to-many target is shared, so a member "replace" drops only loses its membership and is always unlinked; that kind has no orphan and no delete_service, and its deleted and removed stay empty.

updated records every matched row the write ran through update_from_input or the spec's update_service, whether or not that row's own columns actually changed.

docs.title: RelatedObjectChange dataclass
docs.text:
The delta for a relation that holds one row, not a collection.

Carried in ChangeResult.relations, one entry per singular relation declared in relations= — a forward foreign key / one-to-one, or a reverse one-to-one. ChildCollectionChange's five pk tuples cannot report a one-row relation honestly: every one of them would be either empty or a one-tuple, and "which of the five is non-empty" is a worse way to say "what happened" than saying it. So a singular relation reports one outcome and one pk.

outcome is a RelationOutcome, which documents what each value means.

pk is the primary key of the row the outcome is about, read before any delete (Django clears instance.pk afterwards), and None when no row was touched ("untouched" / "cleared").

docs.title: create_model
docs.text:
create_model(
    model: type[ModelT],
    *,
    field_map: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    exclude_fields: list[str] | None = None,
    m2m: Mapping[str, Any] | Callable[[Any], Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None,
    relations: Mapping[str, RelationSpec] | None = None,
) -> Callable[..., ModelT]

A service that builds a row of model from its validated data, and returns the row.

The service a create operation would otherwise write by hand:

def create_author(*, data: AuthorIn, **_: Any) -> Author:
    return create_from_input(Author, data).instance

field_map, exclude_fields and relations are handed to create_from_input as they are, so one relations map writes every nested kind, a reverse foreign key's ChildSpec among them. m2m is a static mapping, or a callable handed the validated data that returns one, which is the usual case when the rows to link arrive in the arguments:

create_model(Post, m2m=lambda data: {"tags": data.tags})

The service returns the row, not the ChangeResult, since the row is what a create's output presents. It opens no transaction: dispatch runs a service inside one, which covers the row and every nested write. It takes **kwargs, so the rest of the pool - the user and any registered seed - is absorbed rather than refused. It names call_context, which a catch-all is never handed, and the same pool with the call's context beside it is handed on as the helper's context, so a row service a relation spec declares can see who is calling and, by naming call_context, the very dict the call's other stages share.

docs.text:
