Reporting is the whole of it: unguarded_specs refuses nothing, and is no authorization boundary. It makes the declaration visible to whoever reads the report.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
Call Returns get(name) The entry, or None all() Every entry, in registration order queries() The SelectorSpec entries, in registration order mutations() The ServiceSpec entries, in registration order specs() A new {name: spec} dict, the shape a transport that takes a mapping of specs accepts name in registry, len(registry), iteration As for a mapping of entries

Registration order is kept so that a transport's listing - a tool list, a help screen - comes out the same on every start.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
Four calls derive a new registry from an existing one:

  • by_tag(*tags) keeps the entries carrying any of the tags. It is a union; chain the calls for an intersection: registry.by_tag("catalogue").by_tag("write"). No tags keeps nothing.
  • subset(*names) keeps the named entries, in the order named. A name that is not registered raises KeyError: a typo is a configuration error, not a quietly smaller surface.
  • merge(*others) combines registries, in order. Names are unique within one registry, so two independent registries may each use a name; merging is where that becomes a conflict, and it raises ValueError.
  • replace(name, spec) puts spec under name in place of the spec registered there. The entry keeps its tags and its place in the order, and the replacement is checked as register checks a spec. A name that is not registered raises KeyError, since a replacement for an operation nobody registered is a typo rather than a registration.

replace is how a transport serves a variant of an operation without a second name for it. The registry holds what every transport shares; a variant shaped for one transport is the registered spec's own derive(...), in the registry that transport is handed:

# The command line is handed a registry with the variant under the operation's
# own name; every other transport keeps reading ``registry``, and the base.
command_line_registry = registry.replace("list_notes", search_only)

search_only is the variant derived from list_notes_spec.

Every view is a snapshot. It shares the spec objects rather than copying them, it never changes its source, and a register() on the source afterwards does not appear in a view taken before it. A transport reads its view once, at configuration time, to build its own table of operations; nothing reads a registry per dispatch.

There is no global registry. A project holds as many registries as it has reasons to, with no state shared between them, and passes each transport the one it should expose.

docs.title: Relation writes
docs.text:
A write that creates or updates a row often writes its related rows in the same call: an author and its books, a post and its tags. The mutation helpers do that inside the service's transaction, reconciling the rows that arrived against the rows that exist, and report what changed.

The helpers are ordinary functions a service calls. Dispatch knows nothing about them: the spec's Validator checks the nested rows before the service runs, and the helpers own persistence only.

docs.title: The helpers
docs.text:
• create_from_input(model, data, ...) builds a row from data, saves it, then writes its relations.
  • update_from_input(instance, data, ...) writes only the fields whose value changed, with a minimal save(update_fields=...) (auto_now fields, and a changed image's width_field and height_field, are added to it), then reconciles its relations. update_fields=False makes it a full save, and a list names the columns exactly.
  • apply_input(instance, data) sets the changed fields without saving, for a service that wants to see what the input would change before deciding to persist.
  • delete_relations(instance, relations=...) disposes of the rows instance owns, before a delete service removes instance itself. See Deleting.
  • acreate_from_input, aupdate_from_input and adelete_relations are the async forms, for an async def service.
  • create_model, update_model and delete_model build the service itself, for an operation whose service would be nothing but one helper call: create_model(Author, relations=BOOKS) is a service taking data, writing the author and its books, and returning the author. update_model takes instance as well, and delete_model takes instance alone, runs delete_relations first when given a map, and returns None. delete_collection deletes the rows a spec's collection_selector_spec resolved. Each takes the rest of the pool as **kwargs, which the three model services hand on as the helper's context, with the call's context beside it, so a nested row service or scope naming call_context is handed the very dict the call's other stages share. Each opens no transaction of its own, since dispatch runs the service inside one, and has an async form: acreate_model, aupdate_model, adelete_model and adelete_collection.

A service of your own that calls a helper and hands its **kwargs on as the helper's context hands on no call context: **kwargs is never handed call_context, which reaches a callable only by its name. One whose nested row services and scopes should see it names call_context and passes it beside the pool, context={**kwargs, "call_context": call_context}, as create_model does.

data is a dataclass, a mapping, or an object with a __dict__ - usually the validated values dispatch passes the service as data. A dataclass gives its __init__ fields only, at every depth: one declared init=False is computed by the dataclass rather than sent, and is never written. A field holding UNSET is left alone, which is what makes a partial update's omitted fields omitted. A file field's value is written as a ModelForm writes it, through the model field's save_form_data: a file replaces the one the row holds, None keeps it, and False, a form's value for a cleared file, leaves no file, reported as a change to "". An upload, or any File a row does not already hold, is always written and reported, even under the name of the file it replaces; the file the row holds, handed back as itself, is no change. field_map renames input keys onto model fields and exclude_fields drops keys. m2m={name: rows} assigns many-to-many rows that already exist; writing the target rows from the payload is a ManyToManySpec, and naming one relation in both is refused.

relations={name: spec} declares the related rows, one spec per relation, and is the one map for every kind of relation.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
An author and their books. Author has a name; Book has a title, a decimal price, a status and a non-nullable foreign key author, whose reverse accessor is Author.books. The input dataclasses are the ones Declaring an operation builds.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal

from django_service_specs import (
    ChangeResult,
    ChildSpec,
    DataclassPresenter,
    DataclassValidator,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    ServiceSpec,
    create_from_input,
    update_from_input,
)
from docs.examples.declaring import AuthorIn, AuthorPatch, IsSignedIn
from tests.adapter_app.models import Author, Book, Status

# One declaration of how the books are written, shared by the create and the update.
BOOKS = {"books": ChildSpec(model=Book, fk="author")}


@dataclass
class BookOut:
    id: int
    title: str
    price: Decimal
    status: Status


@dataclass
class AuthorOut:
    id: int
    name: str
    books: list[BookOut]


def create_author(*, data: AuthorIn) -> ChangeResult[Author]:
    return create_from_input(Author, data, relations=BOOKS)


def update_author(*, instance: Author, data: AuthorPatch) -> ChangeResult[Author]:
    return update_from_input(instance, data, relations=BOOKS)


# The services return what changed; the output selector re-reads the author,
# with its books prefetched, for the presenter.
reread_author = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
    selector=lambda *, result: Author.objects.filter(pk=result.instance.pk),
    prefetch_related=["books"],
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(AuthorOut),
)

create_author_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=create_author,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=DataclassValidator(AuthorIn),
    output_selector_spec=reread_author,
)

update_author_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=update_author,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=DataclassValidator(AuthorPatch),
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=lambda *, pk: Author.objects.filter(pk=pk),
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)),
    ),
    output_selector_spec=reread_author,
)

What each call does:

  • Create with {"name": "Ursula", "books": [{"title": "The Dispossessed", "price": "9.99"}, {"title": "Lathe", "price": 12.5}]} writes the author, then both books pointing at it. The service's ChangeResult reports ChildCollectionChange(relation="books", created=(1, 2)), and the presented result is the author with both books, the prices rendered as "9.99" and "12.50".
  • Update with {"pk": 1, "books": [{"pk": 1, "title": "The Dispossessed", "price": "10.99"}, {"title": "Always Coming Home", "price": "8"}]} matches the first row to book 1 by its pk and updates it, creates the row with no pk, and removes book 2, which the input left out: ChildSpec's default mode is "replace", and because Book.author is not nullable the orphan is deleted. The report is created=(3,), updated=(1,), deleted=(2,). The author's name was not sent, so AuthorPatch delivered it as UNSET and it was not written.
  • Update without books leaves every book alone: the relation arrives as UNSET, and a relation the input omits is untouched. An explicit "books": [] would have removed them all.
  • A row naming a book the author does not have - {"pk": 1, "books": [{"pk": 4, ...}]} where book 4 is someone else's - is refused with ServiceValidationError, at {"books": {0: {"non_field_errors": ["references Book [4], which this write did not match. ..."]}}}. Saving a new row under a primary key it did not match would overwrite the row that holds it, so the write refuses rather than creating.
  • A malformed row - a status of "lost" in the second book - is refused by the Validator before the service runs, as InvalidArguments at {"books": {1: {"status": ["Select a valid choice. lost is not one of the available choices."]}}}.

docs.title: The five relation specs
docs.text:
Spec Writes Named by Written ChildSpec A reverse foreign-key collection: rows whose fk points at the parent The reverse accessor ("books" for Author.books) After the parent's save() ForwardRelationSpec A ForeignKey or OneToOneField declared on the parent The parent's field ("author" for Post.author) Before the parent's save() ReverseOneToOneSpec The one row whose OneToOneField points back at the parent The reverse accessor ("profile" for Author.profile) After the parent's save() GenericRelationSpec A GenericRelation: rows linked by content type and id The GenericRelation on the parent After the reverse kinds ManyToManySpec Target rows from payloads, then the membership Either side's accessor ("tags" for Post.tags) Last

Each spec takes its required fields positionally and every option by keyword: ChildSpec(Book, "author", mode="merge").

The order is a property of the kind, not of how the relations= mapping is spelled: a forward target has to exist before the parent is saved, and a membership needs both rows saved. RelationPhase names the sequence. Within one phase, relations are written in the order they are declared.

How each kind reads its value:

  • Omitted leaves the relation untouched, for every kind.
  • A forward relation set to None clears the parent's column and leaves the row it pointed at alone: a forward target is not the parent's, and may be shared. A mapping writes the target row - creating one, or with a match_key, updating the row it names.
  • A reverse one-to-one set to None removes the related row by the orphan rule below, because that row is the parent's. A mapping updates the existing row, or creates and links one.
  • A collection (child, generic, many-to-many) is reconciled: incoming rows are matched to existing ones by match_key ("pk" by default), matched rows are updated, the rest are created, and in "replace" mode the existing rows the input left out are removed. "merge" mode only upserts. A null row is refused, every one of them and before any row is written, with "This field cannot be null.", coded null, under the row's non_field_errors: a declaration may let one through (list[Row | None]), and nothing in a relation spec says what it stands for.

docs.title: Matching, scope and orphans
docs.text:
A child collection, a generic relation and a reverse one-to-one match inside the parent's own rows, so a key that matches nothing there cannot name anyone else's row. A forward relation and a many-to-many match against rows the parent does not own, so they take a scope: a queryset, or a callable resolved from context (lambda user: Author.objects.filter(owner=user)), of the rows this caller may write. Without a scope the spec is create-only, and a payload carrying a match_key raises ImproperlyConfigured rather than letting any caller write any row of that model by guessing a key. A key outside the scope is refused with ServiceValidationError, at the row, and so is one past the range of the integer column it is matched on, which no row holds, before the lookup hands it to the database. A match_key written as a path, catalog__pk, is held to the column the path ends on, and one naming a relation to the key of the row it reaches.

What removing a row does is the orphan setting of a child collection, a reverse one-to-one or a generic relation. "auto", the default, reads the schema: a nullable link is set to None (unlinked, like on_delete=SET_NULL), a non-nullable one is deleted (like CASCADE). "unlink" and "delete" say it outright, for a spec that means one of them: under "auto", a later migration adding null=True would turn a destructive "replace" into a non-destructive one with nothing in the spec changing. A many-to-many target is shared, so a dropped member only loses its membership, and is reported as unlinked.

A many-to-many with a custom through model is not covered: the helpers let Django write the through row, which cannot carry the extra columns a custom through model exists for.

docs.title: Row services
docs.text:
A row whose write has behaviour of its own - side effects, derived columns, an external call - takes a create_service, an update_service and, where rows are removed, a delete_service. The spec keeps what it never delegates: which rows exist, which incoming row matches which existing one, and what happens to the ones left over. The service is called once per row the helper has already decided about, with data, the parent (except on a forward relation, whose target is written before the parent exists), the instance for an update, and any keys of the helper's context= mapping it declares. That mapping is how a row service or a scope callable sees the acting user: the operation's service declares user and passes context={"user": user} on to the helper.

Row services run with atomic=False, inside the transaction the operation already holds. Declaring one beside the shaping options it replaces (field_map, exclude_fields, m2m, nested relations) is refused at construction, because they would configure nothing. A delete_service owns the disposal, so its rows are reported as removed rather than guessed into deleted or unlinked. In the async helpers, a row service must be async def.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
Every helper returns a ChangeResult:

  • instance and created.
  • changes: a FieldChange with old and new for every field whose value differed, old being UNSET on a create. changed_fields lists their names.
  • children: a ChildCollectionChange per collection - a child, generic or many-to-many relation - holding the primary keys created, updated, deleted, unlinked and removed. get_child_change(name) finds one.
  • relations: a RelatedObjectChange per one-row relation - a forward relation or a reverse one-to-one - holding one RelationOutcome and the pk it is about. get_relation_change(name) finds one.

A ChangeResult is falsy when nothing changed.

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
A delete service that has to take a row's related rows with it calls delete_relations with the same map the writes use, then deletes the row:

from django_service_specs import (
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    ServiceSpec,
    delete_model,
    delete_relations,
)
from docs.examples.declaring import IsSignedIn
from docs.examples.relations import BOOKS
from tests.adapter_app.models import Author


def delete_author(*, instance: Author) -> tuple[int, ...]:
    # The database would take the books with the author and say nothing about
    # them. Cascading first, through the map the writes use, names each one.
    cascade = delete_relations(instance, relations=BOOKS)
    instance.delete()
    books = cascade.get_child_change("books")
    return books.deleted if books else ()


delete_author_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=delete_author,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=lambda *, pk: Author.objects.filter(pk=pk),
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)),
    ),
)

The database's own cascade would remove these books as well, and report nothing. The helper matters where the database will not cascade, or should not be the one to:

  • A PROTECT foreign key, which refuses the parent's delete while a child row exists.
  • A soft delete, which removes no row, so Django never cascades through it. The instance outlives its cascade, and its cached relations are brought in line with the removal, so it renders without the rows it lost.
  • A row service: a spec's delete_service sees each row go, which a database cascade never calls.
  • A report: the returned ChangeResult names every row disposed of, as the example returns them.

The rule is the one a write follows when it removes a row, applied to every row the instance owns. A child, generic or reverse one-to-one row is disposed of after its own declared relations, so a non-nullable grandchild goes first, and each is deleted, unlinked or handed to its delete_service by the spec's orphan setting. A many-to-many loses its membership and its target rows survive. A forward relation is reported untouched: the row it points at is not the instance's, and refusing it would make a map that is right for writing impossible to cascade.

Where the service is nothing but that cascade and the delete, delete_model builds it. It returns None rather than the report, and refuses a value that is not a relation spec when it is built rather than on its first call:

retire_author_spec = ServiceSpec(
    # The books go first, through the map the writes use, then the author.
    service=delete_model(Author, relations=BOOKS),
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    instance_selector_spec=delete_author_spec.instance_selector_spec,
)

soft_delete= calls a function with the row in place of delete(), after the cascade, which is the case Django never cascades through.

docs.title: Errors from a nested write
docs.text:
A refusal inside a row is re-rooted under the row's address, in the tree Arguments and refusals describes, and keeps its class: a ServiceValidationError from a row stays one, an InvalidArguments stays one, because the class says who refused. Its messages are kept as they were, each one's code included. A grandchild's refusal carries both addresses.

Django's own failures to write a row's data - a value a field cannot coerce, a key the model has no field for - carry no detail and would otherwise escape as an unhandled error naming no row. They become InvalidArguments at the row. A ValidationError keeps each message's own code, which is the one DRF gives the same mistake, and its field names where it has them; a message raised with no code, and the message of a TypeError or ValueError, is coded invalid.

Code the caller wrote is treated differently. Any other error a row service, a scope callable or an m2m callable raises passes through untouched, at any depth: reading its TypeError as a refusal of the arguments would report the caller's own bug as the client's mistake. An IntegrityError is left alone too: a constraint is a conflict with rows that exist rather than a shape, and the backend's message can quote another row's values.

docs.title: A refusal from another library
docs.text:
A row service written for another library may raise that library's own validation error, which this package cannot name: the one djangorestframework-services registers is DRF's ValidationError. Register the class with a function reading its detail, and a relation write re-roots it as it does its own two:

from django_service_specs import ChildSpec, create_from_input, register_row_error
from tests.adapter_app.models import Author, Book


class CatalogueRefusal(Exception):
    """A validation error from another library, which a row service written for it raises."""

    def __init__(self, detail: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(detail)
        self.detail = detail


def read_refusal(exc: CatalogueRefusal) -> Any:
    return exc.detail


def ready() -> None:  # an AppConfig.ready(), or the adapter's own import
    register_row_error(CatalogueRefusal, read_refusal)


def create_book(*, data: dict[str, Any]) -> Book:
    if data["title"].isupper():
        raise CatalogueRefusal({"title": ["No titles in capitals."]})
    return Book.objects.create(**data)


def create_author(*, data: dict[str, Any]) -> Author:
    books = {"books": ChildSpec(model=Book, fk="author", create_service=create_book)}
    return create_from_input(Author, data, relations=books).instance

The detail is placed at the row's address by the same rule, a list or a string under non_field_errors inside the row, and the class is rebuilt from the re-rooted tree, so a caller catching CatalogueRefusal here reads {"books": {1: {"title": ["No titles in capitals."]}}}. Registering the same pair again does nothing; a second reader for one class, or a class overlapping one the kernel re-roots already, is refused with ImproperlyConfigured. See register_row_error.

docs.title: JSON Schema
docs.text:
A transport that hands an operation to a client describes it first: an MCP server lists each tool with an input and an output schema, an agent toolset gives the model the same, a form builder picks its widgets from one. The kernel emits that description from the spec's own declarations - Parameters for what goes in, Output for what comes out - so no adapter describes itself.

That is the point of emitting it here. Every adapter already reads its library's declaration into Parameters and Output, and the schema is read from those alone, so there is one dialect whichever library declared the spec. A pydantic model's own model_json_schema() is not used: it speaks a different dialect - references, titles on every field, a decimal as an anyOf - and a transport would hand its clients whichever one the project happened to install.

docs.title: The functions
docs.text:
• spec_input_schema(spec, *, unknown_arguments=REJECT) describes everything spec.parameters() declares: the arguments dispatch checks. A many service spec's is its reads, its shapes and the one required list many_argument names, each row an object of the Validator's parameters. A spec's shapes are properties like any other, closed set included, though only the presenter reads what is sent for them.
  • spec_output_schema(spec, *, paginate=False, projection=None, handle_description=None) describes what present returns for the spec, or None when the spec declares no output. With paginate=True a list is described as the page envelope, and with a projection as an agent audience is served it; see paging and projection.
  • parameters_schema(parameters, *, unknown_arguments=REJECT) and output_schema(output) are the same over a bare declaration, for a transport describing something that is not a whole spec.

Each schema is a plain dict, built anew on every call, so a transport can add its own keys - a $schema, an annotation of its own - without reaching the declaration or another transport's copy.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
The notes list and the author write from the earlier pages, described:

from django_service_specs import (
    DataclassPresenter,
    Output,
    OutputField,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    ServiceSpec,
    UnknownArguments,
    output_schema,
    parameters_schema,
    spec_input_schema,
    spec_output_schema,
)
from docs.examples.declaring import IsSignedIn, NoteRow, list_notes_spec
from docs.examples.relations import create_author_spec
from tests.dispatch_app.models import Note

# What a transport advertises for the notes list: its arguments, and its rows.
notes_input = spec_input_schema(list_notes_spec)
notes_output = spec_output_schema(list_notes_spec)

# The author write, as a transport that refuses an undeclared argument...
author_input = spec_input_schema(create_author_spec)
# ...and as one that drops it, which must not claim to refuse it.
lenient_author_input = spec_input_schema(
    create_author_spec, unknown_arguments=UnknownArguments.IGNORE
)
author_output = spec_output_schema(create_author_spec)

The notes list takes a search term with help text and an ordering with two choices and a default, and refuses any other argument:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "search": {"type": "string", "description": "Part of the title, in any case."},
    "ordering": {"type": "string", "enum": ["title", "-title"], "default": "title"}
  },
  "additionalProperties": false
}

It returns a list, so its output is an array of rows. The rows' fields carry markings - id is a handle, title the label - which this schema does not apply; see what is not emitted.

{
  "type": "array",
  "items": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"id": {"type": "integer"}, "title": {"type": "string"}},
    "required": ["id", "title"]
  }
}

The author write takes rows, and each row is described in full and closed as the top is. A book's price is a decimal, its status has choices and a default, and published_on and pk may be null:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "name": {"type": "string"},
    "books": {
      "type": "array",
      "maxItems": 1000,
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "title": {"type": "string"},
          "price": {"type": "string", "format": "decimal"},
          "status": {
            "type": "string",
            "anyOf": [
              {"const": "draft", "title": "Draft"},
              {"const": "published", "title": "Published"}
            ],
            "default": "draft"
          },
          "published_on": {"type": ["string", "null"], "format": "date", "default": null},
          "pk": {"type": ["integer", "null"], "default": null}
        },
        "required": ["title", "price"],
        "additionalProperties": false
      }
    }
  },
  "required": ["name"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}

Its output selector re-reads the author once the write has committed, so the output may be null (see what a spec returns), and the book's status states each choice's display as a title:

{
  "type": ["object", "null"],
  "properties": {
    "id": {"type": "integer"},
    "name": {"type": "string"},
    "books": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "id": {"type": "integer"},
          "title": {"type": "string"},
          "price": {"type": "string", "format": "decimal"},
          "status": {
            "type": "string",
            "oneOf": [
              {"const": "draft", "title": "Draft"},
              {"const": "published", "title": "Published"}
            ]
          }
        },
        "required": ["id", "title", "price", "status"]
      }
    }
  },
  "required": ["id", "name", "books"]
}

docs.title: Precise: never false, and not incomplete where the declaration knows
docs.text:
A schema is a claim a client acts on. A model that reads "this may not be null" never sends null; a form builder that reads an enum offers nothing else. So the rule is that the schema never states something the kernel would contradict, and states everything the declaration knows.

  • Nullable is stated for every node, objects and arrays included, as a type list: ["string", "null"]. Parameters carries nullable whichever library declared the field, so the schema does not depend on it. An array's element states its own, from items_nullable, on items: the array and its elements may each be null or not, independently.
  • An enum lists every accepted value. An enum claims to be the whole set, so leaving a value out is a falsehood rather than an omission. A nullable parameter with choices therefore lists null among them, because the shape check accepts a null before it reads the choices. An array's choices constrain each element, so they sit on items, and gain null there by the element's nullability alone, never by the array's. So do an array's format, minimum and maximum, which describe each element: a CSV number filter's items are {"type": "string", "format": "decimal", "minimum": -1e+50, "maximum": 1e+50}, and the array node states only its own "minItems" and "maxItems".
  • Labelled choices are an anyOf of {"const": value, "title": label} in place of the enum, where some label says more than its value, as the book's status above shows; labels that only repeat their values keep the enum. A choice with no label is a bare {"const": value}, and a null is {"type": "null"}, titled when it is labelled: the null a nullable parameter gains among them. Each value is listed once, so the entries are disjoint and anyOf admits exactly what oneOf would. It is anyOf because a model provider's schema dialect is narrower than JSON Schema: an OpenAI strict schema refuses oneOf, and so does Gemini, while Google's transform empties a {"const": null} into {}, which matches every value. A title is rendered when the schema is built, so a lazy label is in the language active then, and it constrains nothing. What a spec returns still states labelled choices as a oneOf.
  • A file is {}. No JSON value is one, so any type stated for it would be false, and JSON Schema has no keyword for a multipart part. Whether it is required, and its description, are still stated.
  • An any is {} too, since every JSON value is one; its default and description are stated as on any other node. Like a file's, its node admits null whether or not it is nullable, and the shape check is what refuses a null it does not allow. An output field may be any as well, for a value whose JSON type is open (a computed field, a JSON column): its node is {}, with its title if it has a label, rather than a string the value may not be.
  • required lists what the shape check refuses when absent: a required parameter with no default. A required parameter that declares a default is not refused when omitted, because the Validator supplies the default, so it is not listed.
  • A partial update requires only its reads. A partial spec's Validator parameters are listed in no required, at any depth, because dispatch refuses none of them absent; see a partial update.
  • A value JSON cannot carry is left out whole. A default of Decimal("9.99") or date.today, or a choice set holding one, would break the encoding every transport performs on the schema, so it is not stated rather than restated in a form the declaration did not choose. Leaving out only the unencodable choices would claim the others are refused.

What stays incomplete is only what the declaration does not carry. A Parameter's minimum and maximum are stated as "minimum" and "maximum"; a bound only the Validator holds, a maxLength or a form field's max_value, is not, unless the Parameter's json_schema_extra states it. An array's min_length is stated as "minItems", and its "maxItems" is the maximum in force: the declared max_length, or where none is declared the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting's, 1000 unless the project sets another. It is the one bound stated without being declared, because the shape check refuses past it and a client told nothing would send a call that cannot run. Under a setting of None, an array with no max_length states none. The setting is read each time a schema is built, so building one for an array with no max_length reads Django's settings and needs them configured: outside a configured Django it raises ImproperlyConfigured, as the shape check does, rather than state the default when a project configured later may set another. JSON Schema reads minimum and maximum on a number instance alone, so on a decimal string a validating client enforces neither: the shape check does, and the schema tells a reader where the line is.

docs.title: Keywords no field spells
docs.text:
A Parameter and an OutputField each take json_schema_extra: a mapping of the JSON Schema keywords none of their fields spells, which parameters_schema and output_schema add to that declaration's node last, at any depth, as spec_input_schema and spec_output_schema do through them:

isbn = Parameter(
    "isbn",
    "string",
    help="The 13-digit ISBN, digits only.",
    # Keywords no field of a Parameter spells, added to its node as written.
    json_schema_extra={"pattern": "^97[89][0-9]{10}$", "maxLength": 13},
)
isbn_input = parameters_schema(Parameters.of(isbn))

tags = OutputField("tags", "array", items="string", json_schema_extra={"uniqueItems": True})
tags_output = output_schema(Output((tags,)))

isbn_input is:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "isbn": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The 13-digit ISBN, digits only.",
      "pattern": "^97[89][0-9]{10}$",
      "maxLength": 13
    }
  },
  "additionalProperties": false
}

and tags_output:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}, "uniqueItems": true}
  },
  "required": ["tags"]
}

It is how an adapter whose library declares more than a Parameter carries keeps it on every route rather than on its own; none of the adapters this package ships sets it. Because the node already holds everything the declaration states, a keyword a field states is refused when the declaration is built, naming the field to declare it on, whether or not this declaration sets that field:

On Refused keywords Parameter type, format, default, the choices' enum, anyOf and const, minimum, maximum, minItems, maxItems, items, description, properties, required and additionalProperties OutputField type, format, items, the choices' enum, oneOf and const, title, properties and required

So a custom format is refused too, since format is a field, and either side winning would advertise what the declaration does not say or drop what was written. Refusing a keyword only when one build happened to state it would make one declaration valid until the array cap came on or a spec moved to REJECT. A value JSON cannot carry - a Decimal, a lazy translation - is refused too, at any depth, naming its key, since every transport encodes the schema as JSON. The mapping is held as a deep copy, so changing it afterwards leaves the declaration as written, and its values are placed in each schema as the declaration holds them, as a default's are.

It is advertised, not enforced. The shape check never reads it, so on a Parameter what it states holds only where the spec's Validator enforces it, and on an OutputField it describes what the presenter renders.

docs.title: A partial update
docs.text:
A spec declaring partial=True takes any subset of its Validator's parameters, so its schema lists none of them in required: not at the top, not in an object's fields, not in an array's rows. A client reading required to decide what to send would otherwise never send the partial call the spec exists for. The spec's reads and its target selector's keep their required, as dispatch keeps them, so the schema still says which row the update names. An update whose target selector reads pk and whose Validator requires title and body has "required": ["pk"].

On a many spec the list stays required and each row requires nothing. parameters() is unchanged: it still says what a whole update needs, and the schema is where the relaxing happens, through the one function the shape check relaxes a partial call with, so the two cannot drift. A read a kwargs provider fills is still listed as declared; server_owned_keys is how a transport finds those, and the schema's required less that set is exactly what dispatch refuses when it is absent. A transport that binds or withholds parameters of its own subtracts its ServerArguments' names() too: see arguments the server supplies.

docs.title: The decimal convention
docs.text: A decimal is {"type": "string", "format": "decimal"}. The shape check also accepts a JSON number for one, because every decimal validator does, and the schema does not advertise that: a string is the form every validator reads without a binary float's rounding, so it is the one a client is told to send.

docs.title: The closed set follows the policy
docs.text:
Dispatch closes the argument set under UnknownArguments.REJECT, the default, and the schema says so with "additionalProperties": false, at exactly the levels the shape check closes: the top, every object parameter that declares its fields, and every row of an array of rows. A declared object with no fields at all is closed too, since it refuses every key.

Under UnknownArguments.IGNORE an undeclared key is accepted and dropped, so a schema saying false would tell the client a call that runs is invalid. The schema leaves the keyword out at every level instead, as lenient_author_input in the example does: the same description as author_input with every "additionalProperties": false gone. Pass the policy the transport dispatches with.

docs.title: Flat and self-contained
docs.text:
Every schema is inline. There is no $defs and no $ref, however deeply the declaration nests: most MCP clients refuse a tool schema holding a reference, and none of the family's transports resolve one.

A declaration that refers to itself - a category tree, a threaded comment - cannot be inlined without end, so an adapter bounds it where it reads the declaration: past the bound, a nested object is declared with no fields. The schema of that node is {"type": "object"}. It is the one thing still known to be true, it is what a caller can still send, and it constrains nothing a valid call could fail. An object parameter declared without fields is described the same way for the same reason.

docs.title: What a spec returns
docs.text:
spec_output_schema describes what dispatch presents, which depends on the kind of spec as well as on its presenter:

Spec Schema No presenter, on the spec or its output selector None A LIST selector spec {"type": "array", "items": <item>} A LIST selector spec with allow_none=True {"type": "array", "items": <item>}: its selector's None is presented as [] A RETRIEVE selector spec the item A RETRIEVE selector spec with allow_none=True the item, with "null" in its type A service spec whose output selector is a LIST {"type": "array", "items": <item>} A service spec whose output selector is a RETRIEVE the item, with "null" in its type A service spec with no output selector the item A service spec with no output selector, with allow_none=True the item, with "null" in its type A many service spec with no output selector {"type": "array", "items": <item>}, with "null" in its type under allow_none=True A returns_many service spec {"type": "array", "items": <item>}, with "null" in its type under allow_none=True; never paged, with or without paginate=True

Where the table says "null" is can_present_nothing's answer, exported for a transport that writes an output schema of its own, so the two cannot disagree. It reads neither many nor returns_many: either service's list may be None exactly where any service's return may.

A RETRIEVE selector spec without allow_none answers a missing row as not-found, which a transport reports in its own terms and never presents, so its item is not nullable. A service spec's RETRIEVE output selector is nullable whatever its allow_none says: once the service has run, a re-read that finds nothing is None rather than not-found, because not-found would tell the caller a committed write did not happen.

A service spec that presents what the service returned is described as the item, and dispatch presents a None it returned as None. Whether a service may return one is not otherwise in its declaration, so the spec says it with allow_none=True, the name a selector spec already uses, and the item gains "null":

def archive_oldest(*, user: Any) -> Note | None:
    note = Note.objects.filter(owner=user, archived=False).order_by("pk").first()
    if note is not None:
        note.archived = True
        note.save(update_fields=["archived"])
    return note  # None once there is nothing left to archive


archive_oldest_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=archive_oldest,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteRow),
    # It presents what it returned, which may be nothing: said here, so the
    # schema a transport advertises admits the null it will serve.
    allow_none=True,
)
archive_output = spec_output_schema(archive_oldest_spec)

Left undeclared, a None is not stated, and the item stays the strict object its presenter declares: a schema that admitted null for every write would describe every service as one that may return nothing. On a service spec with an output selector, allow_none changes nothing: a RETRIEVE re-read admits "null" already, and a LIST one presents its rows rather than the service's return.

docs.title: A spec that declares shapes
docs.text:
A spec's shapes say what its presenter renders, and a fields selection there leaves keys out of a row, so whether a key is present depends on what the caller sent. Nothing in the presenter's declaration says that for every value a caller may send, so for a spec declaring any shapes the item lists no required: not at its top, not in a nested object's fields, not in an array's rows. Every field is still described, nested ones included, so a client still knows what a key means when it is there.

The trigger is any shape, not one marked as a field selection. A shape is a Parameter, the presenter reads it however it likes - a query over each row leaves keys out as surely as a fields list - and a flag saying "this one selects fields" would be a claim nothing could check.

What the kernel writes around the item keeps its own required, wherever the item sits: the affordances object dispatch adds to each row stays required, with its answers' schema whole, and a page's envelope still requires items, page, totalPages and hasNext. A spec declaring no shapes is described exactly as before, with the required its presenter's always_present states. Shaping each row by the call shows a shaped list.

docs.title: What is deliberately not emitted
docs.text:
• No title on an input property. A Parameter has no label of its own; on input a title is only ever a choice's. On output, a field's label becomes its title, and adapters set a label only where the author wrote one, so a title is never the field's name restated.
  • No additionalProperties on output. Output is not a set a caller can get wrong, and a transport may add keys of its own to what it sends.
  • No default or description on output. A default says what happens when a caller omits an argument, which means nothing for a value that came back. A projected schema is the exception for description: a marking's description, or the transport's handle_description on a handle, is stated there.
  • No marking, unless a projection is passed. Without one, a field marked as a handle, a label or hidden is described like any other, which is what present and every HTTP response return. With one, spec_output_schema describes what present_for_audience returns; see paging and projection.
  • No $schema key. A transport whose wire wants one adds it.
